n: Susurluk crash — MP, police chief and Grey Wolves gunman in one car
rank: deputy chief of Istanbul police; member of parliament
d: On 3 November 1996 a Mercedes crashed near Susurluk, Balikesir province. Inside were Huseyin Kocadag, deputy chief of the Istanbul police; Sedat Bucak, a True Path Party MP and village-guard clan leader; and Abdullah Catli, a Grey Wolves leader on Interpol's wanted list for murder and drug trafficking. Parliament set up an inquiry on 12 November 1996; its chairman Mehmet Elkatmis issued a 350-page report in April 1997 concluding that state bodies had used the Grey Wolves. In February 2001 a court sentenced Ibrahim Sahin and Korkut Eken to six years each.
cite: Turkish Grand National Assembly Susurluk inquiry commission (Elkatmis), report April 1997; Istanbul court verdict 12 February 2001

n: Mehmet Agar — interior minister signed papers for Grey Wolves fugitive
d: After the Susurluk crash, investigators found that Abdullah Catli carried a false passport and a gun licence signed by Interior Minister Mehmet Agar, who had met the group shortly before the crash. Agar resigned on 8 November 1996. Parliament voted on 11 December 1996 to lift his immunity and that of MP Sedat Bucak. Agar was not punished and was later re-elected to parliament.
cite: Turkish Grand National Assembly Susurluk inquiry commission, report April 1997

n: Counter-Guerrilla — Turkey's NATO stay-behind in the army
rank: Special Warfare Department of the General Staff
d: Prime Minister Bulent Ecevit said he learned of the Counter-Guerrilla when General Kemal Yamak asked him for funding after US financing ended around 1973-74. The unit sat in the army's Special Warfare Department (renamed from STK in 1967; later Special Forces Command). Ecevit suspected its involvement in the 1977 Taksim Square shooting; the gunmen were never caught. A December 1990 Prime Ministry statement said the Special Warfare Department was not a counter-guerrilla force.
cite: Statements of PM Bulent Ecevit; Prime Ministry press release December 1990; academic histories of NATO stay-behind networks

n: Alparslan Turkes — MHP/Grey Wolves leader as deputy prime minister
d: Alparslan Turkes, leader of the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), whose youth wing is the Grey Wolves, served as deputy prime minister in Suleyman Demirel's Nationalist Front coalition governments of 1975-77 and 1977-78. The Grey Wolves were active in the street violence of the late 1970s.
cite: Turkish government records of the First and Second Nationalist Front cabinets; academic histories of the MHP

n: Ergenekon verdict — ex-army chief Basbug sentenced to life
rank: former Chief of the General Staff
d: On 5 August 2013 Istanbul's 13th High Criminal Court ruled on 275 defendants accused of belonging to an 'Ergenekon' network plotting to overthrow the government. Former Chief of General Staff Ilker Basbug was sentenced to life. Retired general Veli Kucuk received a double aggravated life sentence plus 99 years, and Workers' Party leader Dogu Perincek aggravated life plus 30 years. These convictions were overturned in 2016 (see separate record).
cite: Istanbul 13th High Criminal Court, verdict 5 August 2013

n: Ergenekon verdict — sitting CHP MPs jailed
d: Three opposition CHP MPs were among those convicted in the 5 August 2013 Ergenekon verdict: Mustafa Balbay (34 years 8 months), Mehmet Haberal (12 years 6 months) and Sinan Aygun (13 years 6 months). The appeals court overturned the Ergenekon convictions in April 2016, finding no evidence that the organisation existed.
cite: Istanbul 13th High Criminal Court, 5 August 2013; Court of Cassation, 21 April 2016

n: Ergenekon convictions overturned — 'no evidence organisation existed'
rank: Court of Cassation ruling on officers, MPs, journalists
d: On 21 April 2016 Turkey's Court of Cassation in Ankara overturned the convictions of 275 Ergenekon defendants, including officers, politicians, lawyers, academics and journalists. It found no evidence that an 'Ergenekon terror organisation' existed and said the 2013 verdict relied on illegal wiretaps, anonymous witnesses and unlawful searches. At retrial in 2019 an Istanbul court acquitted 235 defendants. The Turkish government now attributes the original prosecution to Gulen-linked police and prosecutors.
cite: Court of Cassation ruling, 21 April 2016; Istanbul retrial verdict, July 2019

n: Sledgehammer (Balyoz) — 300 officers convicted of coup plot
d: On 21 September 2012 an Istanbul Heavy Penal Court sentenced about 300 of 365 military defendants for an alleged 2003 coup plan called Sledgehammer. Retired generals Cetin Dogan, Ibrahim Firtina and Ozden Ornek were given aggravated life, reduced to 20 years; 78 others got 18 years and 214 got 16 years. The convictions were later quashed (see separate record).
cite: Istanbul Heavy Penal Court, verdict 21 September 2012
org_note: grouped with the Ergenekon-era 'deep state' trials.

n: Sledgehammer retrial — all 236 acquitted, evidence found forged
d: On 19 June 2014 the Constitutional Court ruled the defendants' rights had been violated and they were released. On 31 March 2015 an Istanbul court acquitted all 236 remaining defendants after the prosecutor said the digital evidence was faked. Experts found documents dated 2003 that used later fonts and named a navy ship, TCG Alanya, that did not exist until 2005.
cite: Constitutional Court of Turkey, 19 June 2014; Istanbul court acquittal, 31 March 2015

n: Dec 2013 graft probe — prosecutors who targeted Erdogan cabinet sacked
d: In December 2013 Istanbul prosecutors and police opened a corruption investigation reaching Prime Minister Erdogan's inner circle; four ministers left office in the fallout. The government called it a plot by Gulen movement members inside the police and judiciary. On 30 December 2014 the judicial council HSYK dismissed the four prosecutors who led the probe: Zekeriya Oz, Celal Kara, Muammer Akkas and Mehmet Yuzgec. The case itself was dropped for lack of evidence.
cite: Supreme Board of Judges and Prosecutors (HSYK) decision, 30 December 2014

n: Police purge after 2013 graft probe
d: In the weeks after the December 2013 corruption probe, the government removed or reassigned police officers across Turkey, including around 1,000 officers that officials described as a 'routine' rotation. The government said the officers belonged to a Gulen 'parallel structure' inside the police.
cite: Turkish government statements reported by Ahram Online and Hurriyet Daily News, January 2014

n: 2016 purge — 2,745 judges removed in one day
d: On 16 July 2016, the day after the failed coup, the HSYK judicial council removed 2,745 judges (about 36% of judges then serving) and ordered their detention for alleged Gulen links. By 19 July 755 judges and prosecutors had been arrested. Over 1,000 more judiciary members were dismissed by decree in July 2018. Turkey designates the movement as the terrorist organisation 'FETO'.
cite: Supreme Board of Judges and Prosecutors (HSYK) decision, 16 July 2016; emergency decrees 2016-2018

n: 2016 purge — about 23,000 police dismissed for Gulen links
d: Turkey's top police chief said in December 2017 that 22,987 police officers had been dismissed over alleged Gulen links since the July 2016 coup attempt. President Erdogan gave a figure of 31,000 police removed in April 2019. Across the public sector, about 150,000 people were dismissed from government jobs by emergency decree.
cite: Statement of the Director General of Security, December 2017; emergency decrees 2016-2018

n: 2016 purge — 15,000 military removed, 150 generals detained
d: On 16 July 2016 Prime Minister Binali Yildirim announced 2,839 soldiers arrested, including at least 34 generals or admirals; by 18 July 103 generals and admirals were detained. A July 2018 decree dismissed over 6,000 more military members. President Erdogan said in April 2019 that 15,000 military personnel had been removed.
cite: Turkish government announcements and emergency decrees 2016-2018

n: Akin Ozturk — ex-air force commander jailed for life
rank: former commander of the Turkish Air Force
d: In June 2019, in the main trial over the 15 July 2016 coup attempt, an Ankara court sentenced former Air Force commander Akin Ozturk to multiple aggravated life terms as the military leader of the attempt. The court treated the coup as an operation of the Gulen movement. Ozturk denied the charges.
cite: Ankara High Criminal Court, General Staff coup trial verdict, 20 June 2019

n: Akinci air base trial — 337 life sentences
d: On 26 November 2020 a court sitting in Sincan, Ankara, ruled on 475 defendants tied to Akinci air base, the coup's command centre. 291 received aggravated life and 46 received life; 70 were acquitted. Civilian Adil Oksuz, described by prosecutors as the Gulen movement's link to the plotters, had been released after arrest in 2016 and remains missing.
cite: Ankara High Criminal Court, Akinci trial verdict, 26 November 2020

n: Mohamed Morsi — Muslim Brotherhood member elected president
d: Mohamed Morsi, a senior Muslim Brotherhood figure and candidate of its Freedom and Justice Party, won Egypt's presidential election in June 2012. The army removed him on 3 July 2013. Most of the Brotherhood's leadership was jailed in the following months.
cite: Egyptian Presidential Election Commission results, June 2012

n: Egypt designates Muslim Brotherhood a terrorist organisation
d: On 25 December 2013 Deputy Prime Minister Hossam Eissa announced that the interim cabinet had declared the Muslim Brotherhood a terrorist organisation, two days after a car bomb at the Mansoura police headquarters killed 14 people. Ansar Bait al-Maqdis claimed the bombing. Membership became punishable by up to five years in prison; a court had already banned the group and seized its assets in September 2013.
cite: Egyptian cabinet decision, 25 December 2013

n: Morsi Qatar case — ex-president's life term upheld
d: Morsi and others were accused of passing state secrets to Qatar while he was president. On 16 September 2017 Egypt's Court of Cassation upheld his life sentence (handed down in June 2016) for leading an illegal group, but threw out a 15-year term for stealing secret documents. Three co-defendants' death sentences were upheld. Qatar denied the accusations.
cite: Egyptian Court of Cassation, 16 September 2017

n: Safari Club — Egypt's intelligence chief Kamal Hassan Ali
d: General Kamal Hassan Ali, head of Egypt's Mukhabarat, was one of five intelligence chiefs who signed the Safari Club charter dated 1 September 1976, with France, Saudi Arabia, Morocco and Iran. In 1977 France flew Egyptian and Moroccan troops into Zaire's Shaba province to back Mobutu. Saudi Arabia paid Egypt $75 million for old Soviet weapons sent to Somalia's Siad Barre. Mohamed Heikal documented the club from the Shah's seized archives (Iran: The Untold Story, 1982).
cite: Mohamed Hassanein Heikal, Iran: The Untold Story (1982); Prince Turki al-Faisal, Georgetown University speech, 2002

n: Safari Club — Saudi intelligence chief Kamal Adham
d: Kamal Adham, head of Saudi intelligence from 1965 until his dismissal on 19 January 1979, signed the 1976 Safari Club charter with the intelligence chiefs of France, Egypt, Morocco and Iran. In a 2002 speech at Georgetown University, his successor-but-one Prince Turki al-Faisal publicly confirmed the club and said it 'included France, Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Morocco, and Iran.'
cite: Prince Turki al-Faisal, former Saudi intelligence chief, Georgetown University speech, 2002

n: Kamal Adham — ex-intelligence chief fronted BCCI's US bank takeover
rank: former head of Saudi General Intelligence
d: Kamal Adham, Saudi intelligence chief until 1979, was a major BCCI shareholder. US prosecutors said he played a key role in BCCI's secret and illegal takeover of First American bank in Washington. Under a plea agreement he paid a $105 million fine in exchange for a reduced sentence and was barred from the finance sector.
cite: US federal and New York County prosecutions in the BCCI case, plea agreement 1992-93

arch.t: Bank of Credit and Commerce International — Abedi and Iqbal: BCCI Was the Largest Bank Fraud in History; CIA Used It for Covert Operations; 62 Countries Affected

n: Saudi Arabia lists Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist
rank: designation by the government (no officials named)
d: On 7 March 2014 the Saudi Press Agency published a list of terrorist organisations including the Muslim Brotherhood, Jabhat al-Nusra, ISIS and the Houthis. It came a day after Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Bahrain withdrew their ambassadors from Qatar. The designation did not name any Saudi officials.
cite: Saudi government designation published by the Saudi Press Agency, 7 March 2014

n: 'UAE 94' trial — Islah members convicted of plot to seize power
rank: ministries, schools and universities (per the Attorney General)
d: 94 Emiratis, many from the Islah group, were tried for plotting to overthrow the government. Attorney General Salem Saeed Kubaish said they had sought to infiltrate state institutions including schools, universities and ministries. On 2 July 2013 the Federal Supreme Court jailed 56 for 3 to 10 years, sentenced 8 in absentia to 15 years and acquitted 26. Those convicted included Sheikh Sultan bin Kayed Al-Qassimi of the Ras al-Khaimah ruling family and lawyer Mohammed al-Roken. Islah denies organisational ties to the Brotherhood.
cite: UAE Federal Supreme Court verdict, 2 July 2013

n: UAE cabinet lists Muslim Brotherhood and Islah as terrorist
d: On 16 November 2014 the UAE cabinet approved a list of about 80 terrorist organisations, released through the WAM news agency. It included the Muslim Brotherhood and its local affiliates, and the Emirati group al-Islah.
cite: UAE cabinet terrorist list, 16 November 2014

n: Abu Dhabi government — 77% owner of BCCI
rank: Abu Dhabi Investment Authority and Department of Finance
d: By 5 July 1991 the Abu Dhabi government, its ruling family and their investment company owned 77% of BCCI. Ghanim Al Mazrui, secretary general of the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority (which held 10%), sat on BCCI's board from 1981 and later chaired it. The US Senate subcommittee found Abu Dhabi was told of BCCI's fraud in April 1990, kept it from the auditors until November 1990, and gave evasive and misleading answers; it found Al Mazrui received no-risk benefits from BCCI share deals.
cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Subcommittee (Kerry-Brown), The BCCI Affair, report December 1992, chapter on Abu Dhabi

arch.t: Bank of Credit and Commerce International — Abedi and Iqbal: BCCI Was the Largest Bank Fraud in History; CIA Used It for Covert Operations; 62 Countries Affected

n: Jordan bans Muslim Brotherhood; its party holds 31 seats
rank: largest party in parliament (Islamic Action Front)
d: On 23 April 2025 Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya banned all activities of the Muslim Brotherhood and said its assets would be seized. The ban followed the arrest of 16 people, including Brotherhood members, over an alleged plot involving weapons; the group denied knowledge. The Brotherhood's political arm, the Islamic Action Front, had won 31 of 138 seats in the September 2024 election, making it the largest party.
cite: Jordanian Interior Ministry announcement, 23 April 2025

n: Ennahda-led government in Tunisia
d: After winning the October 2011 Constituent Assembly election, Ennahda led Tunisia's government: Hamadi Jebali was prime minister from December 2011 to March 2013, and Ali Laarayedh from March 2013 to January 2014. Rafik Abdessalem, son-in-law of party leader Rached Ghannouchi, was foreign minister 2011-2013. Ennahda grew out of the Brotherhood tradition but says it has no organisational link to the Egyptian Brotherhood.
cite: Tunisian government records; academic and press histories of Ennahda

n: Ghannouchi, ex-speaker, given 22 more years ('Instalingo' case)
rank: former speaker of parliament; former foreign minister
d: On 5 February 2025 a Tunisian court sentenced Ennahda leader Rached Ghannouchi, speaker of parliament from 2019 to 2021, to a further 22 years for 'plotting against state security' in the Instalingo case. Ex-foreign minister Rafik Abdessalem got 34 years and ex-prime minister Hichem Mechichi 35 years in absentia. Ghannouchi has been jailed since April 2023; Ennahda calls the case political. In July 2025 he received another 14-year sentence.
cite: Tunisian criminal court, Instalingo case verdict, 5 February 2025

n: 1989 Sudan coup — Bashir and Islamists tried for NIF takeover
d: On 30 June 1989 Brigadier Omar al-Bashir seized power in a coup organised with Hassan al-Turabi's National Islamic Front, the Sudanese Brotherhood-derived movement. After Bashir's fall in 2019, he and other military and Islamist figures were put on trial in Khartoum in 2020 for the 1989 coup; during the trial Bashir admitted his role.
cite: Khartoum criminal court, 1989 coup trial opened 2020
org_note: NIF/National Congress Party is the Sudanese branch of the Brotherhood tradition.

n: Sudan purge of Bashir-era Islamist appointees from judiciary
d: In November 2019 Sudan's transitional government set up the Empowerment Removal Committee to dismantle the 30 June 1989 regime and remove people placed in state jobs under it. It dismissed judges, prosecutors and judicial staff. On 7 October 2021 the High Court's appeals department overturned the dismissals and on 12 October ordered 15 judicial staff back to work; the committee rejected the ruling.
cite: Empowerment Removal Committee decisions 2019-2021; Sudan High Court ruling, 7 and 12 October 2021

n: Kuwait — Brotherhood's party Hadas in parliament and cabinet
rank: members of parliament; occasional cabinet ministers
d: After the 1990 Iraqi invasion the Kuwaiti Muslim Brotherhood broke with the international Brotherhood and founded the Islamic Constitutional Movement (Hadas). Hadas regularly won several seats in parliament in the 1990s and 2000s and occasionally sent members to the cabinet. A coalition including Hadas was out of parliament after it boycotted the 2013 elections.
cite: Foreign Policy / Carnegie analysis, 20 November 2013

n: Safari Club — SAVAK chief Nematollah Nassiri
d: General Nematollah Nassiri, head of the Shah's SAVAK, signed the 1976 Safari Club charter with the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Morocco. The club's documents were found in the Shah's archives after the 1979 revolution, where journalist Mohamed Heikal read them for his 1982 book Iran: The Untold Story.
cite: Mohamed Hassanein Heikal, Iran: The Untold Story (1982); Prince Turki al-Faisal, Georgetown speech, 2002

n: Hojjatieh Society suspended after Khomeini's attack
org_note: Hojjatieh (Anjoman-e Imam-e Zaman), Shi'a society founded 1953 by Sheikh Mahmoud Halabi
rank: officials in government, judiciary and education bodies
d: In a speech on 12 July 1983 Ayatollah Khomeini attacked the Hojjatieh Society; its founder Mahmoud Halabi announced its suspension the same day, followed by a purge of its affiliates from decision-making, academic and educational bodies. Former members are reported to have later held posts in the judiciary, security system and government staffing offices. Claims of membership by senior figures, and of influence under President Ahmadinejad, are contested.
cite: Baqer Moin, Khomeini: Life of the Ayatollah (1999); RFE/RL reporting 2006

n: Jafar Sharif-Emami — Grand Master and twice prime minister
d: Jafar Sharif-Emami was Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Iran for several years. He was the Shah's prime minister from 31 August 1960 to 5 May 1961, and again from 27 August to early November 1978 in the last months before the revolution.
cite: Biographical and historical accounts of Iranian Freemasonry

n: Safari Club — Moroccan intelligence chief Ahmed Dlimi
d: General Ahmed Dlimi, head of Morocco's DGED, signed the 1976 Safari Club charter with the intelligence chiefs of France, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Iran. In 1977 France airlifted Moroccan troops into Zaire's Shaba province to defend Mobutu, the club's first major operation.
cite: Mohamed Hassanein Heikal, Iran: The Untold Story (1982); Prince Turki al-Faisal, Georgetown speech, 2002

n: Broederbond — D.F. Malan, first apartheid prime minister
d: D.F. Malan, prime minister 1948-1954, was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male Afrikaner society founded in 1918 with 37 members by 1920. Every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 was a member. The 1978 book The Super-Afrikaners by journalists Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom printed a near-complete list of about 7,500 members.
cite: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)

n: Broederbond — J.G. Strijdom, prime minister
d: J.G. Strijdom, prime minister 1954-1958, was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, as listed in Wilkins and Strydom's 1978 study of the society.
cite: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)

n: Broederbond — H.F. Verwoerd, prime minister
d: H.F. Verwoerd, prime minister from 1958 until his assassination in 1966, was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond.
cite: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)

n: Broederbond — B.J. Vorster, prime minister and state president
d: B.J. Vorster, prime minister 1966-1978 and state president 1978-1979, was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond.
cite: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)

n: Broederbond — P.W. Botha, defence minister and prime minister
d: P.W. Botha, defence minister and then prime minister from 1978 (state president from 1984), was a Broederbond member who later left the organisation.
cite: Ivor Wilkins and Hans Strydom, The Super-Afrikaners (1978)

n: Broederbond — F.W. de Klerk, state president
d: F.W. de Klerk, state president 1989-1994, was a member of the Afrikaner Broederbond, the last of the unbroken line of members to lead the apartheid state.
cite: Afrikaner Broederbond membership records as reported in published histories

n: Smuts orders civil servants out of the Broederbond
d: Prime Minister Jan Smuts denounced the Broederbond as a fascist organisation and ordered civil servants and state schoolteachers to give up their membership or resign. The order lapsed after Smuts's United Party lost the 1948 election to Malan's National Party.
cite: Order of the Smuts government, mid-1940s

n: Broederbond — all but two cabinet ministers were members (1979)
d: A 1979 report put Broederbond membership at about 12,000 in 800 cells and said all but two ministers in the government were members. The two exceptions were Finance Minister Owen Horwood, who was English-speaking, and Marais Steyn, a former United Party member. The same report counted 49 Broeders in key posts at the state broadcaster SABC.
cite: The Spectator, 'South Africa's secret government', 13 January 1979, drawing on the 1978 Wilkins and Strydom exposé

n: Broederbond — Defence Force chief Magnus Malan
rank: chief of the South African Defence Force
d: General Magnus Malan, head of the South African Defence Force (and later defence minister), was reported in 1979 to be a Broederbond member. The same report named the Broederbond's close ties to the security police and BOSS.
cite: The Spectator, 13 January 1979

n: Broederbond — BOSS spy chief Hendrik van den Bergh
rank: head of the Bureau for State Security (BOSS)
d: Hendrik van den Bergh, head of apartheid South Africa's state security apparatus including the Bureau for State Security, was a Broederbond member who later left the organisation.
cite: Published histories of the Afrikaner Broederbond

n: Gerrit Viljoen — Broederbond chairman to cabinet minister
rank: Administrator-General of South West Africa; minister of education
d: Gerrit Viljoen chaired the Broederbond from 1974 to 1980. While chairman he was appointed Administrator-General of South West Africa (Namibia) in 1979; he then served as minister of education 1980-1989 and minister of constitutional development 1989-1992.
cite: Official records of South African government appointments; The Spectator, 13 January 1979

n: Omar Bongo — president and founder of Gabon's grand lodges
d: Omar Bongo, initiated as a Freemason in 1953, was president of Gabon from 28 November 1967 until his death on 8 June 2009. He founded two Masonic bodies: the Grand Rite Equatorial, affiliated with the Grand Orient de France, and the Grand Lodge of Gabon, linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise (GLNF), and held the grand mastership until his death.
cite: Afrik-News, 'Freemason Presidents in Africa: Ali Bongo ordained Grand Master of Gabon', 2009; Nicholas Shaxson, Poisoned Wells (2007)

n: Ali Bongo — sitting president installed as Grand Master by GLNF
d: In 2009 Francois Stifani, Grand Master of the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise, installed Ali Bongo as Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Gabon and the Grand Equatorial Rite, succeeding his father; Ali Bongo became president the same year. He kept the post until after his overthrow in the August 2023 coup.
cite: Afrik-News, 2009; Africa Intelligence, October 2023

n: Gabon lodge passes to a provincial governor after 2023 coup
d: In October 2023 the Grand Lodge of Gabon replaced deposed president Ali Bongo with Jacques Denis Tsanga, governor of Haut-Ogooue province and minister of water and forests in 2018-19. The grand mastership had traditionally gone to the head of state; transitional president Brice Oligui Nguema reportedly declined it.
cite: Africa Intelligence, 20 October 2023, as reported by Connection Ivoirienne

n: Denis Sassou-Nguesso — Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Congo
d: Denis Sassou-Nguesso, president of the Republic of Congo, is reported to be Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Congo-Brazzaville, which is linked to the Grande Loge Nationale Francaise.
cite: Afrik-News, 2009; Jeune Afrique dossier as republished by L'Hebdo Ivoirien, May 2013

n: Idriss Deby — president reported as Freemason
d: Idriss Deby, president of Chad from 1990 to 2021, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting on African heads of state in Masonic lodges, and again in a 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier. No lodge is named.
cite: Afrik-News, 2009; Jeune Afrique dossier as republished by L'Hebdo Ivoirien, 29 May 2013

n: Mamadou Tandja — president reported as Freemason
d: Mamadou Tandja, president of Niger from 1999 to 2010, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting on African heads of state in Masonic lodges. No lodge is named.
cite: Afrik-News, 'Freemason Presidents in Africa', 2009

n: Francois Bozize — president initiated under Sassou's sponsorship
d: Francois Bozize, president of the Central African Republic from 2003 to 2013, was named as a Freemason in 2009 reporting. A 2013 Jeune Afrique dossier said he joined under the sponsorship of Congo's president Denis Sassou-Nguesso.
cite: Afrik-News, 2009; Jeune Afrique dossier as republished by L'Hebdo Ivoirien, 29 May 2013

n: Paul Biya and the Templar order OSTI — state oil money traced
org_note: Ordre Souverain du Temple Initiatique (OSTI) and its charity CIRCES, esoteric Templar order founded by Raymond Bernard, former head of AMORC (Rosicrucians) in France
d: Le Monde reported in December 1999 that President Paul Biya gave Raymond Bernard's OSTI and CIRCES tens of millions of francs between 1988 and 1992, including 40 million francs personally. 11.2 million francs moved from Cameroon's state oil company SNH to Bernard's personal account. The presidency called Bernard an 'old friend' and would not comment on the payments. Bernard was questioned in the Solar Temple inquiry but not charged.
cite: Le Monde, 'L'argent africain des Templiers', 24 December 1999; Le Monde, 17 August 2000

n: William Tolbert — Liberia's president was Masonic Grand Master
d: William Tolbert, vice-president 1952-1971 and president 1971-1980, was Grand Master of the Masonic Order of Liberia. Lodge membership was widely seen as a requirement for leadership in the ruling True Whig Party, and by the 1970s most high officials were Masons. Tolbert was killed on 12 April 1980 in Samuel Doe's coup, and much of the Masonic leadership was killed.
cite: Histories of the Masonic Order of Liberia

n: Samuel Doe bans Freemasonry, later joins it
d: After the April 1980 coup, Samuel Doe banned Freemasonry in Liberia. He later lifted the ban; the order was formally reinstated in 1988, and Doe himself was initiated in 1989.
cite: Histories of the Masonic Order of Liberia

n: Senegal closes Gulen schools, hands them to Turkey's Maarif
d: In 2017 Senegal's government closed more than a dozen schools linked to the Gulen movement, attended by about 3,000 children, after Turkish requests. President Erdogan said they were transferred to Turkey's state-backed Maarif Foundation, which opened three schools in Senegal in November 2017.
cite: Senegalese government closure, 2017, reported by AFP/IOL, 18 March 2018

n: Chad's president orders Gulen schools handed to Maarif
d: In November 2017 a statement on the Chadian presidency's website said President Idriss Deby had agreed to hand schools run by the Gulen movement to Turkey's Maarif Foundation by 18 December 2017 and to expel people linked to the movement.
cite: Statement of the Presidency of Chad, November 2017

n: Niger hands Gulen schools to Turkey's Maarif Foundation
d: By June 2017 Gulen-linked schools in Niger had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry, as also happened in Guinea, Sudan and Somalia.
cite: Turkish government and Maarif Foundation statements, June 2017

n: Guinea hands Gulen schools to Turkey's Maarif Foundation
d: By June 2017 Gulen-linked schools in Guinea had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry.
cite: Turkish government and Maarif Foundation statements, June 2017

n: Somalia hands Gulen schools to Turkey's Maarif Foundation
d: By June 2017 Gulen-linked schools in Somalia had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry.
cite: Turkish government and Maarif Foundation statements, June 2017

n: Sudan hands Gulen schools to Turkey's Maarif Foundation
d: By June 2017 Gulen-linked schools in Sudan had been taken over by Turkey's state Maarif Foundation after talks through Turkey's Foreign Ministry.
cite: Turkish government and Maarif Foundation statements, June 2017

n: Morocco shuts Gulen-linked schools
d: Morocco's government ordered Gulen-linked schools in the country shut down, one of several African states (with Tunisia and Sierra Leone) reported in June 2017 to have closed them.
cite: Turkish government statements reported June 2017

n: Shinzo Abe assassination — Yamagami life sentence
d: Former prime minister Shinzo Abe was shot dead in Nara on 8 July 2022 by Tetsuya Yamagami. Yamagami said he acted after seeing a video message Abe sent to a group affiliated with the Unification Church, which he blamed for his family's ruin, and that he wanted to expose the church's ties to Abe. He said he first planned to target the church's leader but switched to Abe. On 21 January 2026 the Nara District Court sentenced him to life in prison after he pleaded guilty to murder.
cite: Nara District Court verdict, 21 January 2026 (AP report)

n: LDP internal survey — 179 of 379 lawmakers tied to church
rank: ruling-party members of the National Diet
d: On 8 September 2022 LDP secretary-general Toshimitsu Motegi released the party's own survey of its 379 Diet members: 179 reported ties to the Unification Church or affiliated groups. Of these, 96 had attended church or affiliated events, 20 gave speeches, nearly 50 paid money at events, 29 accepted donations and 17 used church followers as campaign volunteers. Abe was left out of the survey because he was dead. The survey relied on lawmakers reporting on themselves.
cite: Liberal Democratic Party internal survey, 8 September 2022 (AP report)

n: Nobuo Kishi — defense minister helped by church members
d: After Abe's killing in July 2022, Defense Minister Nobuo Kishi, Abe's younger brother, said Unification Church members had helped him in past elections. In the LDP's September 2022 survey he was named among the 17 lawmakers who had accepted church followers as campaign volunteers.
cite: Statement by Defense Minister Kishi, July 2022 (The Diplomat); LDP survey 8 September 2022 (AP)

n: Koichi Hagiuda — church volunteers in campaigns
rank: former economy and industry minister, senior LDP lawmaker
d: Koichi Hagiuda, a former Minister of Economy, Trade and Industry, was named in the LDP's 8 September 2022 survey among the 17 lawmakers who had accepted Unification Church followers as election campaign volunteers.
cite: Liberal Democratic Party internal survey, 8 September 2022 (AP report)

n: Daishiro Yamagiwa — minister resigns over church ties
d: Daishiro Yamagiwa resigned as economic revitalization minister on 24 October 2022 after scrutiny of his links to the Unification Church. He confirmed he appeared in a 2019 group photo with church leader Hak Ja Han and had attended a church-organized event in 2018. He said he regretted that his attendance at several of the group's meetings had given it credit. Prime Minister Fumio Kishida accepted the resignation; the week before, Kishida had ordered a government probe into the church.
cite: Resignation accepted by Prime Minister Kishida, 24 October 2022 (AFP via Philstar)

n: Nobusuke Kishi — co-founded church's political arm (IFVC)
d: Former prime minister Nobusuke Kishi, Abe's grandfather, founded the International Federation for Victory over Communism (Shokyo Rengo) in 1968 with Ryoichi Sasakawa and Yoshio Kodama; it handled the Unification Church's political operations in Japan. A 1975 FBI report named Kishi and Sasakawa as heads of its Japanese branch. The church built its Tokyo headquarters next to Kishi's former residence in Shibuya, and Kishi gave speeches to followers there in 1970, 1971 and 1973.
cite: The Diplomat, July 2022 (citing 1975 FBI report); Tansa investigative series 'The True Mother Files' (citing Kishi's memoirs and Arita 2024)

n: Unification Church dissolution order — Tokyo courts
rank: ruling party (context of the government case)
d: After the 2022 revelations about church ties to LDP lawmakers, the culture ministry asked the courts to dissolve the church. In March 2025 the Tokyo District Court issued the first dissolution order based on a group's illegal acts under the Civil Code, finding roughly 40 years of damage: 1,559 victims of unlawful donation solicitation and about 20.4 billion yen taken. On 4 March 2026 the Tokyo High Court upheld the order, stripping the church of religious-corporation status and starting liquidation. The 'inquiry' status here marks a court finding against the organization, not a criminal conviction of any official.
cite: Tokyo District Court dissolution order, March 2025; Tokyo High Court ruling, 4 March 2026 (Adnkronos/Jiji)

n: Nippon Kaigi — 15 of 19 ministers in Abe's 2014 cabinet
rank: cabinet ministers including the prime minister
d: After Shinzo Abe's September 2014 cabinet reshuffle, 15 of the 19 cabinet members, Abe among them, were reported to be members of Nippon Kaigi, a nationalist lobby that campaigns for constitutional revision and patriotic education. The count comes from press reporting of the Diet members' association membership lists, not from an official finding.
cite: Korea JoongAng Daily, 'Abe's reshuffle promotes right-wingers', 5 September 2014 (as cited in Wikipedia's Nippon Kaigi article)

n: Shinto Seiji Renmei — 16 of 19 Abe cabinet members
org_note: New key: Shinto Seiji Renmei (Shinto Association of Spiritual Leadership), the political arm of the Association of Shinto Shrines; works closely with Nippon Kaigi.
d: Researcher Ernils Larsson (Uppsala University) reported in December 2014 that 296 Diet members were listed supporters of Shinto Seiji Renmei's Diet members' league, including 16 of the 19 members of Abe's then-current cabinet. He also wrote that a majority of cabinet ministers belonged to Nippon Kaigi.
cite: Ernils Larsson, 'Abe's cabinet reshuffle reflects growing influence of the religious right', East Asia Forum, 3 December 2014

n: Soka Gakkai's Komeito in ruling coalition, 1999–2025
d: Komeito, whose electoral support is closely tied to the lay Buddhist group Soka Gakkai (about 8.3 million member households), was a formal coalition partner of the LDP from 1999. On 10 October 2025 Komeito announced it was leaving the coalition after 26 years, citing the LDP's weak response to its proposal for stricter rules on political donations.
cite: Komeito press conference, 10 October 2025; CSIS analysis 'Japan's 26-Year-Old Ruling Coalition Collapses'

n: Aum member in Tokyo police — Kunimatsu shooting
rank: Tokyo Metropolitan Police officer; target was the National Police Agency chief
d: On 30 March 1995, ten days after the Tokyo subway sarin attack, National Police Agency chief Takaji Kunimatsu was shot and wounded. Toshiyuki Kosugi, a Tokyo Metropolitan Police Department officer and Aum Shinrikyo follower, confessed to a role, but in June 1997 prosecutors declined to charge him for lack of supporting evidence. Kosugi and three other Aum-linked men were arrested in July 2004; on 17 September 2004 prosecutors again declined to indict, doubting Kosugi's changed confession.
cite: Tokyo District Public Prosecutors Office decisions, June 1997 and 17 September 2004 (The Japan Times)

n: Aum Shinrikyo — former Self-Defense Force members
d: A 1995 US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations staff report on Aum Shinrikyo listed three former Japanese Self-Defense Force members in the sect: Shinya Asano, Takahisa Shirai and Akira Yamagata. Yamagata, a subordinate in Aum's 'Home Affairs Ministry', was alleged to have used VX nerve agent to kill members who had left. The report also named a Mitsubishi employee arrested on suspicion of helping an Aum member and former SDF member steal company secrets.
cite: US Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, 'Global Proliferation of Weapons of Mass Destruction: A Case Study on the Aum Shinrikyo', staff report 1995, Appendix A

n: Kim Keon-hee — ex-first lady jailed for church gifts
d: On 28 January 2026 the Seoul Central District Court sentenced Kim Keon-hee, wife of former president Yoon Suk Yeol, to one year and eight months in prison. It found that in July 2022 she received a Chanel bag worth 12 million won and a Graff diamond necklace worth 62 million won from the Unification Church, passed through shaman Jeon Seong-bae on behalf of church official Yun Young-ho. She was acquitted over an April 2022 bag, the Deutsch Motors stock case and a political-funds charge.
cite: Seoul Central District Court verdict, 28 January 2026 (Korea Times)

n: Han Hak-ja — church leader jailed for bribery
d: Special counsel Min Joong-ki indicted Unification Church leader Han Hak-ja on 10 October 2025 for bribery, political-funds violations, embezzlement and destroying evidence. On 31 August 2026 the Seoul Central District Court sentenced her to two years, finding she arranged a necklace and handbag for first lady Kim Keon-hee in July 2022 to seek favors and colluded to give 100 million won to lawmaker Kweon Seong-dong in January 2022. The court said the church used its money to expand political influence around the presidential election. Prosecutors had asked for 13 years; the church said it would appeal.
cite: Special counsel indictment, 10 October 2025; Seoul Central District Court verdict, 31 August 2026 (Korea Times)

n: Kweon Seong-dong — PPP floor leader loses seat
rank: five-term lawmaker, People Power Party floor leader until June 2025
d: Kweon Seong-dong, a close ally of Yoon Suk Yeol, accepted 100 million won from Unification Church official Yun Young-ho in January 2022, before the March 2022 presidential election. He was arrested in September 2025 and indicted the next month. On 16 July 2026 the Supreme Court upheld a two-year prison term and forfeiture of 100 million won, and he lost his National Assembly seat.
cite: Supreme Court of Korea ruling, 16 July 2026 (Korea Times)

n: Shincheonji — Lee Man-hee indicted over mass PPP sign-ups
d: A joint prosecutor-police team found that at least 56,472 Shincheonji members were registered as People Power Party members between July 2021 and August 2023 (6,482 in July 2021 alone, before the 2022 presidential election). Founder Lee Man-hee, 94, was arrested on 24 June 2026; on 13 July 2026 the team announced he and seven other leaders were indicted for violating the Political Parties Act, which bars forcing anyone to join a party, and obstruction of business.
cite: Joint investigation headquarters indictment, June–July 2026 (Asia Economy; Korea JoongAng Daily)

n: Sam Dastyari — senator resigns over Huang Xiangmo links
d: Labor senator Sam Dastyari had a company linked to donor Huang Xiangmo pay his legal bills. At a June 2016 press conference for Chinese media, with Huang present, he said China's borders were 'a matter for China', against Labor policy. In October 2016 he reportedly warned Huang his phone was probably tapped by Australian agencies. He lost his party posts on 30 November 2017, announced his resignation on 12 December 2017 and lodged it on 25 January 2018. Huang chaired the Australian Council for the Promotion of Peaceful Reunification of China, described as a peak body for United Front-linked groups.
cite: Australian Senate record; AAP reporting (InDaily, 12 December 2017)

n: Huang Xiangmo — residency cancelled on ASIO advice
rank: major donor to both main parties
d: In February 2019 the Australian government cancelled Huang Xiangmo's permanent residency and rejected his citizenship application. ASIO judged him 'amenable to conducting acts of foreign interference', citing his roles chairing the Australian Council for the Promotion of Peaceful Reunification of China (2014–17) and the Oceanic Alliance of the Promotion of Peaceful Reunification of China. With associates he had given about AU$2 million to Labor and over AU$1 million to the Liberal Party.
cite: Australian Department of Home Affairs decision on ASIO advice, February 2019 (The Diplomat)

n: ICAC Operation Aero — $100,000 cash to NSW Labor
rank: state parliament member and party head office
d: The NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption reported on 28 February 2022 that $100,000 in cash delivered to NSW Labor's offices in 2015 came from Huang Xiangmo, a property developer barred from donating in NSW, disguised as donations from restaurant staff at a Chinese Friends of Labor dinner. ICAC found former NSW Labor MP Ernest Wong engaged in corrupt conduct by concealing illegal donations and trying to get a donor to give false testimony. ICAC did not make a finding about the United Front itself; the link is through Huang's roles in the reunification council.
cite: NSW ICAC, Operation Aero report, 28 February 2022 (AAP)

n: Di Sanh Duong — first foreign interference conviction
rank: acting federal immigration and multicultural affairs minister (target)
d: A County Court of Victoria jury found Melbourne community leader Di Sanh Duong guilty on 19 December 2023 of preparing a foreign interference offence, the first conviction under Australia's 2018 law. The Crown said he used roles in groups such as the Oceania Federation of Chinese Organisations for Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos to reach Alan Tudge, then acting immigration minister, and concealed links to the United Front Work Department, the Ministry of State Security and the Chinese consulate. He was sentenced on 29 February 2024 to 2 years 9 months.
cite: Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions case report; County Court of Victoria, verdict 19 December 2023, sentence 29 February 2024

n: Chang Hsien-yao — ex-lawmaker indicted over 2024 election
org_note: Prosecutors say Chang met Wang Huning, chairman of the CPPCC National Committee, the top body of China's united front system; the indictment speaks of 'sources of infiltration'. Country field: canonical list has no Taiwan entry — caller should decide placement.
rank: former legislator; former deputy head of the Mainland Affairs Council (2013–14)
d: Prosecutors indicted Chang Hsien-yao on 12 February 2025 under Article 4 of the Anti-Infiltration Act and the presidential election law. He was a People First Party legislator for Kaohsiung (2005–08) and special deputy head of the Mainland Affairs Council. Prosecutors allege that from June 2023 he took instructions from people linked to the Chinese government to promote Terry Gou's presidential bid, gave Chinese officials a document on the election on 6 September 2023, and met Wang Huning in Beijing on 11 September 2023 to confirm the plan.
cite: Taiwan prosecutors' indictment, 12 February 2025 (Central News Agency)

n: Gong He Party leader jailed for Beijing-funded campaigns
org_note: Funding came through officials of the Putian Taiwan Affairs Office in Fujian; the court called it 'united front' activity. Country field: canonical list has no Taiwan entry — caller should decide placement.
rank: registered political party and its 2022 local-election candidates
d: Taiwan's Ministry of Justice indicted Gong He Party chairman Chou Ke-chi and Taipei Puxian Association board members Pan Jindong and Chu Chun-yuan on 9 August 2023 under the Anti-Infiltration Act. Prosecutors said money from Fujian funded the party's November 2022 campaigns, including a Taipei mayoral candidate who got 316 votes. In late June 2025 the Taipei District Court sentenced Chou to two years, Pan to 18 months and Chu to one year, finding they took Beijing funds for united front activity. The sentences can be appealed.
cite: Taipei District Court verdict, June 2025 (Taipei Times via ANI); indictment 9 August 2023 (UCA News)

n: Jiangsu united front money for New Taipei council candidate
org_note: Prosecutors allege the Federation of Hong Kong Jiangsu Youth took assignments from the United Front Work Department of the CCP Jiangsu Provincial Committee. Country field: canonical list has no Taiwan entry — caller should decide placement.
d: On 26 February 2024 New Taipei prosecutors indicted Sun Chih-chuan of the Chinese Youth Development Union and a Chinese woman surnamed Da, director of the Federation of Hong Kong Jiangsu Youth, under the Anti-Infiltration Act and the Political Donations Act. They allege 100,000 yuan was sent on Beijing's instructions, via a US$10,000 transfer from Da's Hong Kong account, to fund Labor Party candidate Wang Cheng in the 2022 New Taipei City Council election; Wang received NT$435,000. Both defendants deny ties to Beijing.
cite: New Taipei District Prosecutors Office indictment, 26 February 2024 (Central News Agency)

n: Chinese Unity Promotion Party raided — Bamboo Union founder

Chang said the party received money from China but that it came from his company's profits there. Legislators alleged that money from Chinese officials and state-linked firms was moved through his Taolue Group.
cite: Taipei District Prosecutors Office search operation, August 2018 (Taipei Times)

n: Juan Luis Cipriani — Opus Dei bishop named state mediator by Fujimori
d: Juan Luis Cipriani, an Opus Dei priest and later the first Opus Dei cardinal (2001), was named by President Alberto Fujimori as one of three mediators in the 1996–97 Japanese embassy hostage crisis. Peru's Truth and Reconciliation Commission later concluded that, as bishop and archbishop of Ayacucho, he never questioned rights violations by state forces; Cipriani rejected the finding.
cite: Peruvian Truth and Reconciliation Commission, final report 2003

n: Banco Ambrosiano Andino — guarantee for Peru's Exocet purchase
d: Banco Ambrosiano Andino in Lima was a subsidiary of Roberto Calvi's Banco Ambrosiano. During the 1982 Falklands war, British intelligence found that the guarantee for Exocet missiles bought by Peru, which France then blocked to stop their transfer to Argentina, was a $200 million deposit from Banco Ambrosiano Andino. Ambrosiano's Latin American banks had lent to Panamanian shell companies that the Vatican Bank's letters of patronage described as under its control.
cite: Histories of the Banco Ambrosiano collapse; Time magazine, 1982

n: Luis Arce Gómez — Bolivian interior minister, life term in Condor case
d: Luis Arce Gómez was interior minister and chief of repression under Luis García Meza after the 17 July 1980 coup, which Argentina's junta backed. In July 2019 a Rome appeals court gave him a life sentence in the Operation Condor case, one of 24 such sentences.
cite: Rome Court of Assizes of Appeal, Operation Condor verdict, July 2019 (subject to Cassation)

n: BCCI — nominee owners tied to President Sarney's circle
d: The US Senate BCCI report found that BCCI secretly controlled a Brazilian bank through nominees, including former ambassador Sergio da Costa, paid $150,000 a year as a front-man. It reports that close associates of President José Sarney were among the nominees and that Sarney presented a BCCI-funded prize in 1987.
cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report), Dec 1992, ch. 5

n: Brazil — prosecutors cite Malhães files as proof of Condor role
d: On 24 November 2014 Brazil's federal prosecutors in Rio de Janeiro released documents found at the home of retired colonel Paulo Malhães. They describe 'Operation Gringo', run by the Rio de Janeiro Army Intelligence Center to track foreign nationals, which Attorney-General Rodrigo Janot called the strongest evidence that Operation Condor existed. Brazil's armed forces and foreign ministry deny the collaboration.
cite: Federal Public Prosecutor's Office, Rio de Janeiro (MPF/RJ), 24 Nov 2014

n: TFP Brazil and the 1964 military coup
d: Brazil's Tradition, Family, Property campaign against President João Goulart's land reform is described by historians as helping set the stage for the 1964 military coup. The TFP later urged the military government to arrest Archbishop Hélder Câmara.
cite: Academic histories of TFP

n: BCCI — Noriega's account in the name of Panama's Defense Forces
d: General Manuel Noriega opened a BCCI account in early 1982 in the name of the Panamanian Defense Forces. The US Senate report found he held about $25 million in it at its height, mostly cash deposits, with one deposit of about $4 million. BCCI also lent to Noriega associates Enrique Pretelt and César Rodríguez and absorbed about $10 million in losses.
cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report), Dec 1992, ch. 5

n: BCCI paid mortgage of Noriega's presidential candidate Barletta
d: The US Senate BCCI report found that Noriega directed BCCI to pay off the mortgage of Nicolás Ardito Barletta, his chosen presidential candidate. Barletta became president of Panama in 1984.
cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report), Dec 1992, ch. 5

n: BCCI handled Jamaica's state foreign-currency accounts under Seaga
d: Under Prime Minister Edward Seaga, BCCI handled Jamaica's US commodity financing and most government foreign-currency accounts. A BCCI officer told the Senate: 'we handled every penny that came into or out of Jamaica in terms of foreign currency.' The report lists loans of $33.9 million to the Bank of Jamaica and $45.4 million to state oil firm Petrojam.
cite: US Senate Foreign Relations Committee, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry-Brown report), Dec 1992, ch. 5

n: Ambrosiano's Managua bank — licence cancelled by presidential decree
d: Ambrosiano Group Banco Comercial, a unit of Calvi's Banco Ambrosiano Holding of Luxembourg, was licensed in Nicaragua in 1977–78. Ambrosiano provided funds to both the Somoza government and the Sandinista opposition. Presidential Agreement No. 39, signed by Daniel Ortega on 2 August 1985, approved moving the bank's seat out of Nicaragua and cancelled its operating licence.
cite: Acuerdo Presidencial No. 39, La Gaceta No. 157, 20 Aug 1985

arch.t: Vatican-Masonic Network — Roberto Calvi Murder; Banco Ambrosiano Collapse; P2 Lodge Member Directed Vatican Bank Investments (PROVEN)

n: Ambrosiano Overseas, Nassau — Vatican Bank chief on board; suspended
d: Banco Ambrosiano Overseas in Nassau was a Calvi subsidiary; Archbishop Paul Marcinkus, president of the Vatican Bank (IOR), had been a director. After Ambrosiano's 1982 collapse, Bahamian banking authorities suspended its operations. The Nassau and Luxembourg units owed about half of the $1.2–1.4 billion lent to Panamanian shell companies.
cite: Bahamian banking authorities' suspension, 1982; Time magazine, 9 Aug 1982

n: Mario Sandoval Alarcón — WACL leader and vice-president
d: Mario Sandoval Alarcón, founder of the National Liberation Movement (MLN) in 1960, was vice-president of Guatemala from 1 July 1974 to 1 July 1978. He was a leader of the World Anti-Communist League. Historians link the MLN to killings by the Mano Blanca death squad.
cite: Academic histories of WACL and Guatemala

n: Venezuela — government inquiry into TFP, 1984
d: After parents complained that the group cut teenagers off from their families, a three-month investigation under President Jaime Lusinchi found Venezuela's TFP was operating outside the constitution, and the government was reported to plan a ban. In December 1984 Caracas police arrested a man carrying a TFP card over a possible plot against Pope John Paul II; TFP denied involvement. Whether a ban took effect is not confirmed.
cite: Venezuelan government investigation, 1984 (as reported)

n: El Yunque — Delgado book names PAN leaders and Fox cabinet members
d: In 2003 journalist Álvaro Delgado published 'El Yunque: la ultraderecha en el poder', claiming the secret Catholic group founded in Puebla in 1953 had members among PAN leaders and in President Vicente Fox's cabinet. PAN officials called the claims 'pure fiction'. Former PAN leader Luis H. Álvarez said he believed the group was real but negligible.
cite: Álvaro Delgado, El Yunque (Grijalbo, 2003); Proceso reporting

n: El Yunque — ex-mayor names PAN president Espino, claims 4 states
d: Luis Paredes Moctezuma, former mayor of Puebla, named PAN national leader Manuel Espino Barrientos as a member, said El Yunque helped back Fox's 2000 presidential campaign, and claimed in 2007 that it controlled four state governments. The PAN denied the group had anything to do with the party.
cite: Statements of Luis Paredes Moctezuma, 2007, as reported in Mexican press

n: El Yunque — Guanajuato governor Oliva and chief of staff named
d: Juan Manuel Oliva, PAN governor of Guanajuato (2006–2012), his chief of staff Gerardo Mosqueda and local politician Alberto Diosdado were named as El Yunque members in the 2000s. All three denied it.
cite: Mexican press reporting, 2000s

n: Scientology Operation Snow White — IRS infiltrated by planted clerks
d: Scientology's Guardian's Office placed members inside the IRS; Gerald Bennett Wolfe took a clerk-typist job there around late 1974 and copied files on tax-exempt organisations for the church. Wolfe was arrested in June 1976 with a forged federal pass. After the FBI raided Scientology offices in Los Angeles and Washington on 8 July 1977, eleven Scientologists, including Mary Sue Hubbard, were convicted; Wolfe received five years and a $10,000 fine.
cite: United States v. Mary Sue Hubbard et al., U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, guilty pleas and sentencing 1979

arch.t: Scientology — Operation Snow White: Church Infiltrated 136 Government Agencies in 30 Countries; 11 Senior Officials Including Founder's Wife Convicted of Federal Crimes (PROVEN)

n: Operation Snow White — Justice Department and U.S. Attorney's office
rank: Department of Justice and U.S. Attorney's Office for D.C.
d: The same operation broke into or copied documents from the Justice Department and from the office of Assistant U.S. Attorney Nathan Dodell, who was handling Scientology litigation. Documents were also taken from the D.C. Metropolitan Police, the DEA and the Treasury. Mary Sue Hubbard, wife of L. Ron Hubbard and head of the Guardian's Office, was sentenced to five years and a $10,000 fine; Jane Kember and Mo Budlong were convicted at trial in 1980 after fighting extradition from the UK.
cite: United States v. Mary Sue Hubbard et al., U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, 1979; Kember and Budlong convicted 1980

n: Scientology — 1993 IRS closing agreement and tax exemption
rank: IRS Commissioner and Exempt Organizations division
d: After decades of litigation (about 200 suits by the church and roughly 2,300 by individual Scientologists), the IRS granted the church religious tax exemption in October 1993. Negotiations began after David Miscavige walked into IRS headquarters and met Commissioner Fred Goldberg, likely in 1991. Under the secret closing agreement the church paid $12.5 million and dropped all its lawsuits against the IRS. The terms became public only when The Wall Street Journal published them on 30 December 1997.
cite: IRS–Church of Scientology closing agreement, October 1993; terms published by The Wall Street Journal, 30 Dec 1997

n: Church of Scientology of Toronto — OPP and Attorney General infiltrated
rank: Ontario Provincial Police and Ontario Ministry of the Attorney General offices
d: On 25 June 1992 the Church of Scientology of Toronto was convicted on two counts of breach of the public trust for placing members inside the offices of the Ontario Provincial Police and the Ontario Ministry of the Attorney General; operations against the RCMP were also part of the case. Seven members were convicted in total. The church was fined $250,000 and member Jacqueline Matz $5,000. The Court of Appeal for Ontario rejected the church's appeal.
cite: R v Church of Scientology of Toronto, Ontario Court (General Division), 1992; Court of Appeal for Ontario, 1997

n: Fraser Report — Moon Organization worked with South Korean agencies
rank: U.S. Congress (lobbying of members and offices)
d: The House Subcommittee on International Organizations, chaired by Rep. Donald Fraser, found that Sun Myung Moon's organization had at times acted 'in cooperation with, or at the direction of, ROK agencies and officials'. It found the Moon group set up the Korean Culture and Freedom Foundation, presented as a nonprofit, and used it to advance its own interests and those of the South Korean government. The subcommittee also found the group had 'extensively used the names of Senators, Congressmen, U.S. Presidents' to raise money. It asked the Justice Department, SEC and IRS to form an interagency task force.
cite: House Committee on International Relations, Subcommittee on International Organizations, 'Investigation of Korean-American Relations' (Fraser Report), 31 Oct 1978

n: Moon Organization — disguised bid for Diplomat National Bank
rank: Federally regulated bank in Washington (Diplomat National Bank)
d: The Fraser Report found that the Moon Organization 'attempted to obtain a controlling interest in the Diplomat National Bank by disguising the source of funds', with shares bought in the names of Unification Church members. The subcommittee asked the SEC and other agencies to look at the purchases and asked congressional tax committees to review the tax filings of Moon-run entities.
cite: Fraser Report, House Subcommittee on International Organizations, 31 Oct 1978

n: Sun Myung Moon — federal tax conviction
rank: Federal tax authorities (false returns filed with the IRS)
d: A federal jury in New York convicted Moon in 1982 on three counts of filing false tax returns for 1973–75 and one count of conspiracy, which covered obstruction of justice and false statements to a grand jury. He was sentenced to 18 months and a $15,000 fine; aide Takeru Kamiyama was convicted of conspiracy, obstruction and perjury. The Supreme Court declined to hear the appeal in 1984, and Moon served 13 months at FCI Danbury.
cite: United States v. Sun Myung Moon, S.D.N.Y. 1982; 718 F.2d 1210 (2d Cir. 1983); cert. denied, 466 U.S. 971 (1984)

n: Washington Times — Moon-founded paper read daily by Reagan
rank: President of the United States (Ronald Reagan, as reader)
d: Moon founded The Washington Times through his company News World Communications; its first edition appeared on 17 May 1982, with Bo Hi Pak as founding president. The paper ran at a heavy loss covered by Unification Church income from Japan; Moon had spent an estimated $900 million to $1 billion on it by 1991. Reagan read it every day of his presidency. The paper is still owned by an entity of the Unification movement.
cite: Major-outlet and reference reporting on The Washington Times' ownership and funding

n: Koreagate — Rep. Richard Hanna pleads guilty
d: South Korean businessman Tongsun Park, acting for the Korean Central Intelligence Agency, paid cash to members of Congress to keep U.S. support for the Park Chung-hee government; in 1978 testimony under immunity he admitted giving money to 30 members. Former KCIA director Kim Hyong-uk testified to the scheme before the House. Former Rep. Richard Hanna was the only member convicted; he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to prison.
cite: U.S. District Court for D.C., Hanna plea 1978; House hearings on Korean influence, 1977–78
org_note: koreagate = the 1970s Tongsun Park / KCIA influence network in the U.S. Congress

n: Koreagate — three congressmen reprimanded by the House
rank: U.S. Representatives (Edward Roybal, Charles H. Wilson, John J. McFall)
d: After the House ethics investigation into Tongsun Park's payments, the House reprimanded Representatives Edward Roybal, Charles H. Wilson and John J. McFall in 1978. Reported payments ranged from $100,000 to $200,000 per person. Rep. Edward Patten was investigated and found not guilty.
cite: U.S. House of Representatives, reprimand votes following the Korean influence investigation, 1978
org_note: koreagate = the 1970s Tongsun Park / KCIA influence network in the U.S. Congress

n: Koreagate — Rep. Otto Passman acquitted
d: Former Rep. Otto Passman, who had chaired the House foreign aid appropriations subcommittee, was indicted on bribery, conspiracy, illegal gratuities and tax evasion charges over money from Tongsun Park. His trial was moved to Monroe, Louisiana, where a jury acquitted him.
cite: U.S. v. Passman, federal trial in Monroe, Louisiana (acquittal)
org_note: koreagate = the 1970s Tongsun Park / KCIA influence network in the U.S. Congress

n: The Fellowship — C Street house for members of Congress
d: The Fellowship, also called the Family, runs the National Prayer Breakfast and a townhouse on C Street owned by an affiliated group. Mother Jones named eight lawmakers who lived there: Senators Sam Brownback, Tom Coburn, Jim DeMint and John Ensign, and Representatives Mike Doyle, Heath Shuler, Bart Stupak and Zach Wamp. Residents paid about $950 a month including housekeeping. Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington filed ethics complaints arguing the subsidised lodging broke House and Senate gift rules.
cite: Mother Jones reporting (2010); CREW ethics complaints; Office of Congressional Ethics review reported by Roll Call, June 2010

n: Sen. John Ensign — C Street resident referred to Justice Department
d: Ensign, a longtime C Street resident, admitted in 2009 to an affair with the wife of his aide Doug Hampton. Sen. Tom Coburn, also linked to C Street, took part in negotiating a payment to the Hamptons. Ensign resigned in 2011, and the Senate Ethics Committee's special counsel found 'substantial credible evidence' that he broke Senate rules, including illegal payments and false statements to the FEC. The committee referred the case to the Justice Department and the FEC.
cite: U.S. Senate Select Committee on Ethics, report on Sen. John Ensign, May 2011

n: Gov. Mark Sanford — counselled at C Street before affair became public
d: Sanford, affiliated with the Fellowship during his years in Congress, admitted an extramarital affair in June 2009 and said he had sought counselling at the C Street house before the news broke. Former Rep. Chip Pickering's affair was also linked to his time living at C Street.
cite: Sanford's own public statements, June 2009; reference summary of Fellowship history

n: Maria Butina — used National Prayer Breakfast as Russian agent
rank: National Prayer Breakfast (event attended by the sitting president)
d: Butina, working under Russian official Alexander Torshin, helped arrange for Russians to attend the February 2017 National Prayer Breakfast, which the Fellowship organised; a planned private meeting between Torshin and President Trump was cancelled after a national security aide flagged him. She also worked through the NRA to build back channels to Republican figures. She pleaded guilty on 13 December 2018 to conspiracy to act as an agent of a foreign government and was sentenced on 26 April 2019 to 18 months. The FBI interviewed Fellowship organiser Doug Burleigh about his ties to her.
cite: United States v. Maria Butina, U.S. District Court for D.C., plea 13 Dec 2018, sentence 26 Apr 2019
org_note: The Fellowship was the host of the event she used, not the agent; the vehicle was a Russian state-directed network.

n: George H. W. Bush — Bonesman as Director of Central Intelligence
rank: Director of Central Intelligence; later President
d: George H. W. Bush (Yale, Skull and Bones 1948) served as the 11th Director of Central Intelligence in 1976–77 and as the 41st President in 1989–93. His father, Prescott Bush (Bones 1917), was a U.S. Senator from Connecticut. Membership comes from published Skull and Bones rosters; no forum has found the society directed his official acts.
cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official CIA and White House records of office

n: 2004 U.S. presidential race — both nominees were Bonesmen
rank: President (George W. Bush) and Secretary of State (John Kerry)
d: George W. Bush (Bones 1968) and John Kerry (Bones 1966) were the two major-party nominees in 2004. Bush served as the 43rd President; Kerry later became the 68th Secretary of State (2013–17). Both confirmed their membership publicly while declining to discuss the society.
cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office

n: William Howard Taft — Bonesman as President and Chief Justice
rank: Chief Justice of the United States; President; Secretary of War
d: William Howard Taft (Bones 1878) was Secretary of War, the 27th President (1909–13) and Chief Justice (1921–30). His father Alphonso Taft, Secretary of War, co-founded the society in 1832–33. Another Bonesman, Morrison Waite (1837), had also been Chief Justice.
cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office

n: Henry L. Stimson — Bonesman as Secretary of War and of State
rank: Secretary of War (twice) and Secretary of State
d: Henry L. Stimson (Bones 1888) served as Secretary of War under Taft, Secretary of State under Hoover, and Secretary of War again under Roosevelt and Truman from 1940 to 1945. Robert A. Lovett (Bones 1918), who later became Secretary of Defense, worked under him as Assistant Secretary of War for Air.
cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office

n: McGeorge Bundy — Bonesman as National Security Adviser
d: McGeorge Bundy (Bones 1940) was National Security Adviser to Presidents Kennedy and Johnson from 1961 to 1966. Other Bonesmen in national security posts include CIA officers Charles S. Whitehouse (1947) and William Sloane Coffin (1949), and F. Trubee Davison (1918), CIA Director of Personnel.
cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office

n: Steven Mnuchin — Bonesman as Treasury Secretary
d: Steven Mnuchin (Bones 1985) served as the 77th Secretary of the Treasury from 2017 to 2021. An earlier Bonesman, Franklin MacVeagh (1862), held the same post under Taft.
cite: Published Skull and Bones membership rosters; official records of office

n: Bohemian Grove — Manhattan Project planning meeting, 1942
rank: Wartime atomic bomb programme (S-1 Executive Committee, U.S. military)
d: In September 1942 the Bohemian Club's Grove in Monte Rio, California, hosted a meeting on early Manhattan Project planning. Ernest Lawrence and J. Robert Oppenheimer hosted it in the Clubhouse; attendees included members of the S-1 Executive Committee and representatives of universities, industry and the military. The U.S. Department of Energy's Manhattan Project history carries a photo of the S-1 Committee at the Grove.
cite: Gregg Herken, Brotherhood of the Bomb (2002), ch. 4; U.S. DOE/OSTI Manhattan Project history, S-1 Committee page

n: Herbert Hoover — Bohemian Club member as President
d: Herbert Hoover joined the Bohemian Club in 1913, served as President from 1929 to 1933, and was inducted into the club's Old Guard in 1953. In 1950 he brought Richard Nixon to the Grove as his guest; a 13 May 1971 White House tape records Nixon, then President, describing the Grove in crude terms.

n: Trilateral Commission — Carter, Mondale and 19 others in office
d: Jimmy Carter and Walter Mondale were members of the Trilateral Commission, founded in July 1973 by David Rockefeller with Zbigniew Brzezinski as organiser, before taking office in 1977. The Christian Science Monitor reported in 1980 that 17 other former commission members served in the Carter administration besides Carter, Mondale, Brzezinski and Harold Brown.
cite: Christian Science Monitor, 'The trilateral controversy', 17 Apr 1980; Trilateral Commission membership lists

arch.t: Trilateral Commission — 19/20 Carter Senior Appointments Were Members

n: Trilateral Commission — Brzezinski, Vance and Brown in Carter cabinet
rank: National Security Adviser, Secretary of State, Secretary of Defense
d: Zbigniew Brzezinski, the commission's founding director, became Carter's National Security Adviser. Cyrus Vance, a commission member, became Secretary of State, and Harold Brown, also a member, became Secretary of Defense. The appointments were raised during the 1980 campaign as evidence of the commission's reach.
cite: Christian Science Monitor, 17 Apr 1980; Trilateral Commission membership lists

n: CFR War and Peace Studies — secret planning for State Department
d: From 1939 to 1945 the Council on Foreign Relations ran a confidential programme, the War and Peace Studies, paid for entirely by the Rockefeller Foundation. Four groups (economic, security, territorial, political) produced 682 memoranda for the State Department, which were classified and circulated among government departments. Allen Dulles, later CIA director, led the security and armaments group. Council members outside the project were not told it existed.
cite: Council on Foreign Relations institutional history; Shoup and Minter, Imperial Brain Trust (1977)

n: BCCI — secret ownership of First American, Washington's largest bank
rank: Federal Reserve (bank approval) and the U.S. banking system
d: The Senate Foreign Relations subcommittee found that BCCI secretly controlled CCAH, which took over Financial General Bankshares in 1981 and renamed it First American. The Federal Reserve approved the takeover on assurances that BCCI was neither financing nor directing it; the report found those assurances false. The Treasury did not pass on CIA information about BCCI's ownership in 1985–86, and the Fed did not open a formal investigation until 3 January 1991.
cite: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, 'The BCCI Affair' (Kerry–Brown report), December 1992

n: Clark Clifford — First American chairman indicted in BCCI case
rank: Chairman of First American Bankshares; former Secretary of Defense
d: Clark Clifford, Secretary of Defense under Lyndon Johnson, chaired First American. In July 1992 he and his law partner Robert Altman were indicted by federal and New York prosecutors on fraud and bribery charges for helping BCCI gain control of the bank. In late 1993 New York Justice John Bradley dismissed the state charges because Clifford's 'age and ill health' prevented a trial.
cite: Indictments by the Manhattan District Attorney and U.S. Justice Department, July 1992; New York Supreme Court dismissal, Nov 1993

n: Robert Altman — First American president acquitted
d: Robert Altman, Clifford's partner and president of First American, was tried in New York on charges that he helped BCCI secretly take over the bank and took bribes. A Manhattan jury acquitted him in August 1993. The Senate report had separately found that Clifford and Altman hid their own BCCI-financed holdings of First American shares from regulators.
cite: New York State Supreme Court jury verdict, August 1993; Senate 'BCCI Affair' report, 1992

n: BCCI — cultivation of Bert Lance and Andrew Young
rank: Director of the Office of Management and Budget (Lance); UN Ambassador (Young)
d: The Senate report found that BCCI began cultivating U.S. political figures in 1977 by paying off the debts of Bert Lance, Carter's former budget director, with a $3.5 million loan. It cultivated Jimmy Carter, Jesse Jackson and Andrew Young, and described BCCI payments to Young while he was a public official as unusual and, by all appearances, improper. It also found BCCI hired former senators, congressmen, federal prosecutors and Fed lawyers, which helped slow investigations from 1988 to 1991.
cite: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, 'The BCCI Affair', December 1992

n: BCCI — CIA kept using the bank after knowing it was criminal
d: The Senate report found that by 1985 the CIA knew more about BCCI's U.S. goals than any other part of government, but shared it with Treasury and the OCC rather than the Fed or Justice Department. It found the CIA kept using BCCI and First American for its own operations after it knew BCCI was a criminal enterprise, and that its first information to Congress was untrue.
cite: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, 'The BCCI Affair', December 1992

arch.t: Bank of Credit and Commerce International — Abedi and Iqbal: BCCI Was the Largest Bank Fraud in History; CIA Used It for Covert Operations; 62 Countries Affected

n: BCCI — FDIC approved Pharaon's purchase of Independence Bank
d: The Senate report found that the FDIC approved Ghaith Pharaon's 1985 purchase of Independence Bank in Encino, California, knowing of his BCCI ties and that a senior BCCI officer would run the bank, without consulting the Fed or the OCC. It also found the OCC failed to pass on 1981 information that BCCI might be using nominees to buy U.S. banks.
cite: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, 'The BCCI Affair', December 1992
