n: John Singlaub — WACL chief used as cover for White House Contra aid
rank: White House National Security Council operation (Contra supply)
d: Retired Major General John Singlaub, removed from his Korea command by Carter in 1977, founded the U.S. Council for World Freedom in 1981 as the U.S. chapter of the World Anti-Communist League, and later chaired both. While Congress barred U.S. military aid to the Nicaraguan Contras, he raised private support for them and enlisted members of Congress. An Associated Press report found that 'Singlaub's private group became the public cover for the White House operation'.
cite: Associated Press reporting during the Iran-Contra affair, 1986–87; CIA reading-room press clippings

n: ALEC — Arizona SB 1070 drafted at an ALEC meeting
d: NPR reported that Arizona's immigration law SB 1070 was drafted at an American Legislative Exchange Council meeting in December 2009, attended by legislators and corporate members, and became an ALEC model bill. Arizona enacted it in 2010. In 2012 the U.S. Supreme Court held parts of it preempted by federal law.
cite: NPR investigation, October 2010; Arizona v. United States, 567 U.S. 387 (2012)

n: ALEC Exposed — 850 corporate-drafted model bills published
d: On 13 July 2011 the Center for Media and Democracy and The Nation published about 850 ALEC model bills from 30 years, with the legislators, corporations and states involved. About 1,000 ALEC-based bills were then being introduced each year, with roughly 20% enacted. ALEC's 'Stand Your Ground' model spread to about 30 states; after the 2012 killing of Trayvon Martin, more than 60 corporations and 34 legislators left ALEC. Common Cause filed an IRS complaint in April 2012 over its nonprofit status.
cite: Center for Media and Democracy, 'ALEC Exposed', 13 July 2011; Common Cause IRS complaint, April 2012

n: Gülen movement — about 200 congressional trips to Turkey
rank: Members of Congress and their staff
d: A USA Today investigation found that groups tied to Fethullah Gülen's movement had paid for about 200 trips to Turkey for members of Congress and staff since 2008; it identified 214 trips that appeared improperly disclosed. Some sponsors claimed nonprofit status that state and IRS records did not show, and five admitted a Gülen group in Turkey paid in-country costs. In July 2015 the House Ethics Committee, reviewing a related trip, found outside parties may have lied to it and referred the matter to the Justice Department.
cite: USA Today investigation, October 2015; House Committee on Ethics review, July 2015

n: Gülen-linked charter school staff — clustered campaign donations
d: USA Today found clusters of donations from Turkish Americans linked to the movement's U.S. charter schools, which number over 100. Sen. Kelly Ayotte refunded $43,100 given on a single day by 19 out-of-state donors, five of whom could not be located. Rep. Henry Cuellar received nine $2,500 donations on one day, including from a Toledo charter school teacher earning about $37,000 a year.
cite: USA Today investigation, November 2015 (via Religion News Service)

n: Linda Sun — Hochul deputy chief of staff charged as PRC agent
rank: Deputy chief of staff to the Governor of New York
d: Linda Sun was deputy chief of staff to Governor Kathy Hochul (2021–22) after serving in Andrew Cuomo's administration. She and her husband Chris Hu were charged on 3 September 2024 with acting as illegal agents of China, visa fraud and money laundering. Prosecutors allege she blocked contact between the governor's office and Taiwan's representatives, steered messaging on Uyghurs, and worked with the Henan Association of Eastern America, a united front–affiliated group, to arrange a Hochul visit to Henan. The trial ended in a mistrial on 22 December 2025 after the jury deadlocked; prosecutors said they would retry.
cite: United States v. Linda Sun and Chris Hu, U.S. District Court, Eastern District of New York (indicted 2024; mistrial Dec 2025)

n: Eileen Wang — Arcadia mayor pleads guilty as PRC agent
rank: Mayor and city council member, Arcadia, California
d: Eileen Wang was elected to the Arcadia City Council in November 2022 and later served as mayor. She was charged on 11 May 2026, resigned, and pleaded guilty to acting as an illegal agent of the People's Republic of China. With her then-fiancé Yaoning 'Mike' Sun she ran the website U.S. News Center and posted pro-Beijing material on the orders of PRC officials from 2020 to 2022, including an essay denying abuses in Xinjiang. Prosecutors said the conduct stopped after she was sworn in.
cite: U.S. Attorney's Office, Central District of California, charge 11 May 2026; guilty plea May 2026
org_note: prc_state = PRC government officials or intelligence acting through local proxies, where the forum did not name the United Front Work Department

n: Mike Sun — ran Arcadia council campaign on Beijing's orders
d: Yaoning 'Mike' Sun, campaign treasurer for Eileen Wang, organised a team to help elect her to the Arcadia City Council in November 2022 at the direction of the Chinese government. He pleaded guilty in October 2025 to acting as an illegal agent of a foreign government and is serving four years in federal prison. The Justice Department said Wang had dealt with John Chen, described as a high-level member of the PRC intelligence apparatus, who was sentenced in 2024 to 20 months.
cite: U.S. District Court, Central District of California, guilty plea Oct 2025
org_note: prc_state = PRC government officials or intelligence acting through local proxies, where the forum did not name the United Front Work Department

n: Christine Fang — suspected Chinese operative placed intern with congressman
rank: Office of a U.S. Representative on the House Intelligence Committee
d: Axios reported in December 2020 that Fang Fang (Christine Fang), believed by U.S. officials to be a Chinese intelligence operative, built ties with California politicians from 2011 to 2015. She fundraised for Rep. Eric Swalwell's campaign and placed at least one intern in his office, and kept close contact with the Chinese consulate in San Francisco. She left the U.S. abruptly in 2015. No charges were filed, and the reporting did not accuse Swalwell of wrongdoing.
cite: Axios investigation, December 2020; follow-up reporting
org_note: prc_state = PRC government officials or intelligence acting through local proxies, where the forum did not name the United Front Work Department

n: Han Dong — 2019 Liberal nomination and the PRC consulate
d: Special Rapporteur David Johnston found 'irregularities' in Han Dong's 2019 Liberal nomination in Don Valley North and a 'well-grounded suspicion' that they were tied to the PRC consulate in Toronto, but no evidence Dong knew. Intelligence said international students were bused to the vote; Dong said a school arranged the bus. Dong left the Liberal caucus in March 2023. Johnston found false the claim that Dong urged China to delay freeing Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor; the Hogue Commission report corroborated Dong's denial, and in August 2025 the Commissioner of Canada Elections found no breach of election law in the nomination.
cite: Independent Special Rapporteur on Foreign Interference (Johnston), first report, May 2023; Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference (Hogue Commission), 2024–25; Commissioner of Canada Elections, Aug 2025
org_note: prc_state = PRC government officials or intelligence acting through local proxies, where the forum did not name the United Front Work Department

n: NSICOP — parliamentarians 'witting' in foreign interference
d: Canada's National Security and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians reported in June 2024 that some unnamed parliamentarians were 'semi-witting or witting participants' in foreign states' interference. Listed conduct included accepting disguised funds from foreign missions or proxies, passing colleagues' views to foreign diplomats, and giving confidential government information to a known foreign intelligence officer. The report named China and Russia as the main perpetrators, with India, Pakistan and Iran also active. The Hogue Commission's final report in January 2025 found no evidence of 'traitors' in Parliament plotting with foreign states.
cite: National Security and Intelligence Committee of Parliamentarians, special report on foreign interference, 3 June 2024; Hogue Commission final report, 28 Jan 2025
org_note: foreign_state = state-directed influence networks of several countries (China, India and others) as described by NSICOP, not a single named organisation

n: Hugo Black — Klansman confirmed to the Supreme Court
rank: Associate Justice of the U.S. Supreme Court
d: Hugo Black joined the Ku Klux Klan in September 1923, resigned in July 1925 as he began his Senate run, and was welcomed back with a life membership in September 1926 during the campaign. Weeks after his 1937 confirmation to the Supreme Court, Ray Sprigle of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette exposed the membership and won a Pulitzer Prize. In a radio address on 1 October 1937 Black said: 'I did join the Klan. I later resigned. I never rejoined.' He served on the Court until 1971.
cite: Pittsburgh Post-Gazette (Ray Sprigle), Sept 1937; Black's radio address, 1 Oct 1937
org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (secret fraternal order with state-office reach in the 1920s)

arch.t: US Supreme Court Justice Was Documented KKK Member; Alabama KKK-Masonic Network Used as Political Infrastructure to Reach Highest Judicial Office

n: Robert Byrd — Klan chapter leader who became longest-serving senator
rank: U.S. Senator (West Virginia); West Virginia House of Delegates
d: Robert Byrd organised and led a 150-member Klan chapter in West Virginia in the early 1940s as its 'Exalted Cyclops', and was a recruiter ('Kleagle') until early 1943; a 1946 letter shows continued involvement. He was elected to the West Virginia House of Delegates in 1946, the U.S. House in 1952 and the Senate in 1958, and when he died in 2010 he had served in the Senate longer than anyone. He called the membership a 'sad mistake'.
cite: Byrd's own statements and 2005 memoir; PolitiFact review of the record, 2019
org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (secret fraternal order with state-office reach in the 1920s)

n: Indiana Klan — Governor Ed Jackson tried for Klan bribe offer
d: Indiana Grand Dragon D. C. Stephenson, whose Klan had about 250,000 members, backed Ed Jackson, who won the governorship in 1924. After Stephenson was sentenced to life in 1925 for the death of Madge Oberholtzer, he gave evidence to the Indianapolis Times. Jackson was tried in 1928 for offering Governor Warren McCray a $10,000 bribe in 1923 on Stephenson's behalf to fill offices with Klansmen; the trial ended with a hung jury and the statute of limitations barred a conviction. Stephenson's evidence also ended the career of Indianapolis Mayor John Duvall.
cite: Marion County criminal proceedings, 1927–28; Indianapolis Times investigation (Pulitzer Prize, 1928)
org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (secret fraternal order with state-office reach in the 1920s)

n: Denver — Klansman mayor made a Klansman police chief
rank: Mayor of Denver; Denver police chief
d: Historian Robert Alan Goldberg found that Benjamin Stapleton was Klan member number 1,128 when he ran for mayor of Denver in 1923. Under pressure he appointed Klansman William Candlish police chief, and the department became in effect a Klan body. In the 1924 recall election the Klan gave his campaign more than $15,000, and he told a Klan rally he would work 'heart and soul' for it. In 1925 Stapleton broke with the Klan and fired Candlish.
cite: Robert Alan Goldberg, Hooded Empire: The Ku Klux Klan in Colorado (1981)
org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (secret fraternal order with state-office reach in the 1920s)

n: Colorado Klan — Governor Morley and Senator Means, 1924
rank: Governor of Colorado; U.S. Senator; state House majority
d: In 1924 Colorado elected Clarence Morley, a Klan member who followed Grand Dragon John Galen Locke, as governor, and Rice Means to the U.S. Senate with open Klan support; the state House had a Klan majority. Klan-backed bills proposed firing Catholic and Jewish faculty at the University of Colorado, but a state Senate group led by Billy Adams blocked most of them. Morley and Locke both later went to jail.
cite: Robert Alan Goldberg, Hooded Empire (1981); Colorado Independent historical reporting
org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (secret fraternal order with state-office reach in the 1920s)

n: Oregon Klan — backed Governor Pierce and the anti-Catholic school law
d: In 1922 the Klan backed Democrat Walter M. Pierce after its own candidate lost the Republican primary; Pierce agreed to support the Klan's Compulsory Education Act and won with 57% of the vote. The act, passed by voters the same year, would have forced children into public schools and was aimed at Catholic schools. The U.S. Supreme Court struck it down in Pierce v. Society of Sisters (1925).
cite: Oregon election records, 1922; Pierce v. Society of Sisters, 268 U.S. 510 (1925)
org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (secret fraternal order with state-office reach in the 1920s)

n: Fruitland Park, Florida — deputy chief and officer tied to the Klan
rank: Deputy police chief and police officer
d: An unrelated FBI investigation found that Fruitland Park Deputy Chief David Borst and Officer George Hunnewell had been involved with the Ku Klux Klan between 2005 and 2009; three informants linked Hunnewell. The FBI told the Florida Department of Law Enforcement, which informed the police chief in 2014. Borst resigned and Hunnewell was fired, and the Lake County State Attorney's office began reviewing their arrests for racial profiling.
cite: Florida Department of Law Enforcement report based on FBI information, July 2014
org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (secret fraternal order with state-office reach in the 1920s)

n: FBI — white supremacist 'ghost skins' seeking police jobs
d: An October 2006 FBI intelligence assessment warned that white supremacist groups had a 'historical' interest in infiltrating or recruiting police, and that this 'can lead to investigative breaches'. It described 'ghost skins' who hide their beliefs, and at least one skinhead group urging them to seek police jobs. An April 2015 FBI counterterrorism policy guide said investigations of militia, white supremacist and sovereign citizen extremists had often found active links to law enforcement officers.
cite: FBI Intelligence Assessment, 'White Supremacist Infiltration of Law Enforcement', 17 Oct 2006; FBI Counterterrorism Policy Guide, April 2015 (published by The Intercept, 2017)
org_note: white_supremacist = organised white supremacist groups (Klan, skinhead and similar), as named by the FBI

n: Saskatchewan Klan — 1929 election that ousted the Liberals
d: Klan leaders claimed about 40,000 members in over 100 Saskatchewan towns by 1928. In the 1929 election, Conservatives and Progressives campaigned on issues the Klan had stirred among Protestant voters and defeated Premier J. G. Gardiner's Liberals; Gardiner accused the Klan of being a Conservative tool, which the Klan and Conservative leader J. T. M. Anderson denied. The Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan states no proof of an alliance existed, but a 1930 Klan convention praised the Anderson government's school and immigration changes.
cite: Encyclopedia of Saskatchewan (University of Regina), 'Ku Klux Klan'
org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (secret fraternal order with state-office reach in the 1920s)

n: Morgan affair — Masonic sheriff convicted in abduction of ex-Mason
rank: Sheriff of Niagara County, New York
d: William Morgan of Batavia, New York, announced a book exposing Masonic rituals; he was jailed in Canandaigua on minor charges on 11 September 1826, taken away by men on the night of 12 September, brought to Fort Niagara, and never seen again. Niagara County Sheriff Eli Bruce, a Mason, was removed from office and convicted of conspiracy for his part, serving 28 months; Loton Lawson, Nicholas Chesebro and Edward Sawyer were also convicted. Public anger at the light sentences led to the Anti-Masonic Party, which ran a presidential candidate in 1832.
cite: New York state criminal trials, 1827–1831 (People v. Bruce and related cases)
org_note: freemasonry here = Batavia and western New York lodges

arch.t: Anti-Masonic Party — First Third Party in US History; Formed After Murder of Military Witness; New York State Investigation Confirmed Masonic Obstruction of Justice

n: Know Nothings — secret order takes the Massachusetts legislature
rank: Governor and the entire state legislature of Massachusetts
d: The Know Nothing movement grew out of a secret nativist fraternal order, the Order of the Star Spangled Banner. In the 1854 Massachusetts election it won the governorship (Henry Gardner), all 40 state Senate seats and all but 3 of the House seats. The 1855 legislature passed laws to deport poor or mentally ill Irish residents and to 'inspect' Catholic schools and convents, and required Protestant Bible readings in public schools.
cite: Massachusetts election returns, 1854; Massachusetts legislative records, 1855
org_note: know_nothing = the Order of the Star Spangled Banner, a secret nativist fraternal order and its American Party

n: Tammany Society — Grand Sachem 'Boss' Tweed convicted
rank: New York state senator and city Commissioner of Public Works
d: William M. Tweed became Grand Sachem of the Tammany Society in 1863 and controlled New York City government while holding seats in Congress, the county Board of Supervisors and the state Senate, and serving as Commissioner of Public Works. A New York aldermen's committee in 1877 estimated he stole $25–45 million from the city. At his retrial in November 1873 he was convicted on 204 of 220 counts and sentenced to 12 years and a $12,750 fine; a higher court cut the sentence to one year.
cite: New York Court of Oyer and Terminer, People v. Tweed, Nov 1873; New York Board of Aldermen report, 1877
org_note: tammany = the Society of St. Tammany, a fraternal society with ritual offices (sachems) that ran the New York Democratic machine

n: Orange Order — Toronto city hall run by Orangemen for a century
rank: Mayor of Toronto and city council
d: By 1844 six of Toronto's ten aldermen were Orangemen, and 20 of its 23 mayors in the 19th century were members of the Loyal Orange Lodge. Every Toronto mayor in the first half of the 20th century was an Orangeman, and in 1942 16 of 23 council members were. The run ended in 1954, when Nathan Phillips beat Orange leader Leslie Saunders; William Dennison (1967–72) was the last Orange mayor.
cite: William J. Smyth, Toronto, the Belfast of Canada: The Orange Order and the Shaping of Municipal Culture (University of Toronto Press, 2015)
org_note: orange_order = Loyal Orange Institution (Protestant fraternal lodge)

n: Orange Order — four Canadian prime ministers, one a Grand Master
d: Four prime ministers were Orangemen: Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir John Abbott, Sir Mackenzie Bowell and John Diefenbaker. Bowell, prime minister in 1894–96, was a past Grand Master of the Orange Order in British North America.
cite: Orange Order in Canada membership records as summarised in academic and reference histories
org_note: orange_order = Loyal Orange Institution (Protestant fraternal lodge)

n: Ordre de Jacques-Cartier — secret order placing francophones in posts
rank: Senior federal public service posts; Montreal mayor's office
d: The Ordre de Jacques-Cartier, called 'La Patente', was founded on 22 October 1926 in Vanier (now part of Ottawa) to advance French Canadians and counter the Orange Order, Freemasons and Knights of Columbus. It worked by infiltration, recruiting decision-makers including Montreal mayor Jean Drapeau and journalist-politician Pierre Laporte, and used the network to get francophones appointed to key federal public service jobs. It peaked at 11,300 members in 1955–56. After a former insider, Roger Cyr, exposed it in a 1964 book, it dissolved in February 1965.
cite: The Canadian Encyclopedia, 'Ordre de Jacques Cartier'; Roger Cyr, La Patente (1964)
org_note: jacques_cartier = Ordre de Jacques-Cartier, a secret French-Canadian Catholic society (1926–65)

n: Commons Home Affairs Committee — Freemasonry in police and judiciary
rank: judges, magistrates, police officers, Crown prosecutors
d: In March 1997 the House of Commons Home Affairs Committee published 'Freemasonry in the Police and the Judiciary'. It recommended that police officers, judges, magistrates and Crown prosecutors be required to register membership of the Freemasons or any other secret society, stating that 'nothing so much undermines public confidence in public institutions' as public servants belonging to a secret society. The report counted nearly 350,000 masons in 7,835 lodges in England and Wales (United Grand Lodge of England). The Association of Chief Police Officers refused to back a register; Lord Chancellor Lord Mackay opposed compulsory disclosure for judges.
cite: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee, 'Freemasonry in the Police and the Judiciary', Third Report 1996–97 (March 1997)

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

n: UK masonic declaration rule for new judges, police, prosecutors
rank: new judicial, police, CPS, probation and prison appointees
d: After the 1997 Committee report, Home Secretary Jack Straw's government set a policy, stated to the Commons by minister Alun Michael on 6 May 1998, that all new appointees to the judiciary, the police, legally qualified Crown Prosecution Service staff and the probation and prison services must declare membership of the Freemasons. Serving office holders were only invited to declare on voluntary registers. In March 1999 Home Office minister Paul Boateng told Parliament that disclosure by existing police staff was 'entirely voluntary at present'.
cite: Hansard, HC Deb 6 May 1998 vol 311 cc838–44 (adjournment debate, Freemasons); HC Deb 23 March 1999 written answer

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

n: Grand Lodge and the West Midlands Serious Crime Squad list
rank: detectives of the West Midlands Serious Crime Squad
d: The Home Affairs Committee's second report on Freemasonry (May 1999) said it obtained the United Grand Lodge of England's cooperation only 'through compulsion' after 'months of prevarication and obfuscation'. The Grand Lodge needed five attempts to produce a list of masons in the West Midlands Serious Crime Squad, a police unit disbanded in 1989, and the Committee doubted the final list was complete. The Committee estimated masonic membership at 5–10% of professional judges and 5–20% of magistrates, and called the government's voluntary police register inadequate.
cite: House of Commons Home Affairs Committee, Freemasonry in Public Life, Second Report 1998–99 (May 1999), as reported by SQUALL magazine

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

n: Straw ends masonic declaration for judges, 2009
d: On 5 November 2009 Justice Secretary Jack Straw issued a written ministerial statement ending the rule, in force since 1998, that applicants for judicial office declare Masonic membership. The United Grand Lodge of England had made representations in May 2009 citing the European Court of Human Rights cases Grande Oriente d'Italia di Palazzo Giustiniani v Italy (no. 1 and no. 2). The Ministry of Justice figures given were 205 masons among 3,808 judges (5.4%) and 1,900 among 29,702 magistrates (6.4%); the review found no evidence of impropriety arising from judges being masons.
cite: Written ministerial statement, Secretary of State for Justice, 5 November 2009

n: Daniel Morgan Independent Panel — Freemasonry in the Met
d: The Daniel Morgan Independent Panel reported in June 2021 on the 1987 axe murder of private investigator Daniel Morgan and the Metropolitan Police's handling of it. The Panel found no evidence that Masonic channels were used corruptly in the case. It nonetheless said membership was 'not conducive to a culture of integrity' and recommended that police officers and staff be required to disclose Freemason membership confidentially.
cite: The Report of the Daniel Morgan Independent Panel, HC 11, June 2021

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

n: Met Police makes officers declare Freemasonry; High Court upholds
d: The Metropolitan Police decided on 18 November 2025, and announced on 11 December 2025, that Freemasonry and similar hierarchical organisations would be declarable associations for its officers and staff. By February 2026, 397 officers and staff had declared membership, most of them Freemasons. The United Grand Lodge of England sought judicial review; on 17 February 2026 Mr Justice Chamberlain refused permission on all grounds, finding the requirement a proportionate way to maintain public trust in policing.
cite: R (United Grand Lodge of England) v Commissioner of Police of the Metropolis [2026] EWHC 330 (Admin); Judiciary press summary, 17 February 2026

n: Christine Lee — MI5 interference alert to Parliament
rank: Members of Parliament (Barry Gardiner MP's office)
d: On 13 January 2022 MI5 issued an interference alert, circulated by the Speaker to MPs, stating that solicitor Christine Lee had acted covertly in coordination with the Chinese Communist Party's United Front Work Department. Labour MP Barry Gardiner had received donations from her, the last in June 2020, and her son worked in his office as diary manager until he resigned that week. Lee challenged the alert; on 17 December 2024 the Investigatory Powers Tribunal ruled that MI5 had issued it for legitimate reasons.
cite: MI5 Interference Alert, 13 January 2022; Investigatory Powers Tribunal judgment, 17 December 2024

n: Yang Tengbo — excluded from UK over CCP work; Prince Andrew link
rank: Duke of York (member of the royal family)
d: In March 2023 Home Secretary Suella Braverman excluded businessman Yang Tengbo from the UK for 'covert and deceptive activity' on behalf of the Chinese Communist Party; the Home Office believed he may have worked for the United Front Work Department. Through Prince Andrew he had been a guest at royal residences, and he had met former prime ministers David Cameron and Theresa May. In December 2024 the Special Immigration Appeals Commission upheld the exclusion; the judges said there was 'not an abundance of evidence' of United Front links but found he had played down his ties to the Party.
cite: Home Office exclusion order, March 2023; Special Immigration Appeals Commission judgment, December 2024

n: Le Cercle chaired by sitting Foreign Affairs Committee MPs
rank: members of the Commons Foreign Affairs Committee
d: Le Cercle, a private foreign-policy club founded in 1952–53, was chaired in the UK by Julian Amery (1985–93), Jonathan Aitken (1993–96), Norman Lamont (1996–2008), Michael Ancram (2008–13), Rory Stewart (2013–14) and Nadhim Zahawi (2015–18). PoliticsHome reported in 2019 that Stewart and Zahawi chaired the group while sitting on the Foreign Affairs Select Committee and did not declare the chairmanship to Parliament.
cite: PoliticsHome (John Johnston), 2019; David Teacher, Rogue Agents: The Cercle and the 6I in the Private Cold War (2003)

n: Ruth Kelly — Education Secretary, Opus Dei spiritual support
rank: Secretary of State for Education and Skills
d: Ruth Kelly became Education Secretary in December 2004. In January 2005, on the BBC's Breakfast with Frost, she said she receives spiritual support from Opus Dei. She did not say whether she was a supernumerary (committed lay member).
cite: BBC Breakfast with Frost interview, January 2005, as reported by Catholic News Agency/EWTN, 24 January 2005

n: Taoiseach John A. Costello — Knights of St Columbanus member
org_note: Knights of Saint Columbanus: Catholic fraternal order founded in Ireland in 1915, long described as secretive.
d: John A. Costello, Taoiseach of the first Inter-Party government from 1948, was a member of the Knights of Saint Columbanus; with other cabinet members who were also Knights, his government gave Maynooth seminary a special annual grant. Labour parliamentary chairman William Davin TD, also a Knight, is reported to have countered support within government for the Mother and Child health scheme, which Archbishop John Charles McQuaid opposed. These accounts rest chiefly on John Cooney's biography of McQuaid (1999) and Anthony Jordan's biography of Costello (2007).
cite: John Cooney, John Charles McQuaid: Ruler of Catholic Ireland (1999); Anthony Jordan, John A. Costello 1891–1976 (2007)

n: Justice Minister Seán MacEoin — Knight reporting to the Order
org_note: Knights of Saint Columbanus: Catholic fraternal order founded in Ireland in 1915.
d: Seán MacEoin, Minister for Justice in 1948, was a member of the Knights of Saint Columbanus and reportedly assured the Order's Supreme Council that efforts would be made to prevent conflict between Church and State. The Order also had members in the civil service, including Dublin City chief planner Michael O'Brien and the Taxing Master of the Courts, Henry B. O'Hanlon.
cite: John Cooney, John Charles McQuaid: Ruler of Catholic Ireland (1999)

n: Affaire des Fiches — Grand Orient files on army officers
rank: Minister of War (General Louis André) and army promotions
d: Between 1901 and 1904 the War Ministry of General Louis André used reports gathered through Grand Orient de France lodges to sort officers for promotion: Catholic and nationalist officers were filed as 'Carthage' and generally blocked, republican officers as 'Corinth' and favoured. Historian Serge Berstein counted 18,818 files written between September 1901 and October 1903, out of about 27,000 active officers; Grand Orient secretary-general Narcisse-Amédée Vadecard received the reports and Captain Henri Mollin ran the system in André's office. Deputy Jean Guyot de Villeneuve exposed it in the Chamber on 28 October 1904; André resigned on 15 November 1904 and the Combes government fell on 15 January 1905.
cite: Chamber of Deputies session, 28 October 1904; Serge Berstein (historian), cited in standard histories of the Third Republic

n: Service d'Action Civique — Gaullist militia dissolved after Auriol
org_note: Service d'Action Civique (SAC): Gaullist security association created 1960, led in practice by Jacques Foccart; a parallel network that recruited police officers.
d: The SAC was founded in January 1960 by Jacques Foccart, de Gaulle's adviser on Africa, and Pierre Debizet; its members included Charles Pasqua. On the night of 18 July 1981 police inspector Jacques Massié, the SAC's leader in Marseille, and his family were murdered at Auriol by an SAC commando. A National Assembly commission of inquiry reported in 1982, and the government dissolved the SAC by decree no. 82-670 of 3 August 1982 under the law on private militias. On 1 May 1985 five commando members were sentenced to terms from 15 years to life.
cite: National Assembly commission of inquiry on the SAC, report 1982; Decree no. 82-670 of 3 August 1982; assize court verdict, 1 May 1985

n: OAS — secret army formed by French generals
org_note: Organisation armée secrète: clandestine organisation formed in 1961 by French army officers to block Algerian independence.
rank: army general, former commander-in-chief in Algeria
d: Generals Raoul Salan, Maurice Challe, André Zeller and Edmond Jouhaud organised the failed Algiers putsch of April 1961, after which Salan became chief of the clandestine Organisation armée secrète. Salan was sentenced to death in absentia, arrested in April 1962, tried for treason and sentenced to life imprisonment. He was pardoned and released in June 1968 and later amnestied by Parliament and reinstated as a general in 1982.
cite: French treason verdict against Salan, 1962; pardon June 1968

n: Manuel Valls — Grand Orient de France lodge member 1989–2005
rank: mayor of Évry and National Assembly deputy (later Interior Minister and Prime Minister)
d: According to L'Express, Manuel Valls was initiated into the Grand Orient de France lodge 'Ni maîtres ni dieux' on 26 April 1989, moved in 1995 to 'L'Infini maçonnique', a lodge founded by Alain Bauer, and his resignation was recorded in 2005. During that period he became mayor of Évry (2001) and a National Assembly deputy (2002); he later served as Interior Minister (2012) and Prime Minister (2014). Valls declined to answer L'Express's questions.
cite: L'Express, reproduced by Seneweb

n: Le Cercle founded by Antoine Pinay, with Adenauer and Strauss
d: Le Cercle (first called the Cercle Pinay) was set up in 1952–53 by Antoine Pinay, French Prime Minister in 1952, and Jean Violet. Historian Adrian Hänni counts West German Chancellor Konrad Adenauer and Franz Josef Strauss, later West German Defence Minister, as co-founders. Brian Crozier, chairman 1980–85, presented an agenda listing 'undercover financial transactions for political aims' among the group's objectives (The Independent, 1997).
cite: Adrian Hänni (historian); David Teacher, Rogue Agents (2003); The Independent, 1997

n: Belgian Senate inquiry into Gladio (SDRA VIII, STC/Mob)
rank: military intelligence (SDRA VIII) and State Security (STC/Mob)
d: Belgium's stay-behind network was made public on 7 November 1990 and the government decided to disband it on 23 November 1990. A Senate commission chaired by Senator Roger Lallemand held 57 meetings and heard 37 witnesses between January and July 1991. It described a military section (SDRA VIII) under the military intelligence service and the Defence Minister, a civilian section (STC/Mob) under State Security and the Justice Minister, and a coordination secretariat (SDRA XI) funded by secret NATO payments. It criticised the refusal to name civilian operatives; former SDRA head Paul Detrembleur refused to testify on the secretariat.
cite: Belgian Senate Commission of Inquiry into the stay-behind network (Lallemand commission), report 1991

arch.t: Italy — Operation Gladio: NATO Stay-Behind Network Used for Domestic Terrorism; 'Strategy of Tension'

n: Westland New Post — far-right group with gendarmes and State Security
org_note: Westland New Post: Belgian far-right paramilitary group founded by Paul Latinus with Front de la Jeunesse members.
rank: Gendarmerie (Diane anti-terror unit) and State Security
d: Westland New Post founder Paul Latinus had been an informant for Belgium's State Security service, and State Security agent Christian Smets admitted training members in surveillance; State Security had a mole in the group from 1981 but did not tell police. Former gendarme Martin Leukeu said he was recruited into 'Group G', a neo-Nazi cell inside the Gendarmerie linked to the WNP, and gendarme Madani Bouhouche was named as a member. NATO documents from the Evere transmission centre, passed by member Michel Libert, were found at member Marcel Barbier's home. A parliamentary inquiry found no proof of a conspiracy behind the Brabant killings.
cite: Belgian parliamentary inquiries into the Nijvel (Brabant) gang and banditry; David Teacher, Rogue Agents (2003)

n: Dutch stay-behind (I&O) — Lubbers tells parliament, 1990
rank: secret Intelligence (I) and Operations (O) units of the state
d: In November 1990 Prime Minister Ruud Lubbers told parliament the Dutch stay-behind network was being given a new direction. In April 1992 Defence Minister Relus ter Beek wrote to members that it had become obsolete. It operated from 1945 to 1992 with several hundred recruited citizens and dozens of weapons caches; according to de Volkskrant, the government covered up the theft of some guns later used by members of Willem Holleeder's gang. In February 2021 Prime Minister Mark Rutte and Defence Minister Ank Bijleveld acknowledged the group in a letter to relatives, and in 2022 the government asked the Netherlands Institute for Military History to inventory its records.
cite: Statement of Prime Minister Lubbers to the Tweede Kamer, November 1990; Rutte–Bijleveld letter, February 2021

n: Bommeleeër trial — gendarmerie officers accused of 18 bombings
rank: officers of the Gendarmerie mobile brigade (BMG)
d: In 2013 two former members of the Gendarmerie's mobile brigade (BMG), Jos Wilmes and Marc Scheer, went on trial for 18 bombings in Luxembourg between May 1984 and April 1986, targeting sites such as Cegedel power pylons. The defence argued the attacks were the work of NATO's Stay Behind network; a 2006 recording of Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker, Justice Minister Luc Frieden and intelligence (SREL) chief Marco Mille speculating about Stay Behind involvement was played in court. Prosecutor Robert Biever said 88 of 125 pieces of evidence had disappeared. The trial was suspended in 2014; later, eight former gendarmerie and public-force officers were referred to trial for false testimony, but not for the bombings.
cite: Luxembourg District Court, 9th criminal chamber, Bommeleeër trial (2013–14); Council Chamber referral order

n: Swiss parliament (PUK EMD) uncovers secret army P-26
d: A parliamentary commission of inquiry into the Defence Department (PUK EMD), set up in March 1990 after the secret files scandal, reported in November 1990 that a secret cadre organisation, P-26, existed outside parliamentary and government control. It was led from October 1979 by Colonel Efrem Cattelan, organised in about 40 regions with up to about 1,000 members (about 300 had taken courses by 1990), and cost about 54.3 million francs of federal money from 1979 to 1990. P-26 was dissolved in November 1990.
cite: Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the Federal Military Department (PUK EMD), report of 17 November 1990

n: Cornu report — P-26 cooperation with British services
d: Judge Pierre Cornu's roughly 100-page report on P-26 found that it lacked political or legal legitimacy and that its cooperation with British intelligence services was extensive. Only a 17-page summary, 'P-26 not part of an international network', was published on 19 September 1991; Defence Minister Kaspar Villiger refused to release the full report, which remains sealed until 2041 despite parliamentary motions in 2005 and 2008.
cite: Report of Judge Pierre Cornu to the Federal Council, 1991 (summary published 19 September 1991)

n: German government confirms BND stay-behind, orders dissolution
d: Answering a parliamentary question from Ingrid Köppe and the Bündnis 90/Die Grünen group, the federal government stated on 17 May 1991 that the dissolution of the stay-behind organisation had been ordered and that the BND, which ran it, would complete it before the end of 1991. The government said no staff of the organisation had been deployed in the former GDR and disputed the European Parliament's resolution of 22 November 1990 as resting on incorrect premises for Germany.
cite: Deutscher Bundestag, Drucksache 12/560, 17 May 1991 (answer to Kleine Anfrage 12/393)

n: Reuss group — sitting Berlin judge and ex-MP in coup plot
org_note: Patriotic Union / 'Council' around Heinrich XIII Prinz Reuss: Reichsbürger network charged by the Federal Prosecutor as a terrorist association.
rank: judge at the Berlin Regional Court; former Bundestag member
d: Birgit Malsack-Winkemann, a judge at the Berlin Regional Court and AfD Bundestag member for about four years, was arrested in the December 2022 raids on the group around Heinrich XIII Prinz Reuss; prosecutors say she was to be justice minister in a new government, and she admits being on its 'Council' with responsibility for justice. As a former MP she could bring up to six people into the Reichstag and admits leading co-accused through it twice in September 2022. Prosecutors say up to 16 people, mainly from the KSK and other special units, were to storm the Reichstag. Twenty-six defendants are on trial in Frankfurt, Stuttgart and Munich since 2024; no verdict had been reported as of April 2026.
cite: Federal Prosecutor General indictment; Federal Court of Justice detention ruling (2023); Higher Regional Court Frankfurt trial from May 2024

n: Voice of Europe — Bystron investigated over Russian-network cash
org_note: Voice of Europe: Prague-based pro-Russian outlet and influence network financed by Viktor Medvedchuk, sanctioned by the Czech government in March 2024.
rank: Bundestag member, then Member of the European Parliament
d: In April 2024 the Munich prosecutor's office opened a bribery and money-laundering investigation into AfD Bundestag member Petr Bystron after Czech intelligence (BIS) briefed the Czech parliament's intelligence committee on a recording of a Prague meeting with Artem Marchevsky in which about €20,000 was reportedly handed over. The Bundestag lifted his immunity and police searched his parliamentary office in May 2024. After he became an MEP, the European Parliament lifted his immunity on 6 May 2025. Bystron denies receiving money; no charge had been reported.
cite: Munich I Public Prosecutor's investigation; Bundestag immunity decision (May 2024); European Parliament immunity vote, 6 May 2025

n: Czech government sanctions Voice of Europe network
org_note: Voice of Europe: Prague-based pro-Russian outlet and influence network financed by Viktor Medvedchuk.
d: On 27 March 2024 Petr Fiala's government put Voice of Europe, Viktor Medvedchuk and Artyom Marchevsky on the Czech national sanctions list. The BIS security service said the network was financed from Russia and operated on Czech territory. Deník N, citing a foreign ministry source, reported that payments went to politicians from Belgium, France, Germany, Hungary, the Netherlands and Poland, in particular the AfD.
cite: Czech government sanctions decision, 27 March 2024; Security Information Service (BIS) statement

n: Thule Society members Hess and Frank enter Nazi government
rank: Deputy Führer (Hess); Reich minister and later Governor-General of occupied Poland (Frank)
d: The Thule Society was formed in Munich in 1918 around Rudolf von Sebottendorff's lodge. Historian Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke states that Rudolf Hess and Hans Frank were members before they rose in the Nazi Party, while Alfred Rosenberg, Dietrich Eckart and Gottfried Feder were only guests. He calls longer membership lists that include Hitler and others 'spurious'. Hess became Deputy Führer in 1933; Frank became a Reich minister and, from 1939, Governor-General of occupied Poland.
cite: Nicholas Goodrick-Clarke, The Occult Roots of Nazism (1985, later editions)

n: Austria's OeWSGV — Olah's secret army, later Interior Minister
rank: Minister of the Interior; trade union federation (ÖGB) president
d: In 1951 trade unionist Franz Olah raised a secret anti-communist paramilitary force under the cover name Österreichischer Wander-, Sport- und Geselligkeitsverein (OeWSGV), funded through the camouflage firms Atlanta and Omnia; it operated until 1964. Olah became ÖGB president in 1959 and Interior Minister in 1963, resigning in September 1964 over misuse of union funds. In his 1969 trial, which ended in a one-year sentence for fraud, he defended the OeWSGV as a patriotic measure. In 1991 the defence and interior ministers denied such an army had existed.
cite: Vienna criminal court, Olah trial 1969; statements of Austrian defence and interior ministers, 1991

n: US discloses 80+ hidden stay-behind arms caches in Austria
d: In January 1996 reports revealed that more than 80 caches of US weapons, including machine guns, explosives, mortars and radio equipment, had been hidden in Austria in the early Cold War for a stay-behind network; Austrian officials said they had not been told. US Ambassador Swanee Hunt then made Cold War US intelligence documents public showing that the US created over one hundred secret weapons depots during its occupation. The Austrian government commissioned historian Oliver Rathkolb to seek further US documents; the CIA replied that none were available.
cite: Boston Globe/Seattle Times, 21 January 1996; US Embassy Vienna document release, 1996

n: Finland's Weapons Cache Case — officers hide arms after 1944
org_note: Asekätkentä (Weapons Cache Case): secret network organised from Finnish Military Headquarters after the 1944 armistice to hide weapons for a guerrilla force.
rank: officers of the operational department, Finnish Military Headquarters
d: After the Moscow Armistice of 19 September 1944, Colonel Valo Nihtilä and Lieutenant Colonel Usko Haahti of the operational department of Finnish Military Headquarters began hiding weapons across the country, planned for 8,000 men but estimated to equip about 35,000. Between 5,000 and 10,000 people took part. The scheme was exposed in spring 1945 to the Allied Control Commission; the security police questioned more than 5,000 people and, under a retroactive law of January 1947, 1,488 people were convicted, most receiving 1–4 months in prison.
cite: Finnish courts under the Act of January 1947; Valpo (State Police) investigation

n: IB affair — secret intelligence bureau tied to Social Democrats
org_note: Informationsbyrån (IB): Swedish military intelligence unit with no official status, which registered and infiltrated the far left; directed by Birger Elmér.
rank: military intelligence; Prime Minister and Social Democratic party secretary
d: On 3 May 1973 Jan Guillou and Peter Bratt revealed in Folket i Bild/Kulturfront that IB, a secret military intelligence bureau with no official status, monitored and registered people with far-left views and infiltrated left-wing groups, including break-ins at the Communist Party's offices. Former security chief P.G. Vinge wrote that IB director Birger Elmér had regular contact with Prime Minister Olof Palme and reported to Social Democratic party secretary Sven Andersson; Palme denied any link. The journalists, not IB staff, were convicted of espionage on 4 January 1974. A 2002 public inquiry report, 'Rikets säkerhet och den personliga integriteten', set out IB's operations.
cite: Swedish court verdict, 4 January 1974; Swedish government inquiry report 'Rikets säkerhet och den personliga integriteten' (2002)

n: Ordo Iuris founder Stępkowski made deputy foreign minister
org_note: Ordo Iuris Institute for Legal Culture: Polish Catholic-conservative legal think tank founded in 2013 by the Christian Culture Association.
d: Aleksander Stępkowski co-founded Ordo Iuris in 2013 and chaired its management board in 2013–2015. In November 2015 the new Law and Justice government of Beata Szydło appointed him deputy foreign minister for legal and treaty affairs; he left the Ordo Iuris chair in December 2015. He was recalled in August 2016. In 2016 Ordo Iuris drafted a near-total abortion ban that the Sejm rejected on 6 October 2016 after nationwide protests.
cite: Polish government appointment records; Forsal; Ruleoflaw.pl

n: Ordo Iuris co-founder heads Polish Supreme Court (acting)
org_note: Ordo Iuris Institute for Legal Culture: Polish Catholic-conservative legal think tank founded in 2013.
rank: acting First President of the Supreme Court
d: Aleksander Stępkowski, Ordo Iuris co-founder and board president in 2013–2015 and 2016–2017, was nominated to the Supreme Court in 2018 by the reconstituted National Council of the Judiciary and appointed in February 2019 with no prior judicial experience. On 15 May 2020, after Kamil Zaradkiewicz resigned, President Andrzej Duda entrusted him with the duties of acting First President of the Supreme Court.
cite: Presidential decision of 15 May 2020; Ruleoflaw.pl

n: Serbian officers' May Coup kills King Alexander Obrenović
org_note: The 1903 officer conspiracy led by Dragutin Dimitrijević (Apis) was the core from which the Black Hand (Unification or Death) was formed in 1911.
d: On 11 June 1903 (29 May Old Style), Dragutin Dimitrijević 'Apis' and junior officers stormed the royal palace in Belgrade and killed King Alexander Obrenović, Queen Draga and others, bringing the Karađorđević dynasty to the throne. In 1911 Dimitrijević and fellow officers founded the secret society Unification or Death (Black Hand), which Britannica describes as dominating the army and pressuring the government through intimidation.
cite: Encyclopaedia Britannica; standard histories of Serbia

n: Apis — Black Hand leader as Serbian military intelligence chief
rank: chief of intelligence, Serbian General Staff
d: Black Hand leader Dragutin Dimitrijević was appointed chief of General Staff intelligence of the Serbian army in 1913. Many scholars hold that he sanctioned the 1914 Sarajevo assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand, with the Black Hand supplying weapons and training. In 1917 Prince Regent Alexander had him court-martialled at Salonika for treason; he and two others were shot on 26 June 1917 and more than 200 members were imprisoned. In 1953 the Supreme Court of Serbia retried the case and acquitted them for lack of proof of the alleged plot against the Prince Regent.
cite: Salonika court-martial, 1917; Supreme Court of Serbia retrial, 1953; Encyclopaedia Britannica

n: White Hand officer Petar Živković becomes Prime Minister
org_note: White Hand (Bela ruka): secret Serbian officers' group founded in 1912 by Petar Živković in opposition to the Black Hand.
rank: Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Yugoslavia
d: The White Hand was founded in 1912 at the Hotel Paris in Belgrade by officers led by Petar Živković, as a rival to the Black Hand; Crown Prince Alexander later joined. After the Black Hand was broken at the 1917 Salonika trial, the White Hand gained influence over Alexander. When King Alexander I suspended the constitution on 6 January 1929 with White Hand officers' support, General Živković was appointed Prime Minister, serving until 1932.
cite: Srejović, Gavrilović & Ćirković (eds.), Istorija srpskog naroda (1983); Milivoje Alimpić, Solunski front (1967)

n: Kerensky — Masonic Grand Orient leader and Provisional Govt PM
org_note: Lodge: Grand Orient of Russia's Peoples, an irregular Masonic body formed from Grand Orient de France lodges and openly separate from 1912.
rank: Minister of Justice, Minister of War, then Prime Minister
d: Alexander Kerensky was Secretary General of the Grand Orient of Russia's Peoples from 1916 to mid-1917, succeeding Nikolai Nekrasov, who held the post in 1912–13 and 1914–16. In 1917 Kerensky served in the Provisional Government as Minister of Justice (March), Minister for War (May) and Prime Minister (July). Historians describe most of the lodge's members as associated with the Provisional Government.
cite: Academic histories of the Russian Revolution (Alpha History summary; Grand Orient of Russia's Peoples records as published by historians)

n: Roberto Calvi — Banco Ambrosiano chairman found hanged
rank: chairman of Italy's largest private bank
d: Calvi, chairman of Banco Ambrosiano and a member of Licio Gelli's P2 lodge, was found hanging under Blackfriars Bridge, London, on 18 June 1982. A first London inquest (1982) said suicide; a second (1983) returned an open verdict. A forensic report for an Italian court (2002) concluded he was murdered. Five defendants, including Pippo Calò and Flavio Carboni, were tried in Rome and acquitted on 6 June 2007 for insufficient evidence, while the court treated the death as murder.
cite: Rome Court of Assizes, verdict of 6 June 2007; London inquests 1982 and 1983

n: Calvi convicted for illegal export of $27m
d: In 1981, months after his name appeared on the seized P2 membership list, Calvi was sentenced to four years (suspended) and fined US$19.8 million for moving US$27 million out of Italy illegally. He was released pending appeal and kept his post as chairman of Banco Ambrosiano.
cite: Milan court, 1981 currency-export verdict

arch.t: Vatican-Masonic Network — Roberto Calvi Murder; Banco Ambrosiano Collapse; P2 Lodge Member Directed Vatican Bank Investments (PROVEN)

n: Banco Ambrosiano collapse — $1.3bn hole
rank: private bank used by P2 members
d: In 1982 Banco Ambrosiano could not account for about US$1.287 billion, much of it routed through offshore companies tied to the Vatican Bank (IOR), its main shareholder. The Bank of Italy had warned in a 1978 report. The bank was replaced by Nuovo Banco Ambrosiano in August 1982. In April 1992 a Milan court convicted 33 people of fraud; P2 head Licio Gelli's sentence was set at 12 years, confirmed by the Court of Cassation in April 1998.
cite: Milan Tribunal, fraudulent-bankruptcy verdict April 1992; Court of Cassation April 1998

arch.t: Vatican-Masonic Network — Roberto Calvi Murder; Banco Ambrosiano Collapse; P2 Lodge Member Directed Vatican Bank Investments (PROVEN)

n: Vatican Bank pays Ambrosiano creditors (1984)
rank: Vatican Bank (IOR), state bank of the Holy See
d: The IOR denied legal liability for Banco Ambrosiano's collapse but acknowledged 'moral involvement' and paid US$224 million to about 120 creditor banks under a 1984 agreement. The IOR had been Ambrosiano's main shareholder and was tied to the offshore companies that held the missing funds. Some press accounts give a figure up to about US$244 million.
cite: Settlement between the IOR and Banco Ambrosiano creditors, Geneva, 1984

arch.t: Vatican-Masonic Network — Roberto Calvi Murder; Banco Ambrosiano Collapse; P2 Lodge Member Directed Vatican Bank Investments (PROVEN)

n: Archbishop Marcinkus — IOR president, warrant blocked
d: In February 1987 Milan magistrates issued arrest warrants for IOR president Paul Marcinkus and IOR officials Luigi Mennini and Pellegrino de Strobel as accessories to Banco Ambrosiano's fraudulent bankruptcy. On 17 July 1987 Italy's Court of Cassation held that Article 11 of the 1929 Lateran Treaty shielded the IOR's central bodies from Italian jurisdiction. Marcinkus stayed inside Vatican City, was never tried, and left Vatican service in October 1990.
cite: Italian Court of Cassation, Re Marcinkus, Mennini and De Strobel, 17 July 1987 (International Law Reports)

arch.t: Vatican-Masonic Network — Roberto Calvi Murder; Banco Ambrosiano Collapse; P2 Lodge Member Directed Vatican Bank Investments (PROVEN)

n: Michele Sindona — banker convicted of Ambrosoli murder
d: Sindona, a P2 member who advised the Vatican on its investments, had his Italian banks liquidated by lawyer Giorgio Ambrosoli, appointed by the Bank of Italy. Ambrosoli was shot dead in Milan on 11 July 1979. On 18 March 1986 a Milan court sentenced Sindona to life as the instigator. He drank cyanide-laced coffee in Voghera prison and died on 22 March 1986. He had already been convicted in New York in 1980 on 65 counts over the Franklin National Bank failure.
cite: Milan Court of Assizes, 18 March 1986; US District Court SDNY, 1980

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

n: P2 list seized at Castiglion Fibocchi — 962 names
d: On 17 March 1981 Guardia di Finanza officers under Col. Vincenzo Bianchi, sent by Milan magistrates Gherardo Colombo and Giuliano Turone who were investigating Sindona, searched Licio Gelli's Giole factory at Castiglion Fibocchi (Arezzo). They found a list of 962 names. It included 44 members of parliament, ministers, 195 military officers (12 Carabinieri generals, 5 Guardia di Finanza generals, 22 army generals, 4 air force generals, 8 admirals), and the heads of all three intelligence services. The government published it on 21 May 1981.
cite: Milan investigating magistrates' search of 17 March 1981; Italian government publication 21 May 1981

n: Forlani government falls over P2 list
d: Prime Minister Arnaldo Forlani was accused of delaying publication of the P2 list and resigned in May 1981, bringing down his government. His chef de cabinet was on the list. Justice Minister Adolfo Sarti, listed as a candidate for membership, resigned first; Forlani handed his resignation to President Sandro Pertini three days later.
cite: Resignation of the Forlani government, May 1981; Time, 8 June 1981

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

n: Ministers Enrico Manca and Franco Foschi on P2 list
d: Two ministers in office in the Forlani cabinet appeared on the seized list as full members: Foreign Trade Minister Enrico Manca (Socialist) and Labour Minister Franco Foschi (Christian Democrat). Five undersecretaries were also listed: Costantino Belluscio, Pasquale Bandiera, Francesco Fossa, Rolando Picchioni and Anselmo Martoni.
cite: P2 membership list published 21 May 1981; Anselmi Commission

n: Fabrizio Cicchitto — Socialist MP admits P2 membership
rank: member of parliament, Socialist Party leadership
d: Fabrizio Cicchitto, a director of the Italian Socialist Party, was the only one of about 30 parliamentarians named in early reports who admitted membership. The full list named 44 parliamentarians and a party secretary.
cite: Time, 8 June 1981; P2 list

n: Adm. Giovanni Torrisi — Chief of Defence Staff
rank: Chief of the Defence General Staff
d: Admiral Giovanni Torrisi, Chief of the Defence Staff from 1 February 1980 to 29 September 1981 and before that navy chief of staff, appeared on the P2 list with card no. 631. He left the post months after the list was published.
cite: P2 membership list 1981; Anselmi Commission

n: Gen. Giuseppe Santovito — SISMI director
d: Santovito led SISMI from its creation in 1978 until August 1981 and was on the P2 list. Prime Minister Giovanni Spadolini removed him during the scandal, and the Anselmi Commission questioned him. He was arrested in December 1983 on charges of disclosing secrets and died in February 1984 before trial.
cite: P2 list 1981; Anselmi Commission hearings

n: Gen. Giulio Grassini — SISDE director
d: Grassini, first director of SISDE (appointed January 1978), was enrolled in P2 with card no. 515. He resigned when the list was found and was replaced on 13 July 1981. In October 1981 the P2 commission heard him on possible intelligence involvement in the 1978 kidnapping of Aldo Moro.
cite: P2 list 1981; Anselmi Commission hearing, October 1981

n: Walter Pelosi — head of CESIS intelligence coordination
d: Walter Pelosi, head of CESIS, the body coordinating Italy's intelligence services, was on the P2 list alongside the SISMI and SISDE directors. With him, the heads of all three intelligence bodies in 1981 were listed members.
cite: P2 membership list 1981; Anselmi Commission

n: Gen. Vito Miceli — former SID chief, later MP
d: Miceli led army counter-intelligence (SIOS) 1969–70 and the SID 1970–74, and appears on the P2 list (file 491). Padua judges arrested him on 31 October 1974 in the 'Rosa dei Venti' inquiry into a secret military structure; he was acquitted in 1978, upheld in 1984 and 1985. He sat as an MSI deputy from 1976 to 1987.
cite: Padua investigation 1974; acquittal 1978, Cassation 1985; P2 list

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

n: Gen. Gianadelio Maletti — SID counter-intelligence chief
d: Maletti headed SID counter-intelligence 1971–75 and appears on the P2 list (file 499), though he denied joining. The Catanzaro Court of Assizes on 23 February 1979 sentenced him to 4 years for shielding Guido Giannettini and Marco Pozzan in the Piazza Fontana bombing case; the sentence was cut to 2 years and made final in 1987. He moved to South Africa in 1980.
cite: Catanzaro Court of Assizes, 23 Feb 1979; Bari Appeal Court of Assizes 1987

n: Gen. Orazio Giannini — Guardia di Finanza commander
rank: commander-general of the Guardia di Finanza (financial police)
d: Orazio Giannini, commander of the Guardia di Finanza, appears on the P2 list with card no. 832. During the 17 March 1981 search, the officer leading it, Col. Vincenzo Bianchi, received a call from the force's commander-general saying 'I am in those lists too.'
cite: P2 membership list 1981; Anselmi Commission

n: Gen. Raffaele Giudice — ex-Guardia di Finanza commander
rank: commander-general of the Guardia di Finanza 1974–1978
d: Giudice commanded the Guardia di Finanza from 31 July 1974 to 20 November 1978 and appeared on the 1981 P2 list. In the 'oil scandal' (scandalo dei petroli) over evaded fuel taxes, the Turin Tribunal sentenced him on 30 April 1987 to 3 years 10 months at first instance; his case was separated on appeal.
cite: Turin Tribunal, 30 April 1987 (first instance)

n: 195 military officers on the P2 list
rank: generals and admirals of all services
d: The list included 195 officers: 12 Carabinieri generals, 5 Guardia di Finanza generals, 22 army generals, 4 air force generals and 8 admirals. Names included Admiral Gino Birindelli and generals Giovanni Allavena (former head of SIFAR intelligence) and Giovanbattista Palumbo of the Carabinieri.
cite: P2 membership list 1981; Anselmi Commission final report 1984

n: Silvio Berlusconi — P2 member, false testimony finding
d: Berlusconi, then a television entrepreneur, was on the 1981 list; inquiry findings and his own earlier testimony showed membership from 1978. In a 1989 libel case in Verona he testified he had joined only briefly and paid no fee. In 1990 the Venice Court of Appeal found this was false testimony but could not sentence him because a 1989 amnesty had extinguished the offence.
cite: Venice Court of Appeal, 1990 (offence extinguished by 1989 amnesty)

n: Anselmi Commission — P2 report
d: A parliamentary commission chaired by Christian Democrat Tina Anselmi, set up under Law 527 of 23 September 1981, ran until 1984 and produced six reports. The majority report described P2 as a criminal and subversive organisation aiming to 'undermine our democracy'. A minority report by Massimo Teodori argued P2 was part of the system rather than an outgrowth of it.
cite: Parliamentary Commission of Inquiry into the P2 Masonic Lodge (Anselmi Commission), final report 1984

n: Law 17/1982 dissolves P2 and bans secret societies
d: Law no. 17 of 25 January 1982 ('Anselmi law') dissolved P2 and made illegal secret associations that seek to interfere with public bodies. The Grand Orient of Italy had already withdrawn the lodge's charter in 1974. The same law was used in the 2010s P3 prosecution.
cite: Italian Law no. 17 of 25 January 1982

n: P2 conspiracy trial — Gelli acquitted
rank: prosecution for conspiracy against the state
d: Rome prosecutors charged Gelli and others with political conspiracy against the state through P2. The Rome court acquitted all defendants on 16 April 1994, and the Rome Court of Appeal confirmed the acquittal on 27 March 1996.
cite: Rome Court of Assizes 16 April 1994; Rome Court of Appeal 27 March 1996

n: Bologna cover-up — Gelli and SISMI officers convicted
d: On 13 January 1981 a suitcase of explosives, weapons and false papers was planted on the Taranto–Milan train to send the Bologna station bombing inquiry toward a false foreign lead. In 1995 the Court of Cassation made final the convictions of Licio Gelli, SISMI general Pietro Musumeci (P2 list no. 487), SISMI colonel Giuseppe Belmonte and SISMI collaborator Francesco Pazienza for aggravated calumny. Musumeci's final sentence was 8 years 5 months.
cite: Bologna Appeal Court 1994; Court of Cassation 1995

n: Bologna prosecutors name Gelli as financier (2020)
d: In February 2020 the Bologna prosecutor-general's office closed a new investigation into the 2 August 1980 station bombing, which killed 85 people. It named the dead Licio Gelli and Umberto Ortolani as financiers and instigators, and Federico Umberto D'Amato and MSI senator Mario Tedeschi as instigators and organisers, and identified Paolo Bellini as an executor.
cite: Procura generale di Bologna, notice of end of investigation, February 2020

n: Bellini verdict — court calls Gelli 'conscious financier'
d: Paolo Bellini, formerly of Avanguardia Nazionale, was sentenced to life in 2022 as a fifth perpetrator of the 1980 Bologna bombing; the appeal court upheld it and the Court of Cassation made it final in 2025. The appeal judges called P2 head Licio Gelli 'il consapevole finanziatore della strage' (the knowing financier of the massacre). Gelli died in 2015 and was never tried for it.
cite: Bologna Court of Assizes 2022; Bologna Appeal Court of Assizes 2024; Court of Cassation 2025

n: Federico Umberto D'Amato — Interior Ministry intelligence
rank: head of the Interior Ministry's Ufficio Affari Riservati
d: D'Amato headed the Interior Ministry's confidential affairs office (Ufficio Affari Riservati) and is reported as a P2 member. Bologna prosecutors in 2020 and the courts in the Bellini case named him, after his death, among the organisers of the 1980 station bombing and its media handling.
