n: Mario Tedeschi — MSI senator named in Bologna case
d: Tedeschi, an MSI senator and journalist described as a P2 member, was named by Bologna prosecutors in 2020 as having helped D'Amato manage press coverage of the 1980 bombing and mislead the inquiry. He was dead and could not be charged.
cite: Procura generale di Bologna, 2020

arch.t: Italian Parliamentary Commission CONFIRMED — P2 Lodge Infiltrated Government, Military, Intelligence, Media, and Banking as Parallel State (962 Documented Members)

n: Licio Gelli — fled Swiss prison, later convicted
d: Arrested in Geneva in September 1982, Gelli escaped Champ-Dollon prison on 10 August 1983 and was extradited to Italy in February 1988. His 12-year sentence for the Banco Ambrosiano fraud was confirmed in April 1998; he vanished in May 1998 and was arrested in Cannes that September. He held an Argentine honorary diplomatic post and is linked to Argentine P2 members Emilio Massera and José López Rega.
cite: Court of Cassation, April 1998

arch.t: Vatican-Masonic Network — Roberto Calvi Murder; Banco Ambrosiano Collapse; P2 Lodge Member Directed Vatican Bank Investments (PROVEN)

n: Andreotti discloses Gladio to parliament
d: On 24 October 1990 Prime Minister Giulio Andreotti told the Chamber of Deputies that a secret stay-behind 'structure of information, response and safeguard' had existed since the 1950s under NATO coordination. He gave the parliamentary massacres commission a list of 622 civilians, said 127 arms caches had been dismantled, and denied any role in bombings. On 22 November 1990 the European Parliament called on member states to dismantle such networks.
cite: Statement to the Chamber of Deputies 24 Oct 1990; European Parliament resolution 22 Nov 1990

arch.t: Italy — Operation Gladio: NATO Stay-Behind Network Used for Domestic Terrorism; 'Strategy of Tension'

n: Gladio membership confirmed by SISMI to commission
d: On 29 November 1990 General Paolo Inzerilli, SISMI chief of staff, told the parliamentary commission on terrorism and massacres that 'the true number is 622'. He broke it down as 215 active, 339 reserve, 65 dead and 3 'frozen' members of the network's units.
cite: Parliamentary Commission on Terrorism and Massacres, hearing of 29 Nov 1990

arch.t: Italy — Operation Gladio: NATO Stay-Behind Network Used for Domestic Terrorism; 'Strategy of Tension'

n: Peteano bombing — Casson uncovers Gladio
d: On 31 May 1972 a car bomb at Peteano killed three Carabinieri. Venice magistrate Felice Casson reopened the case and identified neo-fascist Vincenzo Vinciguerra, who confessed and is serving life. In 1984 Vinciguerra described a 'secret force parallel to the armed forces' helped by the secret services; Casson's inquiry led to Gladio's exposure.
cite: Venice judiciary (Judge Felice Casson); Vinciguerra life sentence

arch.t: Italy — Operation Gladio: NATO Stay-Behind Network Used for Domestic Terrorism; 'Strategy of Tension'

n: President Cossiga — Gladio role and impeachment motion
d: After Andreotti's disclosure, President Francesco Cossiga acknowledged he had been involved in setting up Gladio (he became defence undersecretary in 1966). The Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) filed an impeachment motion; it was dismissed.
cite: Parliamentary impeachment motion (PDS), 1991, dismissed

arch.t: Italy — Operation Gladio: NATO Stay-Behind Network Used for Domestic Terrorism; 'Strategy of Tension'

n: P3 — Flavio Carboni convicted of secret association
rank: network pressing on judges and state appointments
d: On 16 March 2018 a Rome court convicted eight people in the 'P3' case, which prosecutors described as a secret group seeking undue influence on the state. Flavio Carboni received 6 years 6 months for secret association; Arcangelo Martino 4 years 9 months under the Anselmi law against secret societies. Senator Denis Verdini was acquitted of secret association but given 1 year 3 months for illegal party funding.
cite: Rome Tribunal, P3 verdict 16 March 2018
org_note: P3: secret association prosecuted under the 1982 Anselmi law, named by press after P2

n: P3 — senior judge Vincenzo Carbone convicted
rank: senior judge (former First President of the Court of Cassation)
d: In the same 16 March 2018 P3 verdict, Vincenzo Carbone received a 2-year suspended sentence for abuse of office. Former undersecretary Nicola Cosentino received a 10-month suspended term for defamation and private violence. Charges against Sardinia regional president Ugo Cappellacci lapsed.
cite: Rome Tribunal, P3 verdict 16 March 2018
org_note: P3: secret association prosecuted under the 1982 Anselmi law

n: P4 — deputy and magistrate Alfonso Papa
d: In the 2011 'P4' inquiry into go-between Luigi Bisignani, PdL deputy Alfonso Papa, a former Naples prosecutor and Justice Ministry director, was accused of passing confidential information to Bisignani and pressing businessmen for favours. The Chamber authorised his arrest in July 2011 and he spent 101 days in Poggioreale prison. Bisignani took a plea of 1 year 7 months. Papa was convicted in 2016 (4 years 6 months), but the charges lapsed on appeal by 2021; the judiciary's disciplinary body removed him from the bench in 2023.
cite: Naples courts 2016–2021; Superior Council of the Judiciary (CSM) disciplinary section 2023
org_note: P4: press name for the Bisignani information-trading network

n: Anti-Mafia Commission seizes Grand Lodge lists
d: On 1 March 2017 the Anti-Mafia Commission chaired by Rosy Bindi voted unanimously to seize membership lists of lodges in Sicily and Calabria from 1990 onward, after grand masters missed an 8 February deadline citing privacy. The Guardia di Finanza searched the headquarters of the Grand Orient of Italy, the Regular Grand Lodge of Italy, the Serenissima Gran Loggia and the Gran Loggia d'Italia. In 2024 the European Court of Human Rights found the seizure breached Article 8 (privacy); its Grand Chamber upheld that in July 2026.
cite: Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission decision of 1 March 2017; ECHR, Grande Oriente d'Italia v. Italy

n: Anti-Mafia report: 193 lodge members in mafia cases
d: The Commission's report on mafia and Freemasonry, presented by Rosy Bindi in December 2017, found that 193 people listed in lodges were recorded in organised-crime proceedings by the National Anti-Mafia Directorate. It recommended extending bans on lodge membership to magistrates, career military and police.
cite: Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission, report on mafia and Freemasonry, December 2017

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

n: Castelvetrano council — majority of executive were Masons
rank: town executive and council (home town of Matteo Messina Denaro)
d: The Anti-Mafia Commission's 2017 report found that in Castelvetrano in 2016, 4 of the 5 town assessors and 7 of 30 councillors were Freemasons. It also found 11 executives and staff of a Trapani-area cooperative bank belonged to a Grand Orient lodge, and a significant Masonic presence in senior posts at the Locri health authority.
cite: Parliamentary Anti-Mafia Commission, report on mafia and Freemasonry, December 2017

n: Rinascita Scott — ex-senator Giancarlo Pittelli convicted
rank: former senator and Forza Italia regional coordinator
d: In the Rinascita Scott maxi-trial against the Mancuso 'Ndrangheta clan, more than 200 of over 300 defendants were convicted in November 2023, including civil servants, a former police chief and a former mayor. Lawyer and former Forza Italia senator Giancarlo Pittelli, described by prosecutors as a Freemason linking the clan to Masonic circles and business, received 11 years for collusion. In a separate 'Mala Pigna' trial the Palmi Tribunal gave him 14 years for external complicity in 2025.
cite: Vibo Valentia Tribunal, Rinascita Scott verdict November 2023; Palmi Tribunal 2025

n: Roberto Formigoni — CL figure and Lombardy president
d: Formigoni, the unofficial political spokesman of the Catholic movement Comunione e Liberazione, led Lombardy from 1995 to 2013. On 21 February 2019 the Court of Cassation confirmed his corruption conviction in the Maugeri health-care case, with a final sentence of 5 years 10 months. The court ruling concerned bribes, not the movement itself.
cite: Italian Court of Cassation, 21 February 2019

n: Opus Dei technocrats enter Franco's cabinet (1957)
d: In February 1957 Franco appointed two Opus Dei members: Mariano Navarro Rubio as finance minister and Alberto Ullastres as trade minister. Both served until 1965 and drove the Stabilisation Plan that ended autarky. Historians count 8 Opus Dei members among Franco's 116 ministers, none before 1957.
cite: Academic history (Preston; Crozier; Messori; John Allen)

n: Mariano Navarro Rubio — finance minister, then central bank
rank: Finance Minister 1957–65; Governor of the Bank of Spain 1965–70
d: Navarro Rubio, an Opus Dei member, was finance minister from 25 February 1957 to 8 July 1965, then governor of the Banco de España. He was accused in the 1969 MATESA credit scandal and left the central bank.
cite: Spanish government records; academic history

n: Alberto Ullastres — trade minister, then EEC envoy
d: Ullastres, one of the Opus Dei ministers ('Opusdeístas'), was trade minister from 1957 to 1965 and led the Stabilisation Plan's opening of trade. From 1965 to 1976 he headed Spain's mission to the European Communities.
cite: Academic history

n: Laureano López Rodó — architect of development plans
rank: Minister for Development Planning 1965–73; Foreign Minister 1973–74
d: López Rodó, an Opus Dei member and close to Luis Carrero Blanco, was technical secretary of the Presidency 1956–62, Commissioner of the Development Plan 1962–65, minister for development planning 1965–73, and foreign minister from 12 June 1973 to 4 January 1974.
cite: Spanish government records; academic history

n: Gregorio López-Bravo — industry and foreign minister
d: López-Bravo, an Opus Dei member, served as Franco's minister of industry and then foreign minister from 1969 to 1973. He died in the Mount Oiz air crash in 1985.
cite: Spanish government records; academic history

n: MATESA scandal and the 1969 'monocolor' cabinet
rank: finance and trade ministers; state industrial bank
d: The MATESA scandal broke on 23 July 1969: the textile-machinery firm owed about 10 billion pesetas in export credits from the state Banco de Crédito Industrial. Former ministers Mariano Navarro Rubio, Juan José Espinosa San Martín (finance) and Faustino García-Moncó (trade) were charged, and Franco pardoned them before any verdict. The reshuffle of 29 October 1969 produced a 'monocolor' cabinet in which eleven members had ties to Opus Dei.
cite: Spanish Supreme Court proceedings; Franco pardon 1971

n: Spain's stay-behind network — Serra inquiry
d: After the Italian disclosure in 1990, Defence Minister Narcís Serra opened an inquiry into whether Spain had a Gladio network. Former prime minister Adolfo Suárez said he had never heard of it; former prime minister Leopoldo Calvo Sotelo said the Franco regime 'itself was Gladio'.
cite: Spanish Ministry of Defence inquiry, 1990

arch.t: Italy — Operation Gladio: NATO Stay-Behind Network Used for Domestic Terrorism; 'Strategy of Tension'

n: Aginter Press — Lisbon 'news agency' training bombers
d: Aginter Press was set up in Lisbon in September 1966 under Salazar's Estado Novo and run by former French officer and OAS member Yves Guérin-Sérac. It presented itself as a press agency but trained members in bombing and sabotage. Its documents were found at the end of 1974 after the Carnation Revolution, when Guérin-Sérac and associates left Portugal.
cite: Academic history; documents recovered in Lisbon 1974

n: Aginter Press links to Italian bombings — Salvini testimony
d: Italian magistrate Guido Salvini, investigating the 1969 Piazza Fontana bombing, told the Italian parliamentary commission on terrorism in 1997 that his inquiries confirmed links between Aginter Press, Ordine Nuovo and Avanguardia Nazionale. He said Aginter instructors taught Avanguardia Nazionale members to use explosives in Rome in 1967–68.
cite: Italian Parliamentary Commission on Terrorism, Salvini testimony 1997

n: IDEA — secret officers' society behind the junta
d: IDEA (Holy Bond of Greek Officers) was formed in 1945 by officers who had served in the collaborationist Security Battalions; its 1952 manifesto called dictatorship the only solution for Greece. Several leaders of the 21 April 1967 coup, including Georgios Papadopoulos, were members, and IDEA members took key posts under the junta.
cite: Academic history (Kassimeris)
org_note: IDEA: Ieros Desmos Ellinon Axiomatikon, secret society of Greek army officers

n: Junta leaders convicted of high treason (1975)
d: In the trial held at Korydallos Prison from 28 July to 23 August 1975, Georgios Papadopoulos, Stylianos Pattakos and Nikolaos Makarezos were sentenced to death for high treason and mutiny, commuted to life by the Karamanlis government. Dimitrios Ioannidis, former head of the military police, received life. In the separate Polytechnic trial (verdict 31 December 1975) Ioannidis received seven life terms.
cite: Athens court, Trial of the Instigators and Polytechnic trial, 1975
org_note: IDEA: secret society of Greek army officers

n: LOK stay-behind unit seized Defence Ministry in 1967
d: The LOK special forces, integrated into the European stay-behind network after 1952, took over the Greek Defence Ministry during the 21 April 1967 coup under Brigadier General Kostas Aslanides, according to the historical record.
cite: Academic history

n: Operation Sheepskin — Greek Gladio confirmed
d: After Andreotti's 1990 disclosure in Italy, the Greek defence minister confirmed that a Greek stay-behind branch, Operation Sheepskin ('Red Sheepskin'), had operated until 1988. Former prime minister Andreas Papandreou said he learned of it in 1984 and ordered it dissolved.
cite: Statement of the Greek Minister of Defence, 1990

arch.t: Italy — Operation Gladio: NATO Stay-Behind Network Used for Domestic Terrorism; 'Strategy of Tension'

n: Golden Dawn convicted as a criminal organisation
d: Golden Dawn won 21 seats in May 2012, 18 in June 2012 and 17 in January 2015. On 7 October 2020 the Athens Court of Appeals found leader Nikolaos Michaloliakos and six other leading members and former MPs guilty of directing a criminal organisation 'dressed in the mantle of a political party', in a trial of 68 defendants that included the 2013 murder of rapper Pavlos Fyssas. On 4 March 2026 an appeal court upheld the convictions of 42 defendants.
cite: Athens Court of Appeals, 7 October 2020; appeal ruling 4 March 2026
org_note: Golden Dawn: neo-Nazi party ruled a criminal organisation

n: Golden Dawn ties inside the Greek police
d: After the May 2012 election, polling stations used by officers of the Attica police directorate showed just over 20% for Golden Dawn against about 6% at civilian stations in the same district. In 2012 an officer was suspended over a raid on migrant stalls in Missolonghi alongside party members. In 2013 Council of Europe human rights commissioner Nils Muižnieks said he had strong evidence of ties between police and the party.
cite: Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, 2013; election returns 2012
org_note: Golden Dawn: neo-Nazi party ruled a criminal organisation

n: Narendra Modi — RSS pracharak before office
d: Modi joined the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh as a boy and served as a full-time organiser (pracharak) from the early 1970s before the RSS seconded him to the BJP in 1985. He became prime minister in 2014. The RSS does not publish membership rolls; Modi's RSS career is set out in his official biographies and was acknowledged by the organisation.
cite: Official PM biography; RSS statements; widely documented in Indian and international press

n: Brig. Ali Khan — Hizb ut-Tahrir cell in Pakistan's army
d: A military court convicted Brigadier Ali Khan and four majors in August 2012 of links to Hizb ut-Tahrir, which is banned in Pakistan, after he was arrested in May 2011. He was sentenced to five years. The army said the group had tried to recruit officers to its programme of a coup and a caliphate.
cite: Pakistan Army field general court martial, August 2012; reported by Reuters, BBC, Dawn

n: Bangladesh army foils Hizb ut-Tahrir-linked coup plot
d: In January 2012 the Bangladesh army announced it had stopped a coup attempt by serving and retired officers it described as religious extremists, and named Hizb ut-Tahrir, banned in Bangladesh since 2009, among those behind it. Two retired officers were arrested and a serving major was named as a fugitive.
cite: Bangladesh Army press briefing, 19 January 2012; reported by BBC, Reuters

n: Apollo Quiboloy — spiritual adviser to President Duterte
d: Quiboloy, founder of the Kingdom of Jesus Christ church, was described by Rodrigo Duterte as his spiritual adviser and lent him his jet during the 2016 campaign. A US federal grand jury indicted him in 2021 on sex-trafficking and other counts; Philippine police arrested him in September 2024 after a two-week siege of his Davao compound on domestic child-abuse and trafficking charges.
cite: US v. Quiboloy, C.D. Cal., indictment 2021; Philippine National Police arrest, September 2024

n: Indonesia bans Hizb ut-Tahrir Indonesia
rank: civil servants and members of the security forces
d: The government revoked Hizb ut-Tahrir Indonesia's legal status in July 2017 under a new decree on mass organisations, citing its aim of replacing the state with a caliphate. Officials then warned that civil servants who were members would be dismissed; the ban was upheld by the courts in 2018.
cite: Government Regulation in Lieu of Law (Perppu) 2/2017; Ministry of Law and Human Rights decision, 19 July 2017; Jakarta State Administrative Court, May 2018

n: Iglesia ni Cristo endorses Marcos Jr., Duterte and 12 Senate bets
d: On 3 May 2022 the Iglesia ni Cristo announced on its NET 25 channel that it backed Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for president, Sara Duterte for vice-president and 12 Senate candidates, including Jinggoy Estrada, Loren Legarda, Francis Escudero, Juan Miguel Zubiri, Joel Villanueva and Robin Padilla. The church calls its bloc voting the 'Unity Vote'; the 2015 census counted about 2.6 million members. It had backed Benigno Aquino III in 2010 and Rodrigo Duterte in 2016.
cite: Manila Bulletin, 3 May 2022; Wikipedia 'Iglesia ni Cristo' (endorsement history)

n: Eduardo Manalo — INC executive minister named presidential special envoy
rank: Special Envoy of the President for Overseas Filipinos' Concerns (Department of Foreign Affairs)
d: Rodrigo Duterte appointed Eduardo Villanueva Manalo, executive minister (head) of the Iglesia ni Cristo, as Special Envoy of the President for Overseas Filipinos' Concerns under the Department of Foreign Affairs. The appointment papers were dated 13 February 2018 and set a term from 30 January 2018 to 29 January 2019. The church had backed Duterte in the 2016 election.
cite: Presidential appointment papers dated 13 February 2018, reported by Philippine Daily Inquirer, 14 February 2018

n: INC protest at the Justice Department and EDSA over De Lima probe
d: From 27 to 31 August 2015 Iglesia ni Cristo members protested outside the Department of Justice and then occupied parts of EDSA after Justice Secretary Leila de Lima acted on an illegal-detention complaint by Isaias Samson Jr., a minister the church had expelled. Police put the crowd at about 15,400 at its peak. Vice-President Jejomar Binay backed the church's 'mass action'; the church ended the protest after talks with government officials, and the presidential palace said no deal had been struck.
cite: Wikipedia '2015 Iglesia ni Cristo protests' (citing Inquirer, Philstar, Rappler)

n: INC rallies for member-senator Marcoleta facing graft charge
d: Senator Rodante Marcoleta, an Iglesia ni Cristo member elected in 2025 with the church's support, was set to be charged by Ombudsman Jesus Remulla for failing to declare 75 million pesos in unused campaign contributions. On 30 June 2026 the church held a rally along EDSA that police estimated at about 12,000; its spokesman called the case 'selective justice'. Marcoleta was expected to vote against convicting Vice-President Sara Duterte at her Senate impeachment trial.
cite: Malay Mail (AFP), 30 June 2026; Wikipedia 'Iglesia ni Cristo' (2025 Senate support)

n: Pakistan Supreme Court orders Gulen group banned, schools to Maarif
d: A three-judge Supreme Court bench headed by Chief Justice Mian Saqib Nisar ordered the government on 28 December 2018 to ban the Gulen movement (FETO) and the Pak-Turk International Cag Education Foundation, which ran the Pak-Turk schools, and to hand its schools and other institutions to Turkey's state Maarif Foundation. The court said Pakistan was bound by an Organisation of Islamic Cooperation declaration naming the group.
cite: Supreme Court of Pakistan, order of December 2018; Arab News Pakistan, 28 December 2018

n: Malaysia deports three Turks accused of Gulen links
d: Malaysian police arrested Turgay Karaman and Ihsan Aslan, and two days later academic Ismet Ozcelik, in May 2017 under a security law allowing 28 days' detention without trial. They were deported to Turkey on the night of 11 May 2017; police chief Khalid Abu Bakar said Ankara had cancelled their travel documents, so they were treated as illegal immigrants. Turkey accused them of Gulen ('FETO') links; Human Rights Watch condemned the deportations.
cite: Royal Malaysia Police statement, 11–12 May 2017; Al Jazeera, 12 May 2017

n: Veysel Akcay — Mongolia grounds plane to stop removal to Turkey
rank: Mongolian civil aviation and security authorities
d: On 27 July 2018 Veysel Akcay, general manager of the Empathy Worldwide Educational Institution, which ran Turkish-Mongolian schools linked to the Gulen movement, was seized in Ulaanbaatar. Mongolian authorities temporarily grounded a plane at the airport and he was released the same day. Turkish Minute and the Stockholm Center for Freedom reported that Turkey's MIT intelligence service carried out the abduction; Mongolian authorities said they had no specific knowledge of an abduction and were investigating.
cite: Euronews, 28 July 2018; Turkish Minute, 27 July 2018

n: Orhan Inandi — Sapat schools head taken from Bishkek to Turkey
rank: State Committee for National Security border service
d: Orhan Inandi, president of the Sapat network of Turkish-founded schools in Kyrgyzstan and a Kyrgyz citizen, disappeared in Bishkek in mid-2021. On 5 July 2021 President Erdogan said on TRT Haber that Inandi, whom he called a FETO leader, had been 'captured and taken to Turkey'. In August 2021 Kyrgyzstan's Military Prosecutor's Office opened proceedings for negligence and breach of border-service rules against border officers of the State Committee for National Security who allowed him to be taken out of the country.
cite: Kyrgyz Military Prosecutor's Office, pre-trial proceedings, August 2021 (24.kg, 17 August 2021); Erdogan on TRT Haber, 5 July 2021

n: Azerbaijan state oil company takes over Gulen-linked schools
d: On 18 June 2014 Gulen-linked educational facilities in Azerbaijan — 11 high schools, 13 university-entrance preparation centres and a private university — were taken over by the Azerbaijan International Education Company, in which the state oil company SOCAR holds shares. The company gave financial viability as the reason; the takeover followed requests from Turkish Prime Minister Erdogan for help against the Gulen movement.
cite: Eurasianet, 19 June 2014

n: Tajikistan closes seven Gulen-linked schools by presidential decree
d: In May 2015 President Emomali Rahmon issued a decree overruling a 1994 cabinet decision that had let the schools operate, closing seven Gulen-linked Turkish schools from September 2015. The schools were transferred to the state and rebranded as schools for gifted children; they had been under investigation since January 2015.
cite: Presidential decree, May 2015; The Diplomat, August 2015

n: Turkmenistan closes Gulen schools and jails 18 men
d: Turkmenistan closed or nationalised most of the Gulen-linked schools opened in the 1990s in 2011. After more than 100 people, most with some Gulen affiliation, were detained in late 2016, 18 men were convicted in closed trials and given 12 to 25 years for inciting hatred and involvement in a criminal organisation, according to a joint statement by Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and the Norwegian Helsinki Committee.
cite: Joint statement of Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and Norwegian Helsinki Committee, 2017, as reported by The Diplomat, June 2017

n: Kazakhstan — 33 Turkish-Kazakh schools renamed after coup attempt
d: After Turkey's July 2016 coup attempt Ankara asked Central Asian governments to close Gulen-linked schools; Kazakhstan declined to close them. On 18 October 2016 the sponsoring foundation KATEV announced that its 33 Turkish-Kazakh lyceums, co-founded by the Gulen movement, would be renamed 'Bilim' Innovative Lyceums. RFE/RL reported no Kazakh government order behind the renaming.
cite: RFE/RL, 18 October 2016

n: Fraser subcommittee — Moon group as Seoul's M-16 maker and envoy
rank: South Korean defence industry and senior officials (Kim Jong-pil, Pak Chon-kyu)
d: The US House Subcommittee on International Organizations (Fraser committee) found in 1978 that the Moon Organization had influential allies in the South Korean government, naming Kim Jong-pil, founder of the KCIA, and Pak Chon-kyu. It found that a Moon Organization business was an important Korean defence contractor producing M-16 rifles, and that in late 1977 Moon representatives tried to renegotiate the Colt–ROK Government M-16 co-production agreement in circumstances suggesting they were secret envoys of the Korean government. It also found the Moon-founded Korean Cultural and Freedom Foundation advanced the political interests of the Seoul government.
cite: US House Subcommittee on International Organizations, 'Investigation of Korean-American Relations', final report 1978 (excerpt on Wikisource)

n: Lin Hsueh-feng — jailed for China-funded tours of village chiefs
rank: village and ward chiefs (local elected officials)
d: Chiayi District Court sentenced Lin Hsueh-feng, a former KMT city council candidate, on 28 May 2025 to four years in prison under the Anti-Infiltration Act and the presidential election law. In 2023 she took Chiayi village and ward chiefs on trips to Zhejiang arranged with the Taiwan Affairs Office of Taizhou City, which paid for lodging and local travel; prosecutors said Chinese officials urged them to vote for a particular party's candidate. The ruling could be appealed.
cite: Chiayi District Court, judgment of 28 May 2025; Tribune India (citing CNA), 31 May 2025

n: Ex-DPP aides in Presidential Office and Foreign Ministry jailed as spies
rank: Presidential Office consultant; assistant to the foreign minister
d: On 25 September 2025 Taipei District Court convicted four former DPP members of spying for Chinese Central Military Commission intelligence: Huang Chu-jung, ex-assistant to a New Taipei councillor and the recruiter (10 years); Ho Jen-chieh, ex-assistant to Foreign Minister Joseph Wu (8 years 2 months); Chiu Shih-yuan, ex-deputy director of the Taiwan Foundation for Democracy (6 years 2 months); and Wu Shang-yu, a former Presidential Office consultant (4 years). They passed on William Lai's travel schedules and records of Joseph Wu's talks with foreign envoys. The sentences could be appealed.
cite: Taipei District Court, judgment of 25 September 2025; Taipei Times, 26 September 2025

n: Cardinal Becciu convicted over London property, then mistrial
rank: Substitute for General Affairs, Secretariat of State; later prefect
d: Cardinal Angelo Becciu, Substitute at the Secretariat of State from 2011 to 2018, was convicted of embezzlement by the Vatican tribunal on 16 December 2023 and sentenced to five and a half years, with eight other defendants also convicted. The case centred on the Secretariat of State's €350 million investment in a London building, where prosecutors said brokers and officials cost the Holy See tens of millions in fees and extorted €15 million to give up control. On 17 March 2026 the Vatican appeals tribunal nullified the indictment over unpublished papal decrees and undisclosed evidence and ordered a retrial from 22 June 2026.
cite: Vatican City tribunal verdict 16 December 2023; Vatican appeals tribunal ruling 17 March 2026 (PBS NewsHour/AP); Wikipedia 'Giovanni Angelo Becciu'
org_note: Holy See finance case filed under the ior key for the Vatican's financial institutions; the money came from the Secretariat of State, not the IOR.

n: Angelo Caloia — ex-IOR president convicted of embezzlement
rank: president of the Institute for the Works of Religion (Vatican Bank)
d: On 21 January 2021 the Vatican City tribunal convicted Angelo Caloia, former president of the IOR, and lawyer Gabriele Liuzzo of embezzlement from the IOR, aggravated embezzlement and self-laundering over IOR property sales between 2002 and 2007; each was sentenced to eight years and eleven months and fined €12,500. Liuzzo's son Lamberto received five years and two months for money laundering. The court ordered forfeiture of about €38 million.
cite: Vatican City State tribunal, judgment of 21 January 2021 (Vatican News)

arch.t: Catholic Church Financial Fraud — Vatican Bank Scandal: IOR Documented Helping Italian Politicians Hide Money and Evade Taxes; Marcinkus Indicted; Never Extradited (PROVEN)

n: Vatileaks 2 — finance commission secretary jailed for leaks
rank: secretary of the Prefecture for the Economic Affairs of the Holy See
d: Monsignor Lucio Vallejo Balda, a senior official in the Holy See's economic prefecture and member of the papal commission reviewing Vatican finances, was sentenced by the Vatican court in July 2016 to 18 months for leaking confidential documents used in books by Gianluigi Nuzzi and Emiliano Fittipaldi; he began serving in a Vatican cell on 22 August 2016 and was later granted clemency. The court acquitted the two journalists, saying it lacked jurisdiction. In the first 'Vatileaks' case, papal butler Paolo Gabriele was convicted of theft on 6 October 2012 and later pardoned.
cite: Vatican City tribunal verdicts of 6 October 2012 and July 2016; Wikipedia 'Vatican leaks scandal'
org_note: Filed under ior as a Holy See finance case.

n: Rome prosecutors seize €23m from IOR, investigate its president
rank: president of the Vatican Bank (Ettore Gotti Tedeschi)
d: In 2010 Italian magistrates in Rome seized €23 million held by the IOR at an Italian bank, saying anti-money-laundering laws had been broken, and placed IOR president Ettore Gotti Tedeschi and another IOR manager under investigation for money laundering. A Rome court later convicted former IOR officials Paolo Cipriani and Massimo Tulli over reporting omissions on three small transfers, acquitting them of money laundering.
cite: Rome prosecutors' seizure order, 2010; Rome court verdict on Cipriani and Tulli; Wikipedia 'Vatican Bank'

arch.t: Catholic Church Financial Fraud — Vatican Bank Scandal: IOR Documented Helping Italian Politicians Hide Money and Evade Taxes; Marcinkus Indicted; Never Extradited (PROVEN)

n: Uniter — KSK soldier's network put under domestic intelligence watch
rank: Special Forces Command (KSK) soldiers; police and reservists
d: Uniter, an association founded by André Schmitt ('Hannibal'), a former soldier of the Bundeswehr's Special Forces Command (KSK), ran chat groups with soldiers and police that investigators found in 2017; Schmitt himself was an informant in mid-2017. In February 2020 the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution had classed Uniter internally as a review case; in early July 2020 it placed Uniter under surveillance. That same week Defence Minister Annegret Kramp-Karrenbauer disbanded a KSK company after a May raid on a sergeant major's property found PETN explosive, an AK-47 and thousands of rounds believed stolen from the army.
cite: Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution classification 2020; German Defence Ministry, July 2020; Star Tribune (AP), 3 July 2020; t-online, 19 February 2020

n: Heinz Lembke — 33 arms caches on Lüneburg Heath
d: In 1981 forester Heinz Lembke led investigators to 33 illegal arms dumps near Uelzen on the Lüneburg Heath holding automatic weapons, 13,520 rounds, 50 anti-tank weapons, 156 kg of explosives and 258 grenades. Members of the Deutsche Aktionsgruppe had said the day after the 26 September 1980 Oktoberfest bombing that Lembke offered them weapons. He was found hanged in his cell on 1 November 1981, the day before a hearing at which he had said he would name his backers; the inquiry into them was closed. The size and military grade of the caches led to suggestions of a link to NATO stay-behind stocks, which was never officially confirmed.
cite: Federal prosecutor's investigation 1981; Wikipedia 'Heinz Lembke'

n: Norway — Meyer arms cache and defence minister on stay-behind
d: In 1978 Norwegian police found an arms cache and radio equipment at a mountain cabin and arrested businessman Hans Otto Meyer, who said Norwegian intelligence had supplied the weapons. Defence Minister Rolf Hansen then said the network 'was not in any way answerable to NATO and had no CIA connection'. Back in 1957 intelligence chief Vilhelm Evang had protested to NATO about stay-behind-related activity by officers at the Kolsås headquarters, settled in 1958 with assurances on how the networks would be run.
cite: Statement of Defence Minister Rolf Hansen, 1978; Wikipedia 'Operation Gladio'

n: Denmark — stay-behind 'Absalon' inside military intelligence
d: Denmark's stay-behind network, code-named Absalon and led by E. J. Harder, was hidden inside the military intelligence service Forsvarets Efterretningstjeneste, according to historians cited by Wikipedia. Time reported in November 1990 that the Danish and Norwegian units were built 'with official cooperation'. The Guardian reported in January 1992 that after Italy's disclosure Denmark was among the countries that investigated and disbanded their national organisations.
cite: Time, November 1990; The Guardian, 30 January 1992 (as quoted in the Mannheim Pro-Government Militias Database); Wikipedia 'Operation Gladio'

n: Romania — interior minister and gendarmerie chief named as Masons
rank: interim interior minister and deputy prime minister; head of the Gendarmerie
d: Newsweek România reported in September 2019, citing Masonic sources, that Mihai Fifor, then interim interior minister and deputy prime minister, joined Freemasonry in 2008 through Loja Armonia and later Loja Basarab, and that General Constantin Florea, head of the Gendarmerie, belonged to Loja Basarab. Neither had declared membership in their interest declarations, which the magazine said the law required. Fifor neither confirmed nor denied; Costin Mihalache, head of the Government Chancellery and a former foreign-intelligence (SIE) officer, said he had been a Mason but no longer was.
cite: Newsweek România investigation, republished by Alba24, 22 September 2019 (anonymous Masonic sources; the claim rests on that one outlet)

n: Nigeria's constitution bars secret-society members from elected office
rank: President, governors, National and State Assembly members; all public officers
d: Sections 66(1)(g), 107(1)(g), 137(1)(h) and 182(1)(h) of Nigeria's 1999 Constitution disqualify members of secret societies from election to the National Assembly, State Houses of Assembly, the presidency and governorships, and Section 38(4) bars anyone from belonging to one; Section 318 defines the term. Paragraph 10 of the Code of Conduct for Public Officers (Fifth Schedule) says a public officer shall not belong to any society 'the membership of which is incompatible with the functions or dignity of his office'. Commentators name the Ogboni fraternities, Freemasons and AMORC among the societies at issue.
cite: Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria 1999, ss. 38(4), 66, 107, 137, 182, 318 and Fifth Schedule para. 10; ThisDay, 18 October 2022
org_note: Covers Reformed Ogboni Fraternity, Aborigine Ogboni Fraternity and Masonic lodges together.

n: Falae petition alleges president-elect Obasanjo is an Ogboni member
d: After the February 1999 presidential election, runner-up Olu Falae's election petition alleged that Olusegun Obasanjo was an Ogboni member and therefore disqualified, since election rules barred secret-society members from running. The election tribunal dismissed the petition. The Reformed Ogboni Fraternity's general secretary said in March 1999 that it was non-political and not a secret society.
cite: Falae election petition and tribunal ruling, 1999, as summarised by the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (ecoi.net)
org_note: Ogboni fraternity; filed under the generic freemasonry key.

n: Blaise Compaoré — president and former Grand Master in Burkina Faso
d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that President Blaise Compaoré was a former grand master of the Grande Loge du Burkina and had been succeeded in that office by his foreign minister, Djibrill Bassolé. Compaoré ruled from 1987 to 2014.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Djibrill Bassolé — foreign minister as Grand Master in Burkina Faso
d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Djibrill Bassolé, Burkina Faso's foreign minister, was grand master of the Grande Loge du Burkina, having succeeded President Blaise Compaoré in the post.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Amadou Toumani Touré — Mali's president linked to Grand Lodge
d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Amadou Toumani Touré, president of Mali until the coup of 21 March 2012, oversaw ('chapeaute') the Grande Loge du Mali.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Alpha Condé — Guinea's president linked to Grand Lodge
d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that President Alpha Condé oversaw ('chapeaute') the Grande Loge de Guinée.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Abdoulaye Wade — Senegal's president reported initiated
d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that former president Abdoulaye Wade (in office 2000–2012) had been initiated into Freemasonry. Wade's camp accused his successor Macky Sall of membership, which Sall denied.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Côte d'Ivoire — prime minister and interior minister named as Masons
rank: prime minister; minister of the interior
d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Prime Minister Jeannot Ahoussou-Kouadio and Interior Minister Hamed Bakayoko were Freemasons, and that state prosecutor Simplice Koffi Kouadio had been received by the Grande Loge de Côte d'Ivoire. It said President Alassane Ouattara was not officially known to be a member.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Antoine Embinga — Gabon police chief and Grand Master
d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Antoine Embinga, grand master of the Grande Loge symbolique du Gabon, had been removed as head of the police in January 2012. The same report said ministers Paul Toungui and Séraphin Moundounga and National Security Council head Léon Paul Ngoulakia attended Ali Bongo's installation as grand master of the Grande Loge du Gabon on 31 October 2009.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Pascal Lissouba — Congo's president initiated in French lodge
d: Jeune Afrique reported in 2012 that Pascal Lissouba, president of the Republic of Congo from 1992 to 1997, had been initiated at the Grand Orient de France lodge in Besançon.
cite: Jeune Afrique, Pascal Airault, 'Franc-maçonnerie : l'Afrique bien logée' (2012), as reprinted by Dakaractu, 24 April 2012

n: Moon group buys into Banco de Crédito under Uruguay's military rule
rank: de facto president Aparicio Méndez; Uruguayan banking system
d: In 1981 Moon's group bought 49% of Banco de Crédito, one of Uruguay's oldest banks, and founded the daily Últimas Noticias, whose early editorial declared it 'fully identified' with the military 'process'; that year Bo Hi Pak met de facto president Aparicio Méndez, according to a book by Juan de Montemayor. The group also bought Montevideo's Hotel Victoria Plaza. Banco de Crédito closed in 2002; a parliamentary investigative commission on the financial and banking system found it had taken excessive risk by lending about US$100 million to Moon-linked companies out of about US$600 million in total loans.
cite: Uruguayan parliamentary investigative commission on the financial and banking system; El Observador, 1 September 2012; Christianity Today, 13 May 1988

n: Paraguayan Senate votes to expropriate Moon land at Puerto Casado
d: Moon's representatives bought about 600,000 hectares in northern Paraguay, including the town of Puerto Casado, from the Argentine firm Carlos Casado in 2000 for US$22.5 million. In early August 2005 the Senate voted 24 to 14 to expropriate 52,000 hectares around the town for its roughly 6,000 residents; the bill then went to the lower house. President Nicanor Duarte's government sent troops to the area after a community radio station was attacked.
cite: Paraguayan Senate vote, August 2005; MercoPress, 6 August 2005

n: Bo Hi Pak and CAUSA with García Meza after Bolivia's 'cocaine coup'
rank: de facto president Luis García Meza
d: Journalist Robert Parry wrote that the Unification Church published a photo of Moon's aide Bo Hi Pak meeting General Luis García Meza after his July 1980 coup, and quoted Pak saying 'I have erected a throne for Father Moon in the world's highest city'. Parry also wrote, without naming a source, that CAUSA ran joint operations with the junta, and that later Bolivian investigations found Moon's group had invested about US$4 million in the coup. He cited Martin Andersen's 'Dossier Secreto' for García Meza's attendance at a congress of the Latin American Anti-Communist Confederation (CAL), the WACL's regional branch.
cite: Robert Parry, The Consortium, 19 August 1998 (single-author account)

n: APROH — armed forces chief's group took Moon front money
rank: commander of the armed forces (Gen. Gustavo Álvarez Martínez)
d: The Association for the Progress of Honduras (APROH), headed by armed forces commander General Gustavo Álvarez Martínez, joined business leaders and officers; the Library of Congress country study says it received a US$50,000 contribution from a front group for the Unification Church. The Christian Science Monitor reported in March 1984 that APROH and allied forces had taken control of university, professional, teacher, labour and peasant bodies. Fellow officers ousted Álvarez on 31 March 1984 and APROH declined.
cite: Library of Congress, 'Honduras: A Country Study' (1995); Christian Science Monitor, 21 March 1984

n: CIA funds the Congress for Cultural Freedom
rank: US Central Intelligence Agency (International Organizations Division)
d: The Congress for Cultural Freedom was founded in West Berlin in June 1950 and run from Paris by Michael Josselson, a CIA officer. At its height it had offices in 35 countries and published more than 20 magazines, including Encounter (London) and Preuves (Paris). The New York Times named CIA funding in April 1966; Ramparts and the Saturday Evening Post followed in 1967, and Thomas Braden, former head of the CIA's International Organizations Division, admitted in print that the CIA had funded the Congress and Encounter for more than ten years. The CIA's own historians now call it one of its 'more daring and effective Cold War covert operations'. After 1967 it was renamed the International Association for Cultural Freedom and funded by the Ford Foundation until it dissolved in 1979.
cite: New York Times series, April 1966; Thomas Braden, 'I'm Glad the CIA Is Immoral', Saturday Evening Post, May 1967; CIA Center for the Study of Intelligence, 'Origins of the Congress for Cultural Freedom'

n: Asia Foundation set up as a CIA proprietary
d: A CIA memorandum to the White House 303 Committee dated 22 June 1966 describes the Asia Foundation as 'a Central Intelligence Agency proprietary, established in 1954 to undertake cultural and educational activities on behalf of the United States Government in ways not open to official U.S. agencies'. It grew out of the Committee for a Free Asia (1951); CIA support ran under the code name DTPILLAR. After the 1966-67 press disclosures of CIA funding of private groups, a review led by Secretary of State Dean Rusk decided the foundation should be kept and funded openly by the US government.
cite: Foreign Relations of the United States 1964-68, vol. X, doc. 132 (CIA memorandum to the 303 Committee, 22 June 1966)

n: CIA funding of the US National Student Association
d: From the early 1950s until 1967 the CIA secretly paid for the international programme and some domestic work of the National Student Association, the federation of US college student governments, while a few of its officers worked closely with CIA officials. Former staffer Michael Wood exposed the arrangement in Ramparts in February 1967. President Johnson then set up the Katzenbach Committee to review CIA funding of US private voluntary groups, and in August 1967 the NSA formally cut its ties to the CIA.
cite: Ramparts, February 1967; New York Times, 16 Feb 1967; US Senate Church Committee Final Report, Book I (1976), on the Katzenbach Committee

n: CIA money through AFL Free Trade Union Committee, Italy 1948
rank: 1948 Italian general election (party and union politics)
d: The American Federation of Labor's Free Trade Union Committee, run by Jay Lovestone, was set up in 1944 to back non-communist unions abroad. Historian Anthony Carew found that the CIA channelled money to the committee for about 20 years, starting with efforts to influence the Italian elections of 1948. The committee also subsidised Force Ouvrière in France from 1948 through its Paris representative Irving Brown, and according to French journalist Frédéric Charpier the CIA division under Thomas Braden gave Brown and Lovestone about $1 million a year in 1951-54.
cite: Anthony Carew, 'The American Labor Movement in Fizzland: The Free Trade Union Committee and the CIA', Labor History (Feb 1998); Frédéric Charpier, La CIA en France (Seuil, 2008)

n: AIFLD trainees and the 1964 coup against Goulart
rank: President João Goulart (overthrown by the military, 1 April 1964)
d: The American Institute for Free Labor Development was chartered in August 1962 by the AFL-CIO and contracted directly with USAID; it ran training institutes in Recife and São Paulo. Its director William Doherty Jr. later said the institute's Brazilian trainees were 'intimately involved' in the military and civilian conspiracy against President Goulart. Historian Cliff Welch writes that exactly what they did 'remains unclear' and their role was probably less central than Doherty claimed; after the coup, AIFLD graduates helped take over unions whose leftist leaders had been purged. This rests on Doherty's own statement and later historians, not on a court or inquiry finding.
cite: Cliff Welch, 'Labor Internationalism: U.S. Involvement in Brazilian Unions, 1945-1965', Latin American Research Review; Philip Agee, Inside the Company (1974)

n: CIA-linked IBAD funds opposition candidates, 1962 election
rank: Candidates for the National Congress and state governorships, October 1962
d: The Brazilian Institute of Democratic Action (IBAD), linked to the CIA and backed by multinational companies, paid for the campaigns of many opposition candidates in the October 1962 elections for Congress and eleven state governments. A Brazilian Parliamentary Inquiry Commission investigated the funding, and President Goulart closed the institute the following year. In 1977 former US ambassador Lincoln Gordon admitted that the United States had funded the opposition in that election.
cite: Brazilian Chamber of Deputies Parliamentary Inquiry Commission (CPI) on IBAD, 1963; Lincoln Gordon statement, 1977

n: Radio Free Europe and Radio Liberty run on CIA money
d: Radio Free Europe (1949) was created by the National Committee for a Free Europe, a CIA front organised by Allen Dulles in New York, and Radio Liberty followed in 1951; both broadcast from Munich into the Soviet bloc. The CIA and State Department set broad policy directives for the stations. In 1971 Senator Clifford Case introduced a bill to take their funding out of the CIA budget; CIA funding ended in 1971-72, and from 1974 a Board for International Broadcasting passed open congressional appropriations to the stations.
cite: US Congress, S.18 (Senator Clifford Case, 1971); Presidential Study Commission on International Radio Broadcasting (1972-73); Board for International Broadcasting Act 1973

n: Church Committee: CIA used foundations, unions, students, academics
d: The Senate Select Committee on Intelligence Activities (Church Committee) found that, leaving out Ford, Rockefeller and Carnegie, at least 108 of the 700 grants over $10,000 given by 164 other US foundations in 1963-66 involved partial or complete CIA funding, and that CIA money was in nearly half of these foundations' grants for international activities. It found CIA labor, student and media projects peaked in 1964-67 and were cut back after the 1967 Ramparts disclosures and the Katzenbach Committee. It also reported that the CIA was then using several hundred American academics at more than 100 colleges and universities, and until February 1976 had covert ties to about 50 US journalists.
cite: US Senate Select Committee to Study Governmental Operations with Respect to Intelligence Activities, Final Report, Book I, pp. 182-192 (26 April 1976)

n: NED founder: 'what we do today was done covertly by the CIA'
rank: Overt successor to CIA political-action funding
d: The National Endowment for Democracy was created by Congress in 1983 and is funded almost wholly by congressional appropriations. In a September 1991 Washington Post article by David Ignatius, NED founder Allen Weinstein said: 'A lot of what we do today was done covertly 25 years ago by the CIA.' In 1986 NED president Carl Gershman had said NED was set up because it would be 'terrible for democratic groups around the world to be seen as subsidized by the CIA'.
cite: David Ignatius, 'Innocence Abroad: The New World of Spyless Coups', Washington Post, 22 Sept 1991

n: US-funded opposition before Nicaragua's 1990 election
rank: Presidential election won by Violeta Chamorro (UNO), February 1990
d: Historian William LeoGrande writes that NED's roughly $2 million in Nicaragua in 1984-88 was the main source of open aid to the civic opposition, about half of it to La Prensa, the paper run by Violeta Chamorro. In October 1989 the US House voted 263-156 for President Bush's plan to spend a further $9 million to boost the opposition before the 25 February 1990 election, which Chamorro's National Opposition Union won. Critics compared NED's Nicaraguan funding with earlier CIA operations in Chile; NED says its grants are public and nonpartisan.
cite: William M. LeoGrande, Our Own Backyard (1998); Associated Press, 'Nicaragua aid passes House', 6 Oct 1989

n: Russia bans NED as 'undesirable'
rank: Russian government designation (Prosecutor General / Justice Ministry list)
d: In July 2015 Russia declared the National Endowment for Democracy an 'undesirable' organisation, the first group banned under the undesirable-organisations law signed two months earlier. Russian officials and state media blamed NED grants for, among other things, the 2014 Euromaidan protests in Ukraine. The designation is the Russian government's assertion; no court or independent body has found that NED worked inside Russian state institutions.
cite: Russian Ministry of Justice list of undesirable organisations, July 2015; The Guardian, 28 July 2015

n: China sanctions NED over Hong Kong
d: In December 2019 China sanctioned NED and other US groups after Congress passed the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act. In August 2019 its Foreign Ministry had circulated a report naming NED as a US intelligence front and listing 20 years of NED grants to political groups in Hong Kong. This is the Chinese government's assertion, not the finding of an independent forum.
cite: Chinese Foreign Ministry statement, 2 Dec 2019; Washington Post, 2 Dec 2019

n: John Perkins's 'economic hit man' account of Chas. T. Main
rank: Economic forecasts used for foreign borrowing (Perkins's claim)
d: John Perkins worked for the Boston engineering firm Chas. T. Main in the 1970s and became its chief economist. In Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004) he says his job was to inflate growth forecasts so that countries such as Indonesia, Ecuador, Panama and Saudi Arabia would take large loans for infrastructure, and that the National Security Agency screened him for the job. A 2006 New York Times check found 'the arc of Mr. Perkins's career seems to be described accurately' but found no evidence for his 'fancier claims', including the NSA link; Main's former vice president Einar Greve agreed the debt story was 'basically' true but denied the NSA link, and the US State Department called much of the book 'a total fabrication'. All of the hit-man claims are Perkins's own.
cite: John Perkins, Confessions of an Economic Hit Man (2004); New York Times, 'Confessing to the Converted', 19 Feb 2006; Boston Magazine, May 2006; US State Department, Feb 2006

n: US-Saudi Joint Commission (JECOR) run from the US Treasury
rank: Saudi Ministry of Finance and National Economy (co-chaired with the US Treasury Secretary)
d: The US-Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation was set up in 1974, after the Arab oil embargo, with the US Treasury Secretary and the Saudi Minister of Finance as co-chairs. A March 1979 Government Accounting Office report found that US technical assistance under it was 'funded almost entirely from the Saudi Arabian Trust Account in the U.S. Treasury', that it recycled petrodollars and steered US goods, services and technology to Saudi Arabia, and that it had 16 formal projects. John Perkins says Chas. T. Main worked on Saudi projects in this period; that is his claim, while the commission and its Treasury-held Saudi funding are documented by the GAO.
cite: US General Accounting Office, 'The U.S.-Saudi Arabian Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation', ID-79-7, 22 March 1979

n: Berkeley-trained economists run Suharto's planning and finance
rank: Head of BAPPENAS, finance minister and other economic ministries
d: In the late 1950s the Ford Foundation paid for University of Indonesia economists, led by dean Sumitro Djojohadikusumo's faculty, to take graduate degrees at the University of California, Berkeley. After Suharto took power in 1966 he made them his economic team: Widjojo Nitisastro headed the planning agency BAPPENAS (1967-83) and was Coordinating Minister for Economics, Finance and Industry (1973-83); Ali Wardhana was Finance Minister (1968-83); Emil Salim and Mohammad Sadli also held ministries. Their 1966 programme cut inflation from 650% to 13% by 1969 and opened the country to foreign investors.
cite: Ford Foundation, 'Celebrating Indonesia'; Hal Hill and Thee Kian Wie, Bulletin of Indonesian Economic Studies (2008)

n: Widjojo Nitisastro — BAPPENAS head and coordinating minister
rank: Head of National Development Planning Agency (1967-83); Coordinating Minister for Economics, Finance and Industry (1973-83)
d: Widjojo took his doctorate at Berkeley under the Ford Foundation-funded programme for University of Indonesia economists. He led the economists who presented a stabilisation plan to Suharto at the army staff college seminar in August 1966. He then headed BAPPENAS from June 1967 to March 1983 and wrote the Five-Year Development Plans.
cite: Widjojo Nitisastro, The Indonesian Development Experience (ISEAS, 2011)

n: Ali Wardhana — Suharto's finance minister 1968-83
d: Ali Wardhana studied at the University of Indonesia and earned his doctorate at Berkeley in the Ford Foundation-funded programme, and is counted among the 'Berkeley Mafia'. He served as Suharto's Minister of Finance from June 1968 to March 1983, one of the longest-serving ministers in Indonesian history.
cite: Hal Hill and Thee Kian Wie, Bulletin of Indonesian Economic Studies

n: Chicago-trained economists take Pinochet's economic ministries
rank: Ministers of finance, economy, planning; Central Bank presidents
d: The 'Chile Project' began in the mid-1950s as a US government Point Four aid scheme linking the University of Chicago economics department with Santiago's Catholic University. Between 1955 and 1973, 126 Chilean students trained under it, first funded through US aid (to 1964) and then by the Ford Foundation. Their 189-page plan 'El ladrillo' became the junta's economic programme in 1975, and graduates held top posts: Sergio de Castro (Economy 1975-76, Finance 1976-82), Pablo Baraona (Economy 1976-79), Miguel Kast (Planning, Labor, Central Bank), Sergio de la Cuadra (Central Bank, Finance 1982), Rolf Lüders (Economy and Finance 1982-83).
cite: Milton and Rose Friedman, Two Lucky People (1998); University of Chicago-Catholic University exchange records as summarised in the Wikipedia article 'Chicago Boys'

n: Sergio de Castro — Pinochet's economy then finance minister
rank: Minister of Economy (1975-76); Minister of Finance (1976-82)
d: Sergio de Castro studied at the Catholic University of Chile and the University of Chicago under the US-funded Chile Project, and was a co-author of 'El ladrillo'. He was Minister of Economy from April 1975 to December 1976 and Minister of Finance from December 1976 to April 1982, when the 1982 debt crisis ended his term.
cite: Chilean government records; Wikipedia biography citing Chilean sources

n: Miguel Kast — planning minister and Central Bank governor
rank: Minister of Planning (1978-80); Labor Minister (1980-82); Central Bank governor (1982-83)
d: Miguel Kast studied at the Catholic University of Chile and took a master's at the University of Chicago. Under Pinochet he headed the planning office ODEPLAN, then the labor ministry, and in 1982 became governor of the Central Bank of Chile.
cite: Chilean government records; Wikipedia biography citing Chilean sources

n: Meng Hongwei — Interpol president detained in China
rank: Vice-Minister of Public Security (2004-18) while Interpol president (2016-18)
d: Meng Hongwei was elected Interpol's first Chinese president on 10 November 2016 while serving as China's Vice-Minister of Public Security. He disappeared after flying to China on 25 September 2018; on 7 October the Communist Party's discipline commission said he was under investigation for bribery, and Interpol received his resignation. In January 2020 a Tianjin court sentenced him to 13 and a half years for taking more than 14.5 million yuan (about $2.1 million) in bribes. His wife Grace Meng, granted asylum in France, says the case is political.
cite: Tianjin No. 1 Intermediate People's Court, judgment of 21 January 2020; Reuters, 21 Jan 2020

n: Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi — UAE interior official elected Interpol president
rank: Inspector General, UAE Ministry of Interior; Interpol president (2021-25)
d: Major General Ahmed Naser Al-Raisi, inspector general of the UAE Interior Ministry, was elected Interpol president in Istanbul on 25 November 2021 with about 69% of the votes in the third round. Before the vote, 19 NGOs opposed him, 35 French parliamentarians wrote to President Macron, and a report by former UK Director of Public Prosecutions David Calvert-Smith called him unsuited and questioned UAE donations to Interpol. Britons Matthew Hedges and Ali Issa Ahmad accuse him of responsibility for their torture in UAE custody; in March 2022 French anti-terrorism prosecutors opened a preliminary inquiry into the torture complaints. The UAE denies the accusations.
cite: French National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor's Office, preliminary inquiry (March 2022); The Guardian, 24 March 2022

n: UAE gifts to Interpol's foundation
rank: Interpol funding through the Interpol Foundation for a Safer World
d: Through the Interpol Foundation for a Safer World, set up in 2013, the UAE gave donations reported at about $54 million, estimated to equal the statutory contributions of the other 194 member countries combined. Critics say the money helped the UAE win the right to host the 2018 General Assembly and Al-Raisi's 2021 election; the Calvert-Smith report raised the same concern, and Interpol rejected it.
cite: David Calvert-Smith, report on UAE and Interpol (April 2021); The Guardian, 7 April 2021

n: Interpol refuses 773 Turkish Red Notice requests on Gülen suspects
d: After the July 2016 coup attempt Turkey asked Interpol for Red Notices against people it accuses of links to the Gülen movement. In June 2021 Lütfi Çiçek, head of the Interpol department of Turkey's Interior Ministry, said Interpol had refused 773 such requests after finding them political, plus 240 more aimed at people linked to Kurdish and leftist groups. Interpol also refused a Turkish request concerning NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom.
cite: Statement of Lütfi Çiçek, Turkish Interior Ministry, June 2021 (reported by Stockholm Center for Freedom)

n: Interpol deletes China's Red Notice for Uyghur leader Dolkun Isa
rank: Chinese Ministry of Public Security request
d: China had sought Dolkun Isa, a leader of the World Uyghur Congress living in Germany, through an Interpol Red Notice, calling him a terrorist; no Western country acted on it. In February 2018, while China's Meng Hongwei was Interpol president, Interpol removed the notice, and China protested. Rights groups say China has used Interpol channels against Uyghurs abroad and record 1,546 detentions or deportations of Uyghurs from 28 countries since 1997.
cite: Reuters, 'China upset as Interpol removes wanted alert for exiled Uighur leader', 24 Feb 2018

n: Bahrain's Red Notice for refugee footballer Hakeem al-Araibi
d: Bahrain obtained a Red Notice for Hakeem al-Araibi, a footballer and dissident who had fled Bahrain in 2014 and was a refugee in Australia. Thai police arrested him on arrival in Bangkok in November 2018. Interpol withdrew the notice days later because its 2015 policy bars notices sought by the country a refugee fled; Thailand still held extradition proceedings until prosecutors dropped the case on 11 February 2019.
cite: Interpol refugee policy (2015); Thai Office of the Attorney General, 11 Feb 2019

n: Russia's use of Interpol against critics; Prokopchuk candidacy
rank: Russian Interior Ministry; Interpol vice-president Alexander Prokopchuk
d: Interpol refused Russia's repeated requests for a Red Notice against financier Bill Browder as 'predominantly political'. In November 2018 four US senators said Interpol vice-president Alexander Prokopchuk, a Russian Interior Ministry general, had abused Red Notices, and he lost the presidency vote to Kim Jong Yang. In January 2026 the BBC reported leaked files showing Interpol received more complaints about Russia than any other country and that some extra checks added after 2022 were dropped in 2025.
cite: BBC, 'Likely next Interpol chief Prokopchuk fox in the henhouse, US senators say', 20 Nov 2018; Council of Europe PACE and OSCE PA resolutions (2010-2017)

n: Zeltner Committee: tobacco firms worked to undermine WHO
rank: WHO decision-making and member-state health delegations
d: At Director-General Gro Harlem Brundtland's request, a committee of experts chaired by Thomas Zeltner, director of the Swiss Federal Office of Public Health, examined tobacco-industry documents released in US lawsuits. Its 246-page report, received by WHO on 28 July 2000, found an 'elaborate, well financed, sophisticated and usually invisible' effort to undermine WHO tobacco control, working also through FAO, ECOSOC and the World Bank, through consultants and scientists, and through food subsidiaries that offered partnerships to UN agencies. It urged member states to investigate tobacco-company influence on their own national decisions. The report led into the WHO Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (2003).
cite: Committee of Experts on Tobacco Industry Documents, 'Tobacco Company Strategies to Undermine Tobacco Control Activities at the World Health Organization', WHO, July 2000

n: Council of Europe Assembly criticises WHO H1N1 handling
rank: WHO and European health ministries (pandemic vaccine decisions)
d: On 24 June 2010 the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe voted 60-1 for a resolution, from a health committee report by Paul Flynn, saying the H1N1 response of WHO, EU agencies and national governments wasted large sums of public money. It found 'grave shortcomings' in the transparency of decision-making that 'generated concerns about the influence of the pharmaceutical industry', and noted that WHO withheld the names of its Emergency Committee members. The Assembly did not find proven industry control; WHO denied any improper influence but accepted it needed stronger transparency rules.
cite: Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, Resolution 1749 (2010), 'Handling of the H1N1 pandemic: more transparency needed'

n: José Maria Marin — ex-São Paulo governor jailed in FIFA case
rank: Former governor of São Paulo state (1982-83); CBF president (2012-15)
d: José Maria Marin was a São Paulo city councillor, state deputy, vice-governor and, in 1982-83, governor of São Paulo state before heading the Brazilian Football Confederation. Arrested in Zurich in May 2015 in the US FIFA investigation, he was convicted by a Brooklyn federal jury in December 2017 of taking bribes on football marketing contracts. In August 2018 he was sentenced to four years, fined $1.2 million and ordered to forfeit $3.34 million.
cite: US District Court, Eastern District of New York, United States v. Marin et al.; The Guardian, 22 Aug 2018

n: Rafael Callejas — ex-President of Honduras pleads guilty in FIFA case
rank: Former President of Honduras (1990-94); head of Honduran football federation
d: Rafael Leonardo Callejas, President of Honduras from 1990 to 1994, later headed the Honduran football federation until 2015. He was indicted in the US FIFA case on 3 December 2015 and on 27 March 2016 pleaded guilty to taking $500,000 in bribes in 2012 for media and marketing rights. FIFA's Ethics Committee banned him for life in December 2016; he died in April 2020.
cite: US Department of Justice, superseding indictment of 3 Dec 2015 (E.D.N.Y.); New York Times, 12 April 2020

n: Jack Warner — FIFA vice-president and Trinidad cabinet minister
rank: Minister of Works and Transport (from 2010); Minister of National Security (to April 2013)
d: Jack Warner was FIFA vice-president and CONCACAF president until 2011, and from 2010 sat in Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar's cabinet as Works and Transport Minister and then Minister of National Security, resigning from the cabinet on 21 April 2013. A CONCACAF Integrity Committee report in April 2013 concluded he had committed fraud against CONCACAF and FIFA. US prosecutors indicted him in May 2015 for wire fraud, racketeering and money laundering, including a $10 million payment tied to South Africa's 2010 World Cup bid; FIFA banned him for life. On 23 September 2025 Trinidad's High Court blocked his extradition.
cite: US Department of Justice indictment, 27 May 2015 (E.D.N.Y.); CONCACAF Integrity Committee report, 18 April 2013; AP, 24 Sept 2025

n: Héctor Trujillo — Guatemalan judge pleads guilty in FIFA case
rank: Judge (listed as on the Constitutional Court of Guatemala); general secretary of Guatemala's football federation
d: Héctor Trujillo was general secretary of Guatemala's football federation while serving as a judge in Guatemala. He was arrested in December 2015 when a cruise ship docked in Florida, charged in the US FIFA case with taking bribes for World Cup qualifier marketing rights, pleaded guilty, and was jailed.
cite: US Department of Justice superseding indictment, 3 Dec 2015; New York Times, 4 Dec 2015; Sky Sports

n: Carlos Nuzman — Rio 2016 vote-buying conviction
rank: Head of Rio 2016 bid and Brazilian Olympic Committee, working with Rio state governor
d: In the 'Unfair Play' phase of Operation Car Wash, police arrested Carlos Arthur Nuzman, head of the Brazilian Olympic Committee and Rio 2016 organising committee, in October 2017, accusing him of channelling $2 million to IOC member Lamine Diack to secure votes when Rio was chosen in 2009. On 26 November 2021 federal judge Marcelo Bretas sentenced him to 30 years, 11 months for corruption, organised crime, money laundering and currency evasion; he remained free while appealing. The IOC suspended him in October 2017.
cite: 7th Federal Criminal Court of Rio de Janeiro, sentence of 26 Nov 2021; Agência Brasil, 26 Nov 2021

n: Sérgio Cabral — Rio governor admits paying $2m for Olympic votes
rank: Governor of Rio de Janeiro state (2007-14)
d: Sérgio Cabral, governor of Rio de Janeiro state from 2007 to 2014, was arrested in November 2016 in Operation Car Wash and later received sentences totalling over 400 years in many cases, some annulled in 2024. In July 2019 he testified in court that he paid $2 million, through businessman Arthur César de Menezes Soares Filho, to IOC member Lamine Diack to buy votes for Rio's 2009 Olympic bid. He was a co-defendant with Nuzman in the federal case.
cite: Testimony before Judge Marcelo Bretas, 7th Federal Criminal Court, Rio, July 2019; BBC, 5 July 2019

n: Ludwig Erhard — Mont Pelerin Society member in office

He was Chancellor from 1963 to 1966. Membership and office are documented; no forum has found that the society directed his or her decisions.

n: IEA: 14 of Johnson's cabinet were 'alumni of IEA initiatives'

Javid had said in 2015 that the IEA 'deeply influenced' his views. Matthew Elliott, chief executive of Vote Leave, had founded the TaxPayers' Alliance, another Atlas partner. The claim is the IEA's own; the Guardian reported it.
cite: The Guardian, 'How the right's radical thinktanks reshaped the Conservative party', 29 Nov 2019

n: Tim Wilson — IPA policy director to Human Rights Commissioner and minister
rank: Australian Human Rights Commissioner (2014-16); Assistant Minister for Industry, Energy and Emissions Reduction (2021-22)
d: Tim Wilson was policy director at the Institute of Public Affairs, an Atlas Network partner, from 2007 to 2013. The Abbott government appointed him Australia's Human Rights Commissioner in 2014; he entered parliament in 2016 and was an assistant minister in 2021-22.
cite: Australian Parliament biography; Atlas Network partner directory

n: Cristián Larroulet — Libertad y Desarrollo director to Piñera minister
d: Cristián Larroulet was executive director of the Santiago think tank Libertad y Desarrollo, an Atlas Network partner that runs a Free Enterprise Training Centre with Atlas. He had been chief of staff at the Treasury under Hernán Büchi. President Sebastián Piñera made him Minister Secretary-General of the Presidency from 2010 to 2014 and later head of presidential advisers.
cite: Chilean government records; Atlas Network partner listings

n: David Seymour — Atlas-linked think-tank work, now deputy PM
rank: Minister for Regulation (2023-); Deputy Prime Minister (2025-)

He became ACT party leader in 2014, Minister for Regulation in 2023 and Deputy Prime Minister in 2025. Atlas chair Debbi Gibbs is the daughter of ACT co-founder Alan Gibbs.
cite: New Zealand Parliament biography; reporting on Atlas Network links

He served as Deputy Assistant to the President from January to August 2017, and again from January 2025 as senior director for counterterrorism.
cite: The Intercept, 'Sphere of Influence', 9 Aug 2017

n: Fundación Pensar merges into Macri's party

n: Cedice director signs the 2002 Carmona decree
rank: Short-lived coup government of Pedro Carmona (April 2002)
d: Cedice Libertad, Atlas's main think tank in Caracas, received regular grants from 1998 from the Center for International Private Enterprise, an NED core institute; one grant letter lists NED funds for Cedice to advocate 'a change in government'. Cedice's director was among the signers of the 'Carmona Decree', which dissolved the National Assembly and Supreme Court during the April 2002 coup against Hugo Chávez.
cite: The Intercept, 'Sphere of Influence', 9 Aug 2017, citing NED grant records

n: Jameson Raid — Cape premier Rhodes found culpable by Commons committee
rank: Prime Minister of the Cape Colony
d: Leander Starr Jameson led a column of British South Africa Company police into the Transvaal on 29 December 1895 and surrendered at Doornkop on 2 January 1896. Cecil Rhodes, Cape premier and chairman of the company, lost the premiership and left the company board in 1896; the company paid the Transvaal almost £1 million. The 1897 House of Commons Select Committee on British South Africa censured Rhodes ('your Committee can see no excuse'); his solicitor Bourchier Hawksley refused to produce the company's telegrams to it. Quigley, who names Hawksley as a trustee of Rhodes's 1892 will, writes that the Rhodes group 'plotted the Jameson Raid'; that link is Quigley's claim.
cite: House of Commons debate on the Select Committee report, HC Deb 26 July 1897 vol 51; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment (1981), pp. 5, 33–34

n: Alfred Milner — Rhodes's chosen heir as High Commissioner
rank: High Commissioner for Southern Africa; Governor of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony
d: Milner was High Commissioner for Southern Africa and Governor of the Cape from May 1897, administrator and then Governor of the Transvaal and Orange River Colony from 1901 to April 1905, and a Rhodes Trust trustee from Rhodes's death in March 1902. These offices are on the record. Carroll Quigley says Milner was named to the 'Junta of Three' of Rhodes's secret society in 1891 and was Rhodes's chosen successor as its leader, and that the group 'caused the Boer War of 1899–1902'. The membership and the war claim rest on Quigley.
cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 3–5, 33; Wikipedia 'Alfred Milner, 1st Viscount Milner' (offices)

n: Milner's Kindergarten — Oxford men run the Transvaal administration
rank: Transvaal colonial secretary, treasurer, town clerk of Johannesburg, Intercolonial Council secretary
d: From 1901 Milner recruited young Oxford graduates into the colonial government of the conquered Boer republics. Patrick Duncan became Transvaal Treasurer and then Colonial Secretary (1903–07); Richard Feetham and Lionel Curtis served as town clerks of Johannesburg; Robert Brand was secretary of the Intercolonial Council; Geoffrey Robinson (Dawson) was Milner's secretary and then editor of the Johannesburg Star. The appointments are documented. Quigley calls the group the 'Association of Helpers', the outer circle of Rhodes's secret society; that classification is his.
cite: Wikipedia 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 4

n: Kindergarten drafts the case for the Union of South Africa
rank: National Convention of 1908–09; Transvaal Legislative Council
d: Members of the Kindergarten pressed for union of the four colonies: Curtis founded the monthly The State (funded by Abe Bailey) in 1908, Brand served as secretary to the Transvaal delegates at the National Convention and wrote The Union of South Africa (1909), and Feetham sat on the Transvaal Legislative Council (1907–10). The Kindergarten wanted a federal model; the Convention chose a unitary state, and the Union came into being in 1910. Quigley writes that the group 'created the Union of South Africa in 1906–1910'; that is his summary.
cite: Wikipedia 'Robert Brand, 1st Baron Brand', 'Richard Feetham', 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, p. 5

n: Lord Esher — named to Rhodes's 'Junta', chairs War Office reform
d: Reginald Brett, Lord Esher, chaired the War Office (Reconstitution) Committee with Admiral John Fisher and Colonel George Clarke; its 1904 report created the Army Council and a permanent secretariat for the Committee of Imperial Defence. He declined the War Office and the Viceroyalty of India and advised Edward VII almost daily from 1903. Carroll Quigley, citing Esher's journals, says Brett was told of Rhodes's plan on 3 February 1890 and was named with Stead and Milner to the society's 'Junta of Three' in February 1891.
cite: Wikipedia 'Reginald Brett, 2nd Viscount Esher'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 3, 38–39

n: Earl Grey — Rhodes trustee as Governor General of Canada
d: Albert Grey, 4th Earl Grey, was a director of the British South Africa Company, Administrator of Rhodesia after Jameson's 1896 resignation, one of the first trustees of the Rhodes Trust, and Governor General of Canada from 10 December 1904 to 13 October 1911. Quigley lists Grey in the 'Circle of Initiates' drawn up by Rhodes and Stead in 1891.
cite: Wikipedia 'Albert Grey, 4th Earl Grey'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 12, 39

n: Milner joins Lloyd George's five-man War Cabinet
rank: Member of the War Cabinet; Secretary of State for War; Colonial Secretary
d: Lloyd George asked Milner to join the War Cabinet on 8 December 1916; he sat in it until November 1918, was Secretary of State for War from April 1918 to January 1919 and Colonial Secretary from January 1919 to February 1921. Leo Amery, whom Quigley counts in the group, served under him as personal secretary at the Colonial Office (1919–21). Quigley says Milner held regular 'Ginger Group' meetings with close associates in 1913–1919 to coordinate them as a pressure group; that account is his.
cite: Wikipedia 'Alfred Milner, 1st Viscount Milner' and 'Leo Amery'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope (1966), p. 951

n: Philip Kerr and the 'Garden Suburb' at 10 Downing Street
rank: Private secretary to the Prime Minister; Prime Minister's Secretariat
d: In December 1916 Lloyd George set up a personal secretariat in huts in the garden of 10 Downing Street. Its first members were W. G. S. Adams, David Davies, Joseph Davies, Waldorf Astor and Philip Kerr, the founding editor of The Round Table (1910–16); Kerr stayed as the Prime Minister's private secretary until March 1921 and wrote the Fontainebleau Memorandum of March 1919. H. W. Massingham attacked the group in The Nation (24 February 1917) as 'illuminati'. Historian John Turner (Historical Journal, 1977) examined whether it was 'Milnerite penetration' and found Milner's influence on its staffing; Quigley treats it as a Milner Group placement.
cite: J. A. Turner, 'The Formation of Lloyd George's "Garden Suburb": "Fabian-like Milnerite Penetration"?', Historical Journal 20:1 (1977), 165–184; Wikipedia 'Philip Kerr, 11th Marquess of Lothian'

n: Curtis's Round Table study group and India's 'dyarchy'
rank: India Office; Government of India constitution (Government of India Act 1919)
