d: Quigley writes that Lionel Curtis formed a study group inside the London Round Table about 1911, joined by three India Office officials (Sir William Duke, Malcolm Seton, Sir Lionel Abrahams), which settled on 'dyarchy' — transferring some provincial functions to elected Indian ministers. Lord Chelmsford told the Lords in November 1927 he had been handed a pamphlet with the 'diarchic principle' at the India Office in 1916, thinking it came from an official committee. James Meston, a Kindergarten adviser, sat in the Imperial War Cabinet in 1917. Dyarchy was enacted in the Government of India Act 1919; Curtis described the group's work in his book Dyarchy (1920).
cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 11, pp. 202–204; Lionel Curtis, Dyarchy (1920); Wikipedia 'Lionel Curtis'

n: Feetham chairs the Irish Boundary Commission
d: Richard Feetham, a Kindergarten member and South African judge, chaired the Irish Boundary Commission of 1924–25 that was to fix the border between the Irish Free State and Northern Ireland; its report was unacceptable to both governments and was buried. Lionel Curtis had been involved in the making of the 1921 Anglo-Irish Treaty. Quigley writes that most of Feetham's posts 'came to him as a member of the Milner Group' and that the group's part in the Irish settlement was 'considerably more' than The Round Table admitted; those are his claims.
cite: Wikipedia 'Richard Feetham' and 'Lionel Curtis'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 4 and ch. 9

n: Geoffrey Dawson edits The Times through appeasement
rank: Editor of The Times (influence on government policy)
d: Dawson, Milner's secretary in South Africa and a lifelong Fellow of All Souls, edited The Times in 1912–19 and 1923–41. On 23 May 1937 he wrote to Lord Lothian: 'I spend my nights in taking out anything which I think will hurt their susceptibilities', meaning German opinion. A Times leader of 7 September 1938 suggested Czechoslovakia might gain from ceding its German-speaking border districts. Quigley says the group 'controlled The Times for more than fifty years' except 1919–22 and places the 'Cliveden set' near its centre.
cite: Wikipedia 'Geoffrey Dawson'; The Times leader of 7 Sept 1938 as quoted at airminded.org; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 4–5

n: Lord Halifax — Foreign Secretary counted by Quigley in the group
rank: Foreign Secretary; Viceroy of India; Ambassador to the United States
d: Edward Wood, Lord Halifax, a Fellow of All Souls from 1903, was Viceroy of India (1926–31), met Hitler in November 1937, was Foreign Secretary from 21 February 1938 to 22 December 1940 and defended the Munich Agreement in the Lords on 3 October 1938, then was ambassador in Washington until 1946. Quigley writes that Halifax was close to the group from 1903 'but did not really become a member until after 1920' and should 'probably be placed in the inner core'. The membership claim is Quigley's.
cite: Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 5–6; Wikipedia 'E. F. L. Wood, 1st Earl of Halifax'

n: Patrick Duncan — Governor-General who installed Smuts in 1939
rank: Governor-General of the Union of South Africa
d: Duncan, Milner's Transvaal Colonial Secretary, became the first South African citizen appointed Governor-General in 1937 and served until his death on 17 July 1943. In 1939, after Prime Minister Hertzog lost a parliamentary vote and resigned, Duncan refused his request for a general election and commissioned Jan Smuts to form a government. Quigley calls Duncan Smuts's 'chief lieutenant', inherited 'directly from Milner', and counts Smuts in the Milner Group.
cite: Wikipedia 'Patrick Duncan (governor-general)'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, pp. 78–79

n: John Buchan — Kindergarten member as Governor General of Canada
d: John Buchan served on Milner's staff in South Africa until 1903, entered Parliament in 1927 and was Governor General of Canada from 1935 until his death in 1940. He is listed as a member of Milner's Kindergarten; Quigley counts him in the wider Milner Group.
cite: Wikipedia 'Milner's Kindergarten'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment

n: Lord Lothian — Rhodes Trust secretary sent as ambassador to Washington
rank: British Ambassador to the United States
d: Philip Kerr, 11th Marquess of Lothian, was General Secretary of the Rhodes Trust from 1925 until 1939, Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster (August–November 1931) and Under-Secretary for India (1931–32). He met Hitler in January 1935 and May 1937 and argued for revising Versailles in Germany's favour until March 1939. He was ambassador in Washington from 1 September 1939 until he died there on 12 December 1940. Quigley names Kerr leader of the society from 1925 to 1940.
cite: Wikipedia 'Philip Kerr, 11th Marquess of Lothian'; Quigley, The Anglo-American Establishment, p. 4

n: Robert Brand — Lazard director on Britain's wartime missions
rank: Head, British Food Mission; UK Treasury representative in Washington
d: Brand joined Lazard Brothers in 1909 and became a managing director; in 1915 he helped set up the Imperial Munitions Board in Canada. He headed the British Food Mission to the United States (1941–44) and was the Treasury's representative in Washington (1944–46), and was made a peer in 1946. He was married to Nancy Astor's sister. Quigley names Brand leader of the group after Curtis (to 1963) and calls him an 'international financier' of its inner circle.
cite: Wikipedia 'Robert Brand, 1st Baron Brand'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, pp. 950–951

n: Chatham House research service moved into the Foreign Office
rank: Foreign Office (wartime research and press analysis)
d: During the Second World War Chatham House ran a Foreign Research and Press Service directed by Arnold Toynbee, and the service was moved into the Foreign Office from 1943 to 1946. Chatham House itself grew from a meeting Lionel Curtis convened of about 30 British and American delegation experts at the Hotel Majestic, Paris, on 30 May 1919; it held its inaugural meeting on 5 July 1920 and received a royal charter in 1926.
cite: Chatham House, 'The Hotel Majestic and the Origins of Chatham House' (2019); Wikipedia 'Chatham House'

n: Quigley: CFR as the New York branch of the Round Table network
rank: Council on Foreign Relations board (Morgan partners and associates)
d: In Tragedy and Hope (1966) Carroll Quigley wrote that the Council on Foreign Relations 'was a front for J. P. Morgan and Company in association with the very small American Round Table Group', and that in 1928 its board included John W. Davis, Paul Cravath, Russell Leffingwell, Norman Davis and Allen Dulles. He says he studied the network for twenty years and examined 'its papers and secret records' for two years in the early 1960s. CFR's own centennial history records that Morgan partner Russell Leffingwell sat on its board. The 'front' description is Quigley's.
cite: Quigley, Tragedy and Hope (Macmillan, 1966), pp. 950–952; G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021)

arch.t: Council on Foreign Relations — Submergence of US Sovereignty (Insider Testimony)

n: CFR Greenland memo reaches Roosevelt before Denmark falls
d: On 17 March 1940 a confidential memo from Isaiah Bowman's Territorial group in the CFR War and Peace Studies argued that Greenland was strategically important and should be placed within the Monroe Doctrine. CFR's 1947 anniversary book says Roosevelt summoned Bowman to the White House with the memo in hand. After Germany invaded Denmark in April 1940 Roosevelt declared Greenland part of the North American continent, and the Danish government-in-exile later granted US base rights there. The account is CFR's own.
cite: G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021), pp. 25–27, citing CFR's 1947 anniversary book

n: Allen Dulles — CFR armaments group to Director of Central Intelligence
d: Allen Dulles sat on the CFR board in 1928 (Quigley's list) and led the Security and Armaments group of the CFR's 1939–45 War and Peace Studies; CFR's own history says the Office of Strategic Services recruited him to carry out the group's plans for occupied Germany. He became the longest-serving Director of Central Intelligence (1953–61).
cite: G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021), pp. 23–25; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, p. 952

n: John Foster Dulles announces 'massive retaliation' at the CFR
d: On 12 January 1954 Secretary of State John Foster Dulles, described by the Council as 'a long-serving Council member', used a televised CFR address to set out the Eisenhower administration's policy of meeting Soviet aggression 'instantly, by means and at places of our choosing'. CFR's history calls it a break with its off-the-record rule. Earlier CFR members in the same office included Frank Kellogg, who spoke at the Council in 1928 months before the Kellogg–Briand Pact, and Henry Stimson.
cite: G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021), pp. 17–19, 41

n: John J. McCloy — War Department, World Bank, Germany, then CFR chair
rank: Assistant Secretary of War; President of the World Bank; US High Commissioner for Germany
d: McCloy was Assistant Secretary of War (April 1941–November 1945), President of the World Bank (1947–49) and US High Commissioner for Germany (1949–52). He then chaired the CFR board from 1953 to 1970 while also chairing Chase Manhattan Bank (1953–60) and the Ford Foundation (1958–65), and sat on the Warren Commission in 1963. CFR's own history names him as board chair.
cite: Wikipedia 'John J. McCloy'; G. Gavrilis, The Council on Foreign Relations: A Short History (CFR, 2021)

n: CFR members in top US foreign-policy posts, 1945–72
rank: Senior US foreign-policy officials (State, Defense, Treasury, CIA)
d: A study by Laurence Shoup and William Minter (Imperial Brain Trust, 1977) found that more than half of 502 senior US government officials it surveyed between 1945 and 1972 were CFR members. By its count members held about 42% of top foreign-policy posts under Truman, 40% under Eisenhower, 51% under Kennedy and 57% under Johnson. Eisenhower himself was a member.
cite: Shoup and Minter, Imperial Brain Trust (Monthly Review Press, 1977), as summarised in Wikipedia 'Council on Foreign Relations'

n: Institute of Pacific Relations — Senate finds it steered Far East policy
d: The Senate Internal Security Subcommittee under Pat McCarran reviewed about 20,000 IPR documents in 1951–52 and reported in 1952 that 'the IPR was a vehicle used by the Communists to orient American far eastern policies toward Communist objectives'. Owen Lattimore, editor of the IPR journal Pacific Affairs, was a central target. The IRS revoked the IPR's tax exemption in 1955, but the courts rejected all IRS allegations in 1959; the IPR dissolved in 1960. Quigley, who says the IPR's British and dominion branches were dominated by the Milner Group, argued that Boston banker Jerome Greene, who wrote the IPR constitution in 1926 and channelled Wall Street funds into it, mattered more inside the IPR 'than any Communists or fellow travelers'.
cite: US Senate Internal Security Subcommittee, report on the Institute of Pacific Relations (1952); Wikipedia 'Institute of Pacific Relations'; Quigley, Tragedy and Hope, pp. 946–956; The Anglo-American Establishment, ch. 10

n: Pilgrims Society — US ambassadors admitted ex officio
rank: US Ambassador to the Court of St James's; US Secretary of State
d: The Pilgrims of Great Britain (London, 16 July 1902) and of the United States (New York, 13 January 1903) hold dinners to welcome each new US ambassador to Britain, and US secretaries of state and ambassadors in London are customarily admitted ex officio. Winston Churchill addressed the Society as Prime Minister on 18 March 1941. Members have included Henry Kissinger, George Shultz, Caspar Weinberger, Margaret Thatcher and Paul Volcker.
cite: Wikipedia 'Pilgrims Society'

n: Stephen Knight's 'The Brotherhood' — Freemasonry in UK policing
rank: Metropolitan Police and provincial police officers
d: Journalist Stephen Knight's The Brotherhood (Granada, 1983–84) devoted chapters to the police, Birmingham City Police and Operation Countryman; an extract in Police Review (28 October 1983) described City of London Freemasons helping secure a Metropolitan Police Commissioner's post for a candidate. After the book, Met Commissioner Kenneth Newman advised officers to stay away from lodges, and his Principles of Policing manual advised against joining; a lodge for Scotland Yard officers, the Manor of St James, was then formed and included chief officers. Knight died in July 1985.
cite: Stephen Knight, The Brotherhood (1984); Police Review vol. 91 no. 4733 (28 Oct 1983) via Statewatch; The Conversation, 'The Freemasons no longer have significant influence in the British police'; Wikipedia 'Kenneth Newman'

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

n: Operation Countryman — Met corruption inquiry and lodge allegations
d: Operation Countryman, run by outside officers from 1978 to 1982, investigated corruption among London detectives; Assistant Chief Constable Leonard Burt returned to Dorset in May 1980, and evidence was handed to the Met's own internal unit. Chief Constable Arthur Hambleton alleged obstruction by Commissioner David McNee and the DPP; eight officers were prosecuted and none convicted. MP Dale Campbell-Savours later alleged that police membership of particular Masonic lodges was tied to a criminal conspiracy; Knight's The Brotherhood gave the operation a chapter. Parliament's requests for the findings were refused on public-interest immunity.
cite: Wikipedia 'Operation Countryman'; Knight, The Brotherhood (1984), ch. 9

n: DCI Brian Woollard — removed from Islington fraud case, petitions Parliament
rank: Detective Chief Inspector, Metropolitan Police Company Fraud Department
d: Woollard investigated corruption in Islington council's street-property renovation contracts. In a petition presented by Austin Mitchell MP on 20 December 1985 he said he was taken off the inquiry when it 'began to indicate a connection between corruption and Freemasonry', by officers who were Masons, and moved to uniform in April 1982. On 29 July 1988 Home Office minister Douglas Hogg told Jeremy Corbyn that the Home Secretary would not order an inquiry under section 32 of the Police Act 1964, and that Woollard had been dismissed by a disciplinary board on 25 May 1988 for absence from duty.
cite: HC Deb 20 December 1985 vol 89 cc671–2 (petition); HC written answer 29 July 1988

arch.t: UK Investigation: Masonic Network in Police and Judiciary Led to Parliamentary Inquiry and New Legal Disclosure Requirements

n: Blackburn 'Victory' police lodge — false arrest settled for £170,000
rank: Lancashire Constabulary officers; Chief Constable of Lancashire
d: In 1988 a Leicester shop owner and his son were assaulted at a Blackburn hotel during a ladies' night of the Victory Lodge, described as a police lodge; most of the men were serving Lancashire officers, the hotel manager was a lodge member, and the investigating officer was a Mason. The father and son, not their attackers, were charged and were acquitted by a jury in February 1989. Their civil action against seven lodge members, the hotel group and the Chief Constable settled for about £170,000, most paid by the Chief Constable. Account given in Martin Short's evidence to the Home Affairs Committee, reprinted in his foreword to The Brotherhood.
cite: Martin Short, foreword to Stephen Knight, The Brotherhood (Harper Perennial ed., 2007), quoting his 1996 evidence to the Home Affairs Committee

n: Alabama Klan and the lodges — Hugo Black's 1926 Senate race
d: Hugo Black joined the Knights of Pythias and the Masons as a young man and around 1920 was an officer of his Masonic lodge; he joined the Klan in September 1923 (the Birmingham chapter was Robert E. Lee Klan No. 1, led from 1921 by James Esdale, later Grand Dragon). By the mid-1920s the Alabama Klan claimed to speak for the state's elite, 'including Masons, bankers, and ministers', and by 1926 Esdale oversaw 148 klaverns with a reported 94,301 members. Black visited all 148 chapters while winning the 1926 Democratic Senate primary, and after the election Esdale had him thank a Klan meeting alongside Governor-elect Bibb Graves. The existing record on Black covers his 1937 Court appointment and radio address.
cite: Encyclopedia of Alabama, 'Ku Klux Klan in Alabama from 1915–1930' (K. Hébert) and 'Hugo L. Black' (S. Suitts); Bhamwiki 'James Esdale'; The Nation, 'Hugo Black: A Personal History'
org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (existing key)

arch.t: US Supreme Court Justice Was Documented KKK Member; Alabama KKK-Masonic Network Used as Political Infrastructure to Reach Highest Judicial Office

n: Bibb Graves — Klan-backed governor of Alabama
d: Bibb Graves won the 1926 governor's race with the secret endorsement of the Ku Klux Klan and served 1927–31 and 1935–39. He was almost certainly the Exalted Cyclops of the Montgomery Klan; his membership became public when he resigned in 1928, and in 1937, during the Senate row over Hugo Black, Graves acknowledged his own former membership. He and Black received gold Klan 'passports' and were nicknamed 'the Gold Dust Twins'; in 1937 Graves appointed his wife Dixie Bibb Graves to Black's vacated Senate seat.
cite: Wikipedia 'Bibb Graves'; Encyclopedia of Alabama, 'Ku Klux Klan in Alabama from 1915–1930'
org_note: kkk = Ku Klux Klan (existing key)

arch.t: US Supreme Court Justice Was Documented KKK Member; Alabama KKK-Masonic Network Used as Political Infrastructure to Reach Highest Judicial Office

n: Valery Zakharov — Wagner man as CAR president's security adviser
rank: national security adviser to the president
d: The Wagner Group is a Russian private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin that Russia used to place fighters and advisers with African governments. Valery Zakharov, a Russian, served as security adviser to President Faustin-Archange Touadéra from 2018 and publicly told rebels in 2021 to hand over their leaders. Ukraine's SBU said in 2018 he headed Wagner's security firm in the country. The US Treasury put him on its sanctions list under the CAR programme with the note 'linked to: Private Military Company Wagner'; the listing shows he also held a Central African passport issued in June 2018.
cite: US Treasury OFAC sanctions list entry (CAR programme); Ukrainian SBU statement Dec 2018, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Wagner guards the CAR president and fights for the army
rank: presidential close protection and army operations
d: About 1,000 Wagner fighters have been in the Central African Republic since 2018, after a Russia–CAR military agreement in August 2018. Their tasks included close protection for President Touadéra and fighting rebels alongside the national army, for example at Boyali in January 2021. Reporting links the deployment to gold, diamond and timber concessions, including a Lobaye logging operation. Russia's defence ministry is moving these structures under its Africa Corps; the CAR remains its largest African deployment, estimated at 1,500–2,000.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Wagner Group activities in the Central African Republic', citing The Guardian (Feb 2023), Al Jazeera and ISPI

n: Mali's defence minister sanctioned for bringing in Wagner
rank: defence minister; air force chief and deputy chief
d: On 24 July 2023 the US Treasury sanctioned Mali's defence minister, Colonel Sadio Camara, saying he planned and organised Wagner's deployment and made several trips to Russia in 2021 to finalise it. It also sanctioned air force chief of staff Colonel Alou Boi Diarra, who it said promoted Wagner inside the armed forces and worked with Wagner's Mali head Ivan Maslov, and deputy chief Lieutenant Colonel Adama Bagayoko. Mali's military government had asked UN peacekeepers to leave a month earlier.
cite: US Treasury press release JY1645, 24 July 2023

n: Mali — Wagner leaves, Russia's Africa Corps stays with the junta
rank: armed forces partner of the military government
d: Africa Corps is the Russian defence ministry's unit that took over most of Wagner's African operations after Prigozhin's death in 2023. On 6 June 2025 Wagner announced it was leaving Mali; Africa Corps, which had deployed about 1,000 troops in December 2024, became the only Russian force there, with about 2,000 Russian troops remaining. Several Wagner commanders moved across to it. Human Rights Watch and Le Monde have reported killings of civilians by Malian soldiers and Africa Corps members in 2025–26.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Africa Corps (Russia)', citing BBC News and Al Jazeera (June 2025)

n: Burkina Faso — Russia's Africa Corps base near the capital
rank: military partner of the transitional government
d: Burkina Faso's military government under Captain Ibrahim Traoré ordered French troops out in early 2023. Africa Corps personnel arrived on 24 January 2024, an initial 100 to be expanded to 300, and set up their first African base at Loumbila, north-east of Ouagadougou. Ghana's president had earlier alleged a mine was allotted to Wagner as payment, which Burkina's mines minister denied.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Africa Corps (Russia)' and 'Wagner Group activities in Mali'

n: Niger — Africa Corps moves into Niamey air base
rank: military partner of the ruling junta
d: After the July 2023 coup, Niger's junta ended military cooperation with the US and France. Dozens of Africa Corps troops arrived in Niamey in April 2024 and were stationed at Air Base 101 before US forces had left it. Estimates for 2025 put them at 200–300, mostly in intelligence, training and surveillance. Wikipedia's article says they took part in fighting during a January 2026 attack on Niamey airport.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Africa Corps (Russia)'

n: Equatorial Guinea — Russian troops protect President Obiang
d: Teodoro Obiang has ruled Equatorial Guinea since 1979. In autumn 2024 Russia deployed up to 200 Africa Corps troops to protect his presidency and to train elite units in Malabo and Bata, according to the CTC Sentinel and other analyses. Obiang officially received the Africa Corps commander in Malabo in November 2025.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Africa Corps (Russia)', citing CTC Sentinel (Dec 2024)

n: Libya — UN monitors count up to 1,200 Wagner fighters with Haftar
rank: fighting force for the Libyan National Army
d: Khalifa Haftar's Libyan National Army controls eastern Libya. A May 2020 UN report counted 800–1,200 Wagner fighters supporting it, including sniper teams, and Syrians recruited by Wagner flown in on at least 33 flights. In July 2020 the US sanctioned Wagner people and firms over landmines planted around Tripoli. In December 2020 a Pentagon report said the UAE was the main funder of Wagner in Libya. Africa Corps began replacing Wagner there in spring 2024 and Russia uses eastern Libyan bases as logistics hubs.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Libya (2020), US Treasury (July 2020), US Defense Department Inspector General (Dec 2020), as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Sudan — Prigozhin's gold firm sanctioned over plan to crush protests
d: On 15 July 2020 the US Treasury sanctioned M Invest, a company linked to Yevgeny Prigozhin, and its Sudanese gold-mining subsidiary Meroe Gold. Treasury said the network had tried to help suppress the protesters who sought democratic reform in Sudan in 2018–19. Wagner personnel first arrived in Sudan in 2017 and numbered about 300 by 2022.
cite: US Treasury OFAC designations, 15 July 2020, reported by The Sentry

n: Madagascar 2018 — Prigozhin's strategists fund presidential candidates
d: The Russian investigative outlet Proekt and the BBC reported in 2019 that 15–20 Russian political strategists tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin worked in Madagascar's 2018 presidential race and dealt with as many as eight candidates, including the winner, Andry Rajoelina. Candidate André Mailhol said they gave him €5,000 in cash; ex-prime minister Omer Beriziky said he was promised $2 million. Rajoelina denied being Russia's candidate and the BBC found no evidence he took Russian money. Prigozhin's representatives denied any link.
cite: Proekt investigation (March 2019) and BBC, as reported by Meduza, 8 April 2019

n: Facebook removes Prigozhin networks run in eight African countries
rank: election campaigns and political news in eight states
d: On 30 October 2019 Facebook removed three networks of almost 200 fake and compromised accounts, with over a million followers, that it traced to entities tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin. They targeted Madagascar, the Central African Republic, Mozambique, DR Congo, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon, Sudan and Libya, and meddled in the Mozambique and Madagascar elections. Stanford Internet Observatory found operators worked with local people and some accounts appeared linked to Wagner. Placed at Maputo because Mozambique's October 2019 election was a named target.
cite: Facebook announcement, 30 Oct 2019; Stanford Internet Observatory; reported by Al Jazeera

n: AFRIC — Prigozhin-linked 'election observers' at Zimbabwe's 2018 vote
d: AFRIC (Association for Free Research and International Cooperation) presented itself as an independent African research and election-monitoring body. It sent about 40 observers to Zimbabwe's 2018 general election. The European Platform for Democratic Elections reports that investigative journalists later found AFRIC was organised by people and structures linked to Yevgeny Prigozhin.
cite: European Platform for Democratic Elections, 'Fake election observation as Russia's tool of election interference: the case of AFRIC' (2020)

n: Nyerere Leadership School — CCP trains six ruling parties' cadres
d: The Mwalimu Julius Nyerere Leadership School in Kibaha, Tanzania, took its first class on 22 February 2022. It was built with a $40 million grant from the Chinese Communist Party's Central Party School, and CCP theoreticians teach there. It is a joint project of the CCP and six ruling parties: Tanzania's CCM, South Africa's ANC, Angola's MPLA, Mozambique's FRELIMO, Namibia's SWAPO and Zimbabwe's ZANU-PF.
cite: Africa Center for Strategic Studies, 'China's first political school in Africa' (2022)

n: ANC leadership attends CCP-funded party school (2024)
rank: ANC secretary-general and national executive members
d: The ANC is South Africa's largest party and led every government from 1994 to 2024. From 23 to 25 January 2024 ANC Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula led a five-person delegation, including NEC members David Makhura and Nobuhle Nkabane, to the annual meeting of the Nyerere Leadership School, which the ANC says the Communist Party of China supported at its 2022 launch. The ANC says the school has trained over 1,405 participants, including ANC members.
cite: ANC statement, 23 January 2024

n: African Union HQ — China-built building sent data to Shanghai
d: China built and paid for the African Union headquarters in Addis Ababa, opened in 2012. In January 2018 Le Monde, confirmed by the Financial Times, reported that the AU's IT staff found in 2017 that its computers had been sending data nightly to servers in Shanghai, and that microphones were found hidden in walls and furniture. The AU replaced the system. China's ambassador called the report 'ridiculous and preposterous'; Huawei also denied wrongdoing.
cite: Le Monde, 26 January 2018 (Tilouine and Kadiri), as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Uganda — Huawei technicians help police crack opposition phones
d: Huawei is China's largest telecoms equipment maker. In August 2019 the Wall Street Journal reported that Huawei technicians working inside Uganda's police headquarters helped its cyber unit get into the encrypted messages of opposition MP Bobi Wine, and that Huawei staff also helped Zambia's government with domestic spying. The Journal found no evidence that Huawei executives in China or the Chinese state directed this. Huawei denied the report.
cite: Wall Street Journal, 14 Aug 2019, as reported by CNBC

n: Guptas offer the finance ministry to Mcebisi Jonas
d: The Gupta brothers, Indian-born businessmen close to President Jacob Zuma, ran a network the Zondo Commission found had 'captured' parts of the state. Deputy Finance Minister Mcebisi Jonas said the Guptas offered him the finance minister's job shortly before Zuma sacked minister Nhlanhla Nene in December 2015; ex-MP Vytjie Mentor testified she was offered the public enterprises ministry in 2010. The US Treasury later cited a promised payment to a potential finance minister. The Guptas denied it.
cite: Judicial Commission of Inquiry into State Capture (Zondo Commission), report parts 1–5, Jan–June 2022

n: Zondo report — ministers and state firm heads acted for the Guptas
rank: public enterprises minister; Transnet and Eskom chief executives
d: Chief Justice Raymond Zondo chaired the state capture inquiry, which heard over 300 witnesses from 2018 and published its report in five parts between 4 January and 22 June 2022. It found that ministers, senior ANC members and heads of state-owned companies acted corruptly for the Gupta family, naming former public enterprises minister Malusi Gigaba and former Transnet chief Brian Molefe, and found state advertising for the Gupta newspaper The New Age defied 'logic and legal requirements'.
cite: Zondo Commission report, 2022

n: US sanctions the Gupta brothers and Salim Essa
rank: network that offered ministries and paid officials
d: On 10 October 2019 the US Treasury sanctioned Ajay, Atul and Rajesh Gupta and their associate Salim Essa under the Global Magnitsky programme. Treasury said the family offered government members money or posts for cooperation, paid an official to appoint people friendly to its businesses, and took hundreds of millions of dollars through state contracts. The brothers moved to Dubai in 2016; in 2023 the UAE refused to extradite Atul and Rajesh to South Africa.
cite: US Treasury press release SM789, 10 October 2019

n: Bain & Company — Zondo finds it helped capture the tax service
d: Bain & Company is a US management consultancy. The Zondo Commission found Bain worked with President Zuma and SARS commissioner Tom Moyane to take over the revenue service, partly to stop SARS investigating corruption; Bain had been paid for a 2015 restructuring that cut the unit producing a third of revenues. Bain denied 'wilfully' facilitating capture. South Africa's National Treasury barred Bain from state contracts for 10 years on 29 September 2022, and Bain closed its South African consulting business in 2025.
cite: Zondo Commission report (2022); Nugent Commission on SARS (2018); National Treasury restriction, 29 Sept 2022

n: McKinsey admits bribing South African officials, pays $122m
d: McKinsey & Company is a US consultancy. It won large contracts at the state power utility Eskom and rail firm Transnet working with Trillian, a firm owned by a Gupta associate. In 2024 McKinsey entered a three-year deferred prosecution agreement with the US Justice Department and paid a $122 million penalty for bribing South African officials between 2012 and 2016; half goes to South Africa. It had earlier repaid about R1 billion to Eskom and R870 million to Transnet; South Africa's prosecutors charged McKinsey SA and ex-partner Vikas Sagar in 2022.
cite: US Department of Justice deferred prosecution agreement (Dec 2024); Zondo Commission part 4 (April 2022)

n: Bell Pottinger expelled over campaign for Gupta firm
rank: public-opinion campaign for the President's allies
d: Bell Pottinger was a London public relations firm. From 2016 it was paid about £100,000 a month by the Gupta-owned Oakbay Investments and ran a campaign about 'white monopoly capital' using fake bloggers and Twitter accounts to defend the Guptas and President Zuma's circle. After a complaint from the Democratic Alliance, the industry body PRCA expelled it on 4 September 2017, and the firm went into administration on 12 September 2017.
cite: Public Relations and Communications Association ruling, 4 Sept 2017; Herbert Smith Freehills review (2017)

n: Hezbollah holds two ministries in Lebanon's 2025 government
d: Hezbollah is a Shia Lebanese party with an armed wing, aligned with Iran and listed as a terrorist group by at least 28 countries including the US and UK; it holds about 14 of 128 seats in parliament. In the 24-member government Prime Minister Nawaf Salam formed in February 2025, Hezbollah's picks hold the public health ministry (Rakan Nasreddine) and the labour ministry (Mohammad Haidar); with its ally Amal it controls six portfolios.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Hezbollah' (section on Lebanese politics)

n: Lebanon's cabinet orders army plan to disarm Hezbollah
rank: armed force outside the state's control
d: On 7 August 2025 Lebanon's cabinet approved the aim that only the state hold weapons, and Hezbollah- and Amal-aligned ministers walked out. On 5 September 2025 army commander General Rodolphe Haykal presented the 'Homeland Shield' plan to disarm all militias, chiefly Hezbollah, which the cabinet welcomed without a timeline. Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem rejected disarmament. In March 2026 Prime Minister Salam said Hezbollah's rocket and drone strikes were outside the state's authority.
cite: Lebanese cabinet decisions of 7 Aug and 5 Sept 2025, reported by AP and Al Jazeera, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: US sanctions two sitting Hezbollah MPs and its security liaison
rank: members of parliament; liaison to state security agencies
d: On 9 July 2019 the US Treasury for the first time sanctioned sitting Lebanese MPs: Hezbollah's Amin Sherri and Muhammad Raad, saying they acted on its behalf. It also sanctioned Wafiq Safa, head of Hezbollah's Liaison and Coordination Unit, which deals with Lebanon's security agencies. A State Department official urged the Lebanese government to cut ties with them; Hezbollah called it a 'humiliation'. Raad is now Hezbollah's deputy secretary-general.
cite: US Treasury OFAC designations, 9 July 2019, reported by Al Jazeera

n: Iraq's parliament writes Iran-aligned militias into the armed forces
rank: Popular Mobilization Forces, a branch of the armed forces
d: The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF) formed in June 2014 to fight Islamic State and are made up of about 67 mostly Shia factions, almost all backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards. A law passed in November 2016 and signed by President Fuad Masum on 19 December 2016 made them part of Iraq's armed forces under the prime minister, paid from the state budget. In 2024 the PMF chief of staff said publicly that it took orders from Iran's supreme leader. A 2025 reform bill to tighten state control was tabled under US pressure.
cite: Law of the Popular Mobilization Commission (2016); Washington Institute and Carnegie analyses, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Falih al-Fayyadh — PMF chairman sanctioned by the US
rank: chairman of the Popular Mobilization Commission; former national security adviser
d: Falih al-Fayyadh chairs the state body that runs the PMF and was also Iraq's national security adviser. On 8 January 2021 the US Treasury sanctioned him over the killing of protesters in 2019, and on 13 January it sanctioned PMF chief of staff Abu Fadak al-Mohammadawi. Iraq's foreign ministry said it was 'surprised'. Fayyadh remains PMF chairman.
cite: US Treasury press release SM1231, 8 January 2021

n: Kata'ib Hezbollah — US-listed terror group staffs three state brigades
d: Kata'ib Hezbollah is an Iraqi Shia armed group that operates under Iran's Revolutionary Guards; the US listed it as a terrorist organisation in 2009. It is a founding member of the state-funded PMF and staffs its 45th, 46th and 47th Brigades; its commander Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis led the PMF in the field until a US strike killed him in January 2020. The US linked it to the January 2024 Tower 22 drone attack that killed three US soldiers.
cite: US State Department FTO listing (2009); US Treasury designations; Washington Institute analyses, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Kenya convicts two Iranians said to be Quds Force over explosives
rank: operatives of Iran's Revolutionary Guards Quds Force (as alleged)
d: The Quds Force is the foreign operations branch of Iran's Revolutionary Guards. In May 2013 a Kenyan court convicted Iranian nationals Ahmad Abolfathi Mohammad and Sayed Mansour Mousavi of plotting attacks and sentenced them to life. Officials believed more than 100 kg of RDX explosive had been shipped into Kenya; about 15 kg was recovered. The men were alleged to be Quds Force members.
cite: Kenyan court judgment, May 2013, as compiled by Iran Watch (Wisconsin Project)

n: US lists Lebanon's Brotherhood (al-Jamaa al-Islamiya) as terrorist
d: The Muslim Brotherhood is a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 with branches across the region. On 13 January 2026 the US designated its Lebanese branch, which operates as the party al-Jamaa al-Islamiya ('The Islamic Group'), both a Foreign Terrorist Organization and a Specially Designated Global Terrorist, and Treasury named its secretary-general Muhammad Fawzi Taqqosh. These were the first US terrorist designations of any Brotherhood branch.
cite: US State Department and Treasury designations, 13 Jan 2026, as reported by FDD

n: US lists Egyptian and Jordanian Brotherhood branches as terrorists
rank: Brotherhood branches; linked party holds seats in parliament
d: On 13 January 2026 the US Treasury designated the Egyptian and Jordanian branches of the Muslim Brotherhood as Specially Designated Global Terrorists. Egypt has banned the group since 2013, and Jordan banned all its activities in April 2025; Jordan's government spokesman said the group 'has been dissolved for years'. The Brotherhood-linked Islamic Action Front won 31 seats in Jordan's 2024 parliamentary election.
cite: US Treasury designation, 13 Jan 2026, as reported by FDD

n: Ali Karti — Islamic Movement chief and ex-minister sanctioned
rank: former foreign minister; secretary-general of the Sudanese Islamic Movement
d: The Sudanese Islamic Movement is the Brotherhood-rooted organisation behind Omar al-Bashir's 1989–2019 rule. Ali Karti was Bashir's foreign minister (2010–2015) and became its secretary-general in June 2021. In September 2023 the US sanctioned him for undermining the transition to civilian rule and obstructing a ceasefire between the army and the Rapid Support Forces; Canada (April 2024) and the EU (June 2024) followed.
cite: US Treasury designation, Sept 2023; EU Council decision, 24 June 2024, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Sudan's finance minister and Islamist brigade sanctioned (2025)
rank: finance minister; Islamist militia fighting beside the army
d: On 12 September 2025 the US Treasury sanctioned Gebreil Ibrahim, Sudan's finance minister and leader of the Justice and Equality Movement, which it tied to Islamist leader Hassan al-Turabi, and the al-Baraa bin Malik Brigade, an Islamist militia that grew from Bashir's Popular Defense Forces and has supplied up to 20,000 fighters against the RSF. Treasury said the brigade got training and weapons from Iran's Revolutionary Guards and that Gebreil built ties with Tehran. Treasury used the word 'Islamist', not 'Muslim Brotherhood'.
cite: US Treasury press release, 12 Sept 2025

n: Khalid al-Mishri — Brotherhood party member heads Libya's State Council
rank: chairman of the High Council of State
d: Libya's Justice and Construction Party was founded in March 2012 as the political arm of the Libyan Muslim Brotherhood; it won 17 party-list seats in the 2012 congress and had five ministers until 2014. Its member Khalid al-Mishri chaired the High Council of State, the upper consultative body of the Tripoli-based government, from 8 April 2018 to 6 August 2023, and represented it at talks in Palermo, Doha, Moscow and Istanbul.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Khalid al-Mishri' and 'Justice and Construction Party', citing Libya Observer and Reuters

n: Morocco — Brotherhood-inspired PJD leads government for ten years
d: The Justice and Development Party (PJD) is a Moroccan Islamist party historically linked to the Muslim Brotherhood but never an official branch. It won 107 seats in November 2011 and its leader Abdelilah Benkirane became head of government; Saadeddine Othmani succeeded him (2017–2021). In the September 2021 election it lost 113 seats.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Justice and Development Party (Morocco)', citing France 24 (Sept 2021)

n: UN monitors: 'credible' evidence UAE armed Sudan's RSF via Chad
rank: Rapid Support Forces, paramilitary at war with the army
d: The Rapid Support Forces grew out of Bashir-era militias and have fought Sudan's army since April 2023. A UN Panel of Experts report to the Security Council, leaked in January 2024, found 'credible' evidence that the UAE sent weapons to the RSF 'several times per week' through Amdjarass in northern Chad. The UAE denied it and said 122 flights carried aid. Sudan's genocide case against the UAE was dismissed by the International Court of Justice on 5 May 2025 for lack of jurisdiction, without ruling on the facts.
cite: UN Panel of Experts on Sudan report (Jan 2024), reported by Al Jazeera; ICJ order, 5 May 2025

n: UAE-backed southern council's chief as Yemen's vice-president
rank: vice-president of the Presidential Leadership Council
d: The Southern Transitional Council (STC) was formed in May 2017 with UAE help to seek a separate southern state. In April 2022 it joined Yemen's eight-member Presidential Leadership Council and its leader Aidarous al-Zubaidi became a vice-president. After an STC offensive in December 2025 and a Saudi-backed counter-offensive, al-Zubaidi fled to the UAE in January 2026 and was removed from the council; a delegation in Riyadh announced the STC's dissolution, which its UAE-based spokesman rejected.
cite: Wikipedia, 'Southern Transitional Council', citing Al Jazeera (7 Jan 2026)

n: Saad Hariri announces resignation as Lebanese PM from Riyadh
d: On 4 November 2017 Lebanon's prime minister Saad Hariri announced his resignation on television from Saudi Arabia, blaming Iran and Hezbollah. President Michel Aoun told ambassadors Hariri was being held by Saudi Arabia; The New Yorker cited a US official saying he was held for hours and slapped. Hariri returned, suspended the resignation on 21 November and withdrew it on 5 December 2017. Saudi Arabia denied holding him.
cite: Wikipedia, '2017 Lebanon–Saudi Arabia dispute', citing Robert Fisk and The New Yorker

n: Kenya hands four Gülen-linked refugees to Turkey
d: Turkey lists the Gülen movement as a terrorist group, blames it for the 2016 coup attempt, and seeks its members abroad. On 18 October 2024 four Turkish nationals living in Kenya as refugees were returned to Turkey after seven people were abducted in Nairobi. Kenya's foreign affairs principal secretary Korir Sing'oei confirmed the repatriation was 'at the request of the government of Türkiye'. The UN said it was 'deeply concerned'.
cite: Kenyan Foreign Affairs PS statement, 21 Oct 2024, reported by Stockholm Center for Freedom

n: Turkish intelligence brings Gülen's nephew back from Kenya
d: In May 2021 Turkey's state news agency Anadolu reported that the intelligence agency MIT had seized Selahaddin Gülen, a nephew of Fethullah Gülen, in an overseas operation and brought him to Turkey for prosecution; he had been living in Kenya. A Turkish court later jailed him and the top court upheld the sentence.
cite: Anadolu Agency report, 31 May 2021, as reported by VOA

n: NSO Group put on US blacklist over Pegasus sales to governments
rank: spyware supplier to state intelligence and police services
d: NSO Group is an Israeli company that sells Pegasus phone-hacking spyware only to governments, under Israeli defence ministry export licences. Investigations tied its use by state clients to surveillance of journalists and dissidents, including the circle of Jamal Khashoggi before Saudi agents killed him in 2018. In November 2021 the US Commerce Department added NSO to its Entity List for acting against US interests. A New York Times investigation found Pegasus sales coincided with some governments' warmer ties with Israel.
cite: US Commerce Department Entity List addition, Nov 2021; Citizen Lab; New York Times, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Morocco named as Pegasus client targeting 6,000 Algerian phones
rank: Algerian politicians and senior military officers
d: The 2021 Pegasus Project, a consortium of journalists working with Amnesty International, reported that Morocco had selected more than 6,000 Algerian phones, including politicians and senior military officers, as Pegasus targets; Le Monde also reported Morocco selected President Macron and 14 French ministers. Morocco denied using Pegasus. Algeria cut diplomatic relations with Morocco in August 2021, citing alleged Pegasus use among its reasons.
cite: Pegasus Project (Forbidden Stories / Amnesty International), July 2021, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Team Jorge — Israeli firm hacks Kenyan presidential aide's Telegram
rank: digital strategist of the winning presidential campaign
d: Team Jorge is an Israeli hacking and disinformation outfit led by ex-special forces operative Tal Hanan, exposed in February 2023 by a Forbidden Stories consortium after undercover reporters filmed him. Hanan claimed work on 33 presidential elections, many in Africa. In the meeting he showed access to the Telegram account of Dennis Itumbi, digital strategist for William Ruto in Kenya's 2022 election; Itumbi confirmed the account had been compromised.
cite: Forbidden Stories 'Story Killers' investigation; The Guardian, 17 Feb 2023, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Cambridge Analytica and Team Jorge in Nigeria's 2015 election
d: Cambridge Analytica was a British data firm, part of SCL Group. Emails leaked to The Guardian in 2023 showed it worked with Israel's Team Jorge in the 2015 Nigerian election on a campaign to re-elect President Goodluck Jonathan by discrediting Muhammadu Buhari, who won. Cambridge Analytica closed in 2018.
cite: The Guardian, 16 and 18 Feb 2023, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Cambridge Analytica ran Kenyatta's 2013 and 2017 campaigns' data work
d: Cambridge Analytica ran campaigns in secret in Kenya's 2013 and 2017 elections, both won by Uhuru Kenyatta, and said it surveyed 47,000 Kenyans in 2013. After staff boasted of their role on undercover footage in March 2018, the opposition called for an investigation; Kenyatta's Jubilee Party said it had hired the parent company for branding.
cite: Channel 4 News undercover investigation (March 2018), as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Archimedes Group banned by Facebook for African election meddling
rank: election campaigns in several African states
d: Archimedes Group was an Israeli political consulting firm. In May 2019 Facebook removed its networks for 'coordinated inauthentic behavior' aimed mainly at elections in sub-Saharan Africa, including Nigeria, as well as Latin America and Southeast Asia, and found it had spent about $1.1 million on ads. Placed at Abuja because Nigeria's February 2019 election was among those targeted.
cite: Facebook takedown, 16 May 2019, reported by CNN; Atlantic Council DFRLab, as summarised on Wikipedia

n: Oligui Nguema — Gabon's coup leader receives Grand Orient chief
rank: president of the transition (now elected president)
d: The Grand Orient de France is France's largest Masonic body. Gabonreview, citing Africa Intelligence, reported that in November 2023 its Grand Master Guillaume Trichard met coup leader Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema in Libreville in secret and offered support to his transitional council; it described Oligui as a non-practising Freemason. Trichard also met the council of the Grande Loge symbolique du Gabon. Oligui was elected president in April 2025.
cite: Gabonreview, 22 Nov 2023, citing Africa Intelligence

n: Senegal's new president makes early call on the Mouride khalife
d: The Mourides are a Sufi brotherhood centred on the holy city of Touba with millions of followers; their leader, the Khalife général, has long been courted by Senegal's presidents, and Abdoulaye Wade went to Touba the day after his 2000 election. President Bassirou Diomaye Faye, sworn in on 2 April 2024, visited Khalife Serigne Mountakha Mbacké on 15 April 2024, again in August 2024 and March 2025, and pledged state help with Touba's water and sanitation ahead of the Grand Magal pilgrimage.
cite: Le Soleil (Senegal state daily), Aug 2025; Wikipedia, 'Mouride'

n: Bob Menendez — senator convicted as an agent of Egypt
rank: US senator, chair of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee
d: The Foreign Relations Committee shapes US arms sales and aid, including to Egypt. A Manhattan federal jury found Senator Bob Menendez guilty on all counts on 16 July 2024, including bribery, extortion, acting as a foreign agent and conspiracy; prosecutors said he passed sensitive US information to aid the Egyptian government and spoke up for Qatar to help a New Jersey developer get Qatari royal funding, in return for cash, gold bars and other gifts. A halal-meat monopoly granted by Egypt to businessman Wael Hana's company was used to channel bribes. He resigned on 20 August 2024, was sentenced to 11 years on 29 January 2025 and is in prison; his wife Nadine was convicted on 21 April 2025 and sentenced to 4½ years.
cite: US v. Menendez et al., Southern District of New York: jury verdict 16 July 2024, sentence 29 January 2025; Wikipedia 'Bob Menendez'
org_note: Government of Egypt (with Qatari royal-linked funding) — foreign-state influence

n: Manhattan 'secret Chinese police station' — two men convicted
rank: overseas outpost of the Fuzhou Public Security Bureau (Chinese police)
d: Safeguard Defenders, a human-rights group, reported in 2022 that Chinese local police ran 'service stations' abroad to pressure people to return to China. The FBI raided one on a floor of the American Changle Association office in Manhattan's Chinatown in October 2022, and it closed. In April 2023 Lu Jianwang and Chen Jinping, both US citizens, were charged with conspiring to act as unregistered agents of China and with deleting messages exchanged with a Ministry of Public Security official; the same day the Justice Department charged 34 Ministry officers. Chen pleaded guilty in December 2024 and a jury convicted Lu in May 2026.
cite: US Department of Justice, Eastern District of New York charges (April 2023); Chen guilty plea December 2024; Lu jury verdict May 2026; Wikipedia 'Chinese police overseas service stations'

n: Tom Barrack — acquitted as UAE agent, now ambassador to Turkey
rank: chair of Trump's 2017 inaugural committee; US ambassador to Turkey and Syria envoy from 2025
d: Prosecutors charged Tom Barrack on 20 July 2021 with acting as an unregistered agent of the United Arab Emirates while advising the Trump campaign and administration, plus obstruction and false statements; the May 2022 indictment added that he sought hundreds of millions of dollars in UAE investment while lobbying for the UAE. A Brooklyn jury acquitted him and his aide Matthew Grimes on 4 November 2022. The Senate confirmed him as ambassador to Turkey on 29 April 2025 (60–36), and he was named special envoy for Syria in May 2025.
cite: US v. Barrack, Eastern District of New York, acquittal 4 November 2022; Senate confirmation vote 29 April 2025; Wikipedia 'Tom Barrack'
org_note: Government of the United Arab Emirates

n: Michael Flynn — registered after the fact as an agent for Turkish interests
d: The National Security Adviser runs the White House's foreign-policy staff. In autumn 2016 Flynn's consulting firm was paid $530,000 by Inovo BV, a company owned by Turkish businessman Ekim Alptekin, for lobbying work. Flynn served as National Security Adviser from 22 January to 13 February 2017, and on 8 March 2017 filed a retroactive foreign-agent registration acknowledging the work may have benefited Turkey's government. His business partner Bijan Kian was convicted of acting as an unregistered agent of Turkey in 2019, but the judge threw out the verdict for insufficient evidence.
cite: Flynn Intel Group FARA registration, US Justice Department, 8 March 2017; US v. Rafiekian (E.D. Va. 2019); Wikipedia 'Michael Flynn'
org_note: Turkish government interests via Inovo BV

n: Elliott Broidy — RNC finance official pleads guilty as foreign agent
rank: deputy finance chair of the Republican National Committee
d: Broidy was a deputy finance chair of the Republican National Committee, the party's national fundraising body, from April 2017 to April 2018. In October 2020 he pleaded guilty to acting as an unregistered foreign agent: he took money to press the Trump administration to drop the 1MDB investigation of Malaysian financier Jho Low and to have the Chinese dissident Guo Wengui sent back to China, and he forfeited more than $6 million. Trump pardoned him in January 2021, at the end of his first term. Rapper Pras Michel, who prosecutors said paid Broidy, was convicted on 10 counts in April 2023 and sentenced to 14 years in November 2025.
cite: US v. Broidy, D.D.C., guilty plea October 2020; presidential pardon January 2021; US v. Michel, D.D.C., verdict 26 April 2023; Wikipedia 'Elliott Broidy', 'Pras Michel'
org_note: Malaysian (Jho Low) and Chinese government interests

n: Henry Cuellar — congressman charged over Azerbaijan bribes, pardoned
rank: US representative (Texas), senior member of the House Appropriations Committee
d: In May 2024 Representative Henry Cuellar and his wife Imelda were indicted on bribery, money-laundering and honest-services fraud counts; prosecutors said they took about $600,000 from a company controlled by the government of Azerbaijan and from a bank based in Mexico City in exchange for his acting in their interests in Congress. A judge refused to dismiss the case in September 2025. On 3 December 2025, before any trial, President Trump announced a full and unconditional pardon for both.
cite: US v. Cuellar, Southern District of Texas, indictment May 2024; presidential pardon announced 3 December 2025 (Roll Call)
org_note: Government of Azerbaijan (state-controlled company) and a Mexican bank

n: David Rivera — ex-congressman convicted of secret Venezuela lobbying
rank: former US representative (Florida) lobbying Congress and the White House
d: PDV USA, the US arm of Venezuela's state oil company PDVSA, signed a three-month, $50 million consulting contract with former congressman David Rivera's one-man firm in 2017. Prosecutors said he worked to ease US sanctions on the Maduro government without registering as a foreign agent, enlisting Texas congressman Pete Sessions to broker meetings and deliver a letter from Maduro to Trump. A Miami federal jury convicted Rivera on all counts, including failing to register as a foreign agent and money-laundering conspiracy, on 1 May 2026; co-defendant Esther Nuhfer was tried with him.
cite: US v. Rivera and Nuhfer, Southern District of Florida, jury verdict 1 May 2026 (AP via PBS NewsHour)
org_note: Government of Venezuela via state oil company PDVSA

n: Victor Manuel Rocha — ex-ambassador who served Cuban intelligence
rank: US ambassador to Bolivia; White House National Security Council staff; adviser to US Southern Command
d: Rocha joined the US foreign service in 1981, served at the White House and the US Interests Section in Havana, was ambassador to Bolivia and later advised the commander of US Southern Command. Prosecutors said he had acted as an agent of Cuba's General Directorate of Intelligence (DGI) since at least 1981; in recorded conversations he boasted of more than 40 years of service. He pleaded guilty and was sentenced in April 2024 to 15 years in prison and a $500,000 fine.
cite: US v. Rocha, Southern District of Florida, guilty plea and sentence April 2024 (AP via Britannica News)
org_note: Cuba's General Directorate of Intelligence (DGI)

n: Eric Adams — New York mayor charged over Turkish benefits, case dismissed
d: In September 2024 a federal grand jury charged Mayor Eric Adams with bribery, wire fraud, conspiracy and soliciting foreign campaign contributions. Prosecutors said he accepted luxury travel from Turkish officials and businessmen, took straw donations that drew city matching funds, and pressed the fire commissioner to let a Manhattan tower housing Turkey's consulate open in time for a visit by President Erdoğan. After the Justice Department asked to drop the case, Judge Dale Ho dismissed it with prejudice on 2 April 2025, so it cannot be brought again; Adams was never tried.
cite: US v. Adams, Southern District of New York, indictment September 2024, dismissal with prejudice 2 April 2025
org_note: Turkish government officials and businessmen

n: Michael McMahon — ex-NYPD sergeant convicted in China's 'Fox Hunt'
rank: retired New York police sergeant working as a private investigator
d: Operation Fox Hunt is the Chinese government's campaign to force people it accuses of crimes to return to China. A Brooklyn jury convicted McMahon in June 2023 of acting as an illegal agent of China, stalking and conspiracy: he tracked a former Chinese city official living in New Jersey and reported to a Chinese police officer and prosecutor, for more than $19,000. He was sentenced to 18 months on 16 April 2025; President Trump pardoned him on 7 November 2025.
cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of New York, sentencing release 16 April 2025; pardon reported by AP, 7 November 2025

n: Baimadajie Angwang — NYPD officer's China-agent charges dropped
rank: New York police officer and Army reservist
d: In 2020 federal prosecutors charged NYPD officer Baimadajie Angwang with acting at the direction of officials at the Chinese consulate in New York by reporting on Tibetans in the United States; he was held for about six months. His lawyers said the contacts were to get a visa to visit family. On 19 January 2023 a federal judge in Brooklyn granted the government's request to dismiss the case, prosecutors citing new, classified information; the NYPD later fired him.
cite: US v. Angwang, Eastern District of New York, dismissal 19 January 2023 (ABC7 New York)

n: Vikash Yadav — Indian intelligence officer charged in New York murder plot
rank: Indian government intelligence officer (Research and Analysis Wing)
d: US prosecutors unsealed an indictment in October 2024 charging Vikash Yadav, described as a senior field officer of India's foreign intelligence service (RAW) and former paramilitary officer, with directing a 2023 plan to kill Sikh separatist and US citizen Gurpatwant Singh Pannun in New York. The indictment says Yadav gave go-between Nikhil Gupta Pannun's address and routine and sent him video of Hardeep Singh Nijjar's body after Nijjar was killed in Canada. India said Yadav 'is no longer an employee of the Government of India'; he remains at large, while Gupta pleaded guilty in the US in early 2026.
cite: US v. Yadav and Gupta, Southern District of New York, superseding indictment unsealed 17 October 2024 (Al Jazeera); Gupta guilty plea reported February 2026 (The Wire)
org_note: Government of India — Research and Analysis Wing (RAW)

n: Confucius Institutes named a foreign mission; most US branches closed
rank: Chinese-government-funded language centres at US universities, incl. Pentagon-funded programmes
d: Confucius Institutes are Chinese-language centres placed in foreign universities and funded through China's education ministry. On 13 August 2020 the State Department designated the Confucius Institute U.S. Center a 'foreign mission' of China, with Secretary Pompeo calling the network part of the Communist Party's influence and propaganda apparatus. Defense spending laws barred Pentagon language funds for campuses hosting an institute, and none of 13 universities that asked for waivers got one. The National Association of Scholars counted 104 of 118 US institutes closed by June 2022, while reporting that some reopened under new names.
cite: US State Department foreign-mission designation, 13 August 2020 (RFA); National Association of Scholars count, June 2022 (The Diplomat, November 2023)

n: Heritage Foundation — Project 2025 authors staff the second Trump administration
rank: OMB director, FCC chair, CIA director, 'border czar', SEC chair and other senior posts
d: Project 2025 is a governing plan for a conservative administration organised by the Heritage Foundation, a Washington think tank. Axios listed Trump picks tied to it: Russ Vought (OMB director; wrote the plan's chapter on the Executive Office of the President), Brendan Carr (FCC chair; wrote the FCC chapter), Tom Homan (border czar), John Ratcliffe (CIA director; consulted on the intelligence chapter), Paul Atkins (SEC chair), Pete Hoekstra (ambassador to Canada) and Elbridge Colby (Pentagon policy), among others. A CNN review found six cabinet secretaries had authored or contributed to the plan, and Trump revived the 'Schedule F' civil-service order it recommended on 20 January 2025.
cite: Axios, 26 November 2024; CNN review cited in Wikipedia 'Project 2025'; Executive order of 20 January 2025

n: Center for American Progress — alumni staff the Biden White House
rank: White House chief of staff, staff secretary, senior advisers, Veterans Affairs secretary
d: The Center for American Progress (CAP) is a Washington think tank founded by John Podesta in 2003 as a Democratic counterpart to the Heritage Foundation. Biden-administration officials with past CAP posts included chief of staff Ron Klain, economic advisers Brian Deese and Gene Sperling, Veterans Affairs Secretary Denis McDonough, Pentagon chief of staff Kelly Magsamen, Neera Tanden (CAP president 2011–21, then White House staff secretary and senior adviser) and John Podesta (senior clean-energy adviser). Business Insider counted nearly 70 CAP employees who had left for administration posts by mid-2021.
cite: Fox News, 15 September 2022, citing Business Insider (2021); Wikipedia 'Center for American Progress'

n: Federalist Society — 43 of Trump's 51 appeals-court nominees were members
rank: federal appeals-court judges and Supreme Court justices
d: The Federalist Society is a network of conservative and libertarian lawyers founded in 1982, with about 70,000 members. It helped assemble the list of 21 names Trump said he would choose from for the Supreme Court in 2016. The New York Times found that 43 of Trump's 51 appeals-court nominees by March 2020 were current or former members, and at least five sitting justices — Thomas, Alito, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett — are or were members.
cite: New York Times, 16 March 2020; Wikipedia 'Federalist Society'

n: Trump says the Federalist Society was his 'recommending source' on judges
rank: federal judges and Supreme Court justices
d: On 29 May 2025, a day after a trade court with a Trump-appointed judge ruled against his tariffs, President Trump wrote that 'it was suggested that I use The Federalist Society as a recommending source on Judges' and that he did so 'openly and freely'. He called its former leader Leonard Leo a 'sleazebag' who 'brags how he controls Judges, and even Justices of the United States Supreme Court', and blamed the society for 'bad advice' on nominations. The post is the President's own account of the society's role in choosing judges.
cite: Donald Trump, Truth Social posts, 29 May 2025 (American Presidency Project)

n: ALEC — 32 new model bills and a 2025 playbook for state lawmakers
d: The American Legislative Exchange Council (ALEC) brings state lawmakers and corporate members together to write 'model policies' that legislators then file in their own states. At its December 2024 States and Nation Policy Summit in Washington, legislators introduced 32 new model policies, and ALEC handed out an 'Essential Policy Solutions' playbook for 2025 covering taxes, energy plant closures, public-sector unions, school vouchers and bans on ranked-choice voting. More than 400 state lawmakers signed an ALEC letter backing a permanent extension of the 2017 federal tax cuts.
cite: ALEC 2024 Annual Report; Center for Media and Democracy analysis published by Truthout, February 2025

n: National Prayer Breakfast — Congress takes it from the Fellowship
rank: members of Congress who host the annual breakfast attended by the President
d: The Fellowship (also called the Family) is a private Christian network that organised the National Prayer Breakfast for Congress for decades through its Fellowship Foundation. After controversies over who was invited and how the event was paid for, and a boycott call signed by 30 groups, members of Congress moved the official event in 2023 to a new National Prayer Breakfast Foundation. Every president since Eisenhower has taken part; Trump spoke at the breakfast on 5 February 2026.
cite: Wikipedia 'National Prayer Breakfast'; Salon, 2 February 2023

n: India — six diplomats expelled over Nijjar killing and threats
rank: Indian High Commissioner and five other diplomats
d: Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar, a Canadian citizen, was shot dead outside a gurdwara in Surrey, British Columbia, on 18 June 2023. Prime Minister Trudeau told Parliament on 18 September 2023 of 'credible allegations' linking agents of India's government to the killing, and the RCMP charged Indian nationals with murder in May 2024. In October 2024 Canada expelled High Commissioner Sanjay Kumar Verma and five other diplomats; officials said Indian diplomats had pushed Canadians to gather information for India's RAW intelligence agency and that targets were then attacked by the Lawrence Bishnoi gang. India denied it and expelled six Canadians; the two countries restored ties in 2025.
cite: Government of Canada expulsions, October 2024; Trudeau statement to the House of Commons, 18 September 2023; Wikipedia 'Killing of Hardeep Singh Nijjar'
org_note: Government of India — High Commission and RAW

n: Bishnoi gang listed as a terrorist entity by Canada
rank: criminal group named by Canadian officials as used by Indian agents
d: On 29 September 2025 Canada listed the Bishnoi Gang, which it describes as a transnational criminal organisation 'operating primarily out of India', as a terrorist entity under the Criminal Code, letting authorities freeze its property and bring terrorism charges. It became the 87th listed entity. In October 2024 Canadian officials had said Indian diplomats passed information on targets in Canada that the gang then attacked.
cite: Public Safety Canada, news release, 29 September 2025

n: Hogue inquiry — India's proxies may fund Canadian politicians
d: The Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference, led by Justice Marie-Josée Hogue, reported on 28 January 2025 with 51 recommendations. It named India as the second most active state interfering in Canada and cited intelligence that proxy agents of India's government may have given, and may still give, illicit money to various Canadian politicians to get pro-India candidates elected. It found no evidence of 'traitors' in Parliament but noted 'some concerning conduct by parliamentarians'; India rejected the findings.
cite: Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference in Federal Electoral Processes and Democratic Institutions, Final Report, 28 January 2025 (CBC; Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada)
org_note: Government of India

n: Hogue inquiry — China the 'most active' interferer, via the United Front
d: The United Front Work Department is the Chinese Communist Party body that builds influence over overseas Chinese communities and foreign elites. Justice Hogue's final report of 28 January 2025 concluded that China is the 'most active perpetrator of state-based foreign interference' in Canada, working through proxies, diplomats and the United Front Work Department to 'control and influence' the diaspora. She found Canadian institutions had not been seriously affected and criticised the federal government's response as 'far from perfect'. China's embassy called the findings 'groundless accusations'.
cite: Public Inquiry into Foreign Interference, Final Report, 28 January 2025 (Asia Pacific Foundation of Canada, 30 January 2025)

n: Zhao Wei — Chinese consular officer expelled over plan to target MP Chong
rank: Member of Parliament Michael Chong and his relatives
d: A top-secret CSIS assessment, reported in the press and confirmed in substance by Foreign Minister Mélanie Joly, said Zhao Wei, a diplomat at China's consulate in Toronto, was involved with Beijing's intelligence service in targeting Conservative MP Michael Chong and his relatives in Hong Kong. Canada declared Zhao persona non grata on 8 May 2023. China called the report baseless and expelled a Canadian diplomat in return.
cite: Global Affairs Canada, persona non grata declaration, 8 May 2023 (Global News)

n: Chinese 'police stations' in Toronto and Montreal — RCMP probe closed
rank: overseas outposts attributed to Fuzhou city police
d: Safeguard Defenders listed three outposts in Toronto run for the Fuzhou Public Security Bureau. Canada sent a cease-and-desist warning in 2022 and summoned China's ambassador, and in March 2023 the RCMP announced investigations into two alleged stations in the Montreal area. In July 2024 Canada said it had mapped the stations and would share the information with the G7. In September 2025 the RCMP closed its investigation without recommending charges; two Montreal community groups that denied the claims threatened to sue the RCMP.
cite: RCMP statements, March 2023 and September 2025; Wikipedia 'Chinese police overseas service stations'

n: William Majcher — ex-RCMP officer acquitted of helping China
d: The RCMP arrested former officer William Majcher at Vancouver airport in 2023, alleging he used his police knowledge and contacts to get intelligence or services for China's government. At trial the case narrowed to one Security of Information Act count over a 2017 effort to pressure Vancouver resident Kevin Sun, whom China accused of fleeing with tens of millions of dollars, to return. On 13 May 2026 a B.C. judge acquitted him, calling the evidence 'entirely circumstantial'; federal prosecutors filed an appeal in June 2026.
cite: R. v. Majcher, Supreme Court of British Columbia, acquittal 13 May 2026; Crown notice of appeal June 2026 (Global News)

n: Marcelo Crivella — Universal Church bishop, Rio mayor arrested in office
rank: Mayor of Rio de Janeiro; earlier senator and federal minister of fisheries
d: The Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (IURD) is a Brazilian Pentecostal church founded in 1977 by Edir Macedo and now present in many countries. Crivella, an IURD bishop and Macedo's nephew, was a senator (2003–2016), Minister of Fishing and Aquaculture under Dilma Rousseff (2012–2014) and mayor of Rio (2017–2020). Police arrested him at home on 22 December 2020, nine days before his term ended, in an investigation into a kickback scheme in his administration, and he was suspended from office. He has sat in the federal Chamber of Deputies since February 2023.
cite: Rio de Janeiro state prosecutors and courts, arrest of 22 December 2020; Wikipedia 'Marcelo Crivella'

n: Marcos Pereira — Universal Church bishop as minister and party chief
rank: Minister of Industry, Foreign Trade and Services; president of the Republicanos party; vice-president of the Chamber of Deputies
d: Republicanos was founded in 2005 by pastors of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, and commentators describe it as a base from which the church's bishops run for office. Marcos Pereira, an IURD bishop, was Minister of Industry, Foreign Trade and Services under Michel Temer (2016–2018), has led the party since 2018 and has been a federal deputy and vice-president of the Chamber since 2019. The party holds about 40 of 513 Chamber seats and 4 of 81 Senate seats, and São Paulo governor Tarcísio de Freitas is a member.
cite: Wikipedia 'Republicanos' (party history and officeholders)

n: Frente Parlamentar Evangélica — 132 deputies and 14 senators sign on
d: The Frente Parlamentar Evangélica is a registered cross-party caucus in Brazil's Congress that votes as a bloc on issues its churches care about. Agência Pública counted 93 federal deputies tied to evangelical churches in the 2023–2027 Chamber, led by the Assemblies of God (25) and Baptists (15), with the Universal Church among the three largest groups. The front's vice-president, Cezinha de Madureira, said in February 2023 that it brought together 132 deputies and 14 senators; signatories need not be evangelical themselves.
cite: Agência Pública, 'As igrejas que dominam a nova ala evangélica na Câmara', February 2023

n: Kim Kataguiri — MBL leader linked to Atlas partner, now federal deputy
d: The Atlas Network is a US-based network that funds and trains free-market think tanks worldwide. In April 2015 Atlas described Kim Kataguiri, head of the Movimento Brasil Livre (MBL) that led street protests against President Dilma Rousseff, as working with its Brazilian partner Estudantes Pela Liberdade, and said 'many members' of the MBL had passed through its training programme. Kataguiri was elected to the federal Chamber of Deputies in 2018 and re-elected in 2022.
cite: Atlas Network, 'Students For Liberty Plays Strong Role in Free Brazil Movement', 1 April 2015

n: MIRA — Colombian party of the Church of God Ministry of Jesus Christ
d: The Church of God Ministry of Jesus Christ International is a Pentecostal church founded in Colombia with branches in many countries. The MIRA party (Independent Movement of Absolute Renovation), founded in 2000 by Carlos Alberto Baena and Alexandra Moreno Piraquive, lists the church as its religion. The party currently holds 3 Senate seats, 1 seat in the House and 47 local council seats.
cite: Wikipedia 'Independent Movement of Absolute Renovation'

n: Javier Milei — Atlas Network prize-winner as President of Argentina
d: Before entering politics Milei won the Liberty Prize of Fundación Atlas in 2018, sat on the advisory board of Fundación Libre and spoke at events of Atlas Network partners Fundación Libertad y Progreso and Federalismo y Libertad; his adviser Alberto Benegas Lynch is a Mont Pelerin Society director active in several Atlas groups (DeSmog, August 2023). Milei took office in December 2023. In August 2025 the Atlas Network credited its Argentine partners Libertad y Progreso, Fundación Libertad and the Asociación Argentina de Contribuyentes with helping push his deregulation, tax and labour reforms; these are the network's own claims.
cite: DeSmog, 22 August 2023; Atlas Network, 'Sharpening Milei's Chainsaw', 29 August 2025

n: Horacio Cartes — US cites ties to Hizballah, sanctions later lifted
rank: former President of Paraguay; serving Vice-President Hugo Velázquez
d: Hizballah is a Lebanese armed movement and party that the US designates as a terrorist organisation; it has long-standing finance networks in South America's Tri-Border Area. On 26 January 2023 the US Treasury sanctioned former president Horacio Cartes and sitting vice-president Hugo Velázquez for corruption, stating that both 'have ties to members of Hizballah', that Hizballah 'regularly held private events in Paraguay', and that representatives of both men collected bribes at those meetings. The US removed the sanctions on Cartes and several of his companies in 2025.
cite: US Treasury, press release JY1221, 26 January 2023 (E.O. 13818); OFAC delisting reported by WorldECR, October 2025

n: Cristina Fernández de Kirchner — ordered to trial over Iran pact
d: In 1994 the AMIA Jewish centre in Buenos Aires was bombed, killing 85 people; Argentine courts charged Iranian officials. In 2013 President Fernández de Kirchner's government signed a memorandum with Iran on questioning the suspects, which prosecutor Alberto Nisman denounced as a cover-up before his death in 2015. A trial court dismissed the case, saying the pact was not a crime, but the Federal Court of Cassation ordered a trial, and on 5 December 2024 the Supreme Court upheld that order, so she must stand trial for aggravated cover-up.
cite: Supreme Court of Argentina, ruling of 5 December 2024 (El Cronista)
org_note: Government of Iran (AMIA bombing suspects)

n: Rafael López Aliaga — Opus Dei member as mayor of Lima
d: Opus Dei is a Catholic organisation whose lay members seek holiness in ordinary work; it has long had members in Latin American governments. Rafael López Aliaga, leader of the Renovación Popular party, describes himself as an Opus Dei member who keeps celibacy. He was mayor of Lima from 1 January 2023 until he resigned on 13 October 2025 to run for president; he came third in the April 2026 first round with 11.91% and was elected to the national Senate, taking office in July 2026.
cite: Wikipedia 'Rafael López Aliaga' (Opus Dei membership and offices)

n: Eduardo Arana — Peru's prime minister and a Masonic lodge hire
rank: President of the Council of Ministers (prime minister); earlier Minister of Justice
d: In July 2025 the TV programme Cuarto Poder reported that Prime Minister Eduardo Arana reportedly holds the 33rd degree of the Scottish Rite of Freemasonry, and that while he was Justice Minister a lodge member, Elías Falla Villegas, was hired as a consultant in November 2023 at S/15,600 a month, while another reputed lodge member's foundation received an official certification at a July 2024 ceremony Arana attended. Arana said membership of a private association was no grounds to assume favours and that the hire met the job's requirements. No lodge was named.
cite: Canal N, 7 July 2025, citing Cuarto Poder (América TV)

n: José Antonio Kast — Schoenstatt-raised President of Chile
d: Schoenstatt is a Catholic lay movement founded in Germany in 1914 by priest Josef Kentenich and active in more than 100 countries, with nearly 80 of its shrines in Chile, Argentina and Brazil. BBC Mundo reported that Kast and several siblings were raised under Schoenstatt's guidelines; his brother Miguel Kast, Pinochet's planning minister and Central Bank president, was the only other member to hold high office in Chile. Kast won the 14 December 2025 runoff and took office on 11 March 2026.
cite: BBC Mundo, 18 December 2025 (republished by Acento)

n: Russian Interior Ministry training centre in Managua — US sanctions
d: Russia's Interior Ministry opened a police training centre in the Las Colinas district of Managua in October 2017, attended by Russia's ambassador and Laureano Ortega Murillo, the president's son; it was set up as an affiliate of the Russian ministry, with courses for Nicaraguan police and later for Central American and Caribbean officers. On 15 May 2024 the US Treasury sanctioned the centre, saying it trains Ortega-Murillo government officials under the Russian government's 'playbook of oppression' and is a key actor in repressing civil society.
cite: US Treasury sanctions, 15 May 2024 (La Prensa, Nicaragua); Confidencial, 25 October 2017
org_note: Russian Ministry of Internal Affairs

n: Chinese police 'service stations' listed in Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Ecuador
rank: overseas outposts attributed to Chinese county and city police bureaus
d: Safeguard Defenders' 2022 reports listed Chinese police outposts in Rio de Janeiro (Qingtian County police) and São Paulo (Fuzhou city police), and also in Buenos Aires, Viña del Mar in Chile, and Guayaquil and Quito in Ecuador. The group said Chinese police recorded 230,000 fraud suspects 'persuaded to return' between April 2021 and July 2022. A Yale legal scholar found factual errors in the first report, which the group then revised. No Latin American government has announced findings on these sites.
