cite: Safeguard Defenders, '110 Overseas' (September 2022) and 'Patrol and Persuade' (December 2022); Wikipedia 'Chinese police overseas service stations'

n: Sanae Takaichi — Nippon Kaigi Diet league member becomes PM
d: Nippon Kaigi (Japan Conference) is Japan's largest nationalist lobby group, founded in 1997, with about 38,000–40,000 members; it works on politicians through a cross-party league of Diet members. Sanae Takaichi has served in that league, as The Japan Times reported in 2021. She won the Liberal Democratic Party leadership in October 2025 and was elected prime minister by the Diet on 21 October 2025, at the head of an LDP–Japan Innovation Party coalition. She still holds the office.
cite: The Japan Times, 5 September 2021; Wikipedia summary of Nippon Kaigi and of Takaichi's election

n: Takaichi cabinet — 10 of 19 ministers in Nippon Kaigi's Diet league
d: On 23 October 2025 Japan Press Weekly, the English service of the Communist Party paper Akahata, listed the affiliations of the new Takaichi cabinet appointed on 21 October. It named 10 ministers as members of the Nippon Kaigi lawmakers' league: Hiraguchi Hiroshi, Motegi Toshimitsu, Katayama Satsuki, Matsumoto Yohei, Ueno Kenichiro, Kaneko Yasushi, Ishihara Hirotaka, Kihara Minoru, Akama Jiro and Kiuchi Minoru. In Abe's 2014 cabinet the count reported was 15 of 19. Takaichi reshuffled the cabinet in September 2026; the count for the reshuffled cabinet was not checked.
cite: Japan Press Weekly (Akahata), 23 October 2025

n: Takaichi cabinet — 12 ministers in the Shinto Political League
d: Shinto Seiji Renmei (Shinto Political League) is the political arm of the Association of Shinto Shrines and runs a league of Diet members who back its aims, such as constitutional revision and official honours for Yasukuni Shrine. Japan Press Weekly (Akahata) reported on 23 October 2025 that 12 ministers of the new Takaichi cabinet belonged to its Diet league, among them Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu, Finance Minister Katayama Satsuki and Chief Cabinet Secretary Kihara Minoru. Seven of them were also listed as Nippon Kaigi league members.
cite: Japan Press Weekly (Akahata), 23 October 2025

n: Takaichi cabinet — five ministers with Unification Church ties
d: The Unification Church (Family Federation for World Peace and Unification) is a Korean-founded church whose ties to LDP lawmakers came to light after Shinzo Abe's killing in 2022; Tokyo courts ordered its Japanese branch dissolved in 2025. Japan Press Weekly (Akahata) reported on 23 October 2025 that five ministers of the new Takaichi cabinet had ties to it. It listed Matsumoto Yohei (a party branch he headed paid dues to the church-linked Women's Federation for World Peace, revealed in 2019), Ueno Kenichiro (paid fees to affiliated bodies in 2018–19 and attended an affiliated lawmakers' meeting in 2021), Akazawa Ryosei and Ishihara Hirotaka (spoke at affiliated meetings) and Kiuchi Minoru (sent a congratulatory telegram to an affiliated company's event in 2018).
cite: Japan Press Weekly (Akahata), 23 October 2025

n: Komeito quits LDP coalition after 26 years
d: Komeito is the party founded in 1964 by the leader of the Buddhist lay movement Soka Gakkai, whose members supply its votes. It governed with the LDP from 1999 to 2009 and from 2012 to 2025. On 10 October 2025 Komeito leader Tetsuo Saito announced the party was leaving the coalition, citing disagreements with Sanae Takaichi's leadership and the LDP's handling of its slush-fund scandal. Takaichi then formed a coalition with the Japan Innovation Party, and Komeito is now in opposition.
cite: Komeito announcement, 10 October 2025 (NHK, CNBC); Wikipedia: Komeito

n: TM report — church backed 290 LDP lawmakers in 2021 election
d: In January 2026 South Korean media, citing Unification Church documents seized in Korean investigations, reported that Eiji Tokuno, then head of the church's Japan branch, told leader Han Hak-ja that the church backed 290 LDP members in the October 2021 lower-house election. The LDP's own 2022 survey had found 179–180 of its lawmakers with ties to the church. The same documents are reported to describe Abe as pleased with church support at a meeting before the 2019 upper-house election. Akahata separately reported that an August 2021 'TM Special Report' to Han said Takaichi becoming LDP president would be 'Heaven's greatest wish fulfilled'.
cite: Jiji Press, 2 January 2026, citing South Korean media; Akahata/Japan Press Weekly, January 2026

n: Chun Jae-soo — oceans minister quits over Unification Church money
d: Chun Jae-soo, a Democratic Party lawmaker serving as President Lee Jae-myung's oceans minister, resigned on 11 December 2025. Yun Young-ho, former head of the Unification Church's world headquarters, told the special counsel investigating ex-first lady Kim Keon-hee that the church gave Chun 30 million won in cash and two luxury watches in 2018–2020 to seek his help with a Korea–Japan undersea tunnel project. The special counsel passed the matter to police, who booked Chun as a bribery suspect and barred him from travel. Chun denies the allegations.
cite: Reuters/The Star, 11 December 2025; Korea JoongAng Daily, 15 December 2025

n: Hu Peng-nien — retired Executive Yuan official jailed for united front
d: China's united front system works to win over or recruit people abroad, including in Taiwan, for the Communist Party. In September 2026 Taiwan's High Court sentenced businessman Cheng Ming-chia to 10 years and six months for building a network for Communist Party united front officials, arranging meetings in China from 2021 to 2025. It sentenced Hu Peng-nien, a retired official of the Executive Yuan (Taiwan's cabinet), to five years. Prosecutors said Hu tried to recruit military personnel and others for information on the military and on government and legislative work, and carried a Chinese-supplied communications device into Taiwan. Both rulings can be appealed.
cite: Taiwan High Court ruling (Taipei Times, 11 September 2026)

n: Solomon Islands — MPs say both Beijing and Taipei offered money, 2019
d: In September 2019 Prime Minister Manasseh Sogavare ended 36 years of diplomatic ties with Taiwan and recognised the People's Republic of China. The Guardian and the Solomon Star reported that MPs said both Beijing and Taipei had offered them hundreds of thousands of dollars to sway the vote. Riots over the switch followed, and anger over it was a factor in the violent unrest in Honiara in November 2021.
cite: The Guardian and Solomon Star reporting, 2019; Wikipedia: China–Solomon Islands relations

n: Solomon Islands — China-funded PM's fund paid 39 of 50 MPs
d: China agreed in 2019 to fund a discretionary fund run by the Solomon Islands prime minister's office, as Taiwan had done before. At a livestreamed parliamentary budget committee hearing in August 2022, the prime minister's secretary Jimmy Rodgers said China had provided SBD20.9 million (about US$2.49 million) spent in 2021, and that 39 of the 50 MPs received payments in two tranches, on 22 November and 13 December 2021. Sogavare survived a no-confidence vote in December 2021; opposition leader Matthew Wale accused him of using the money to stay in power, which Sogavare's office denied.
cite: Parliamentary budget committee hearing, August 2022 (Reuters via VOA, 25 August 2022)

n: Chinese police inside Solomon Islands policing
d: China sent its first police advisory team to the Solomon Islands in February 2022, after the November 2021 riots, and signed a security agreement in 2022 that lets Honiara ask for Chinese police and military personnel. In 2025 Chinese Ministry of Public Security police in the country began a local pilot of the 'Fengqiao' model of community surveillance policing; it was suspended after local objections. In May 2026 Matthew Wale, a critic of the China relationship, became prime minister and promised to review the security agreement.
cite: East Asia Forum, 7 March 2024; Wikipedia: China–Solomon Islands relations

n: Kiribati — Chinese uniformed police working with local force
d: Kiribati switched diplomatic recognition from Taiwan to China in 2019 and asked China for policing help in 2022. Kiribati's acting police commissioner Eeri Aritiera confirmed to Reuters in 2024 that up to a dozen uniformed Chinese police officers work alongside local police on six-month rotations, doing community policing, martial-arts training and IT support for a crime database.
cite: Kiribati Police Service statement to Reuters (NBC News, 2024)

n: Vanuatu — China's public security minister offers policing pact
d: China has sent police advisers to Vanuatu since 2023. On 19 September 2025 Vanuatu's internal affairs minister Andrew Solomon Napuat met China's Minister of Public Security Wang Xiaohong in Beijing; China donated police equipment worth about NZ$720,000, including motorcycles and drones, and the two sides said they were discussing a wider policing partnership.
cite: Pacific Media Network, 23 September 2025; East Asia Forum, 7 March 2024

n: Fiji — Chinese officers removed from police, 2011 pact kept
d: Under a 2011 police cooperation agreement signed during military rule, China's Ministry of Public Security attached two officers at a time to the Fiji Police Force from 2013 and posted a police liaison officer to its embassy in 2021. In 2017 Chinese police working with local officials arrested 77 Chinese nationals in Fiji and flew them to China. In March 2024 Home Affairs Minister Pio Tikoduadua said Fiji had asked China to withdraw its embedded officers but would keep the agreement, reviewing it every six months, and Fijian officers continue to train in China.
cite: Fiji Home Affairs Minister, ABC interview (BenarNews/RFA, 20 March 2024); East Asia Forum, 7 March 2024

n: Jian Yang and Raymond Huo — two MPs leave over China concerns
d: Jian Yang, a National Party MP from 2011 to 2020, had been a Communist Party member and taught at People's Liberation Army institutions that trained intelligence linguists before moving to New Zealand. Several outlets reported in 2021 that his retirement at the 2020 election came after intelligence agencies raised concerns about his relationship with the Chinese government. The same reports said Prime Minister Jacinda Ardern and opposition leader Todd Muller agreed that Labour MP Raymond Huo would also leave Parliament for the same reason.
cite: New Zealand media reports, 2017 and 2021; Wikipedia: Jian Yang

n: Huang Jing — Singapore expels LKY School professor as foreign agent
rank: foreign-policy academic (target: Singapore foreign policy and opinion)
d: On 4 August 2017 Singapore's Ministry of Home Affairs cancelled the permanent residence of Huang Jing, a US-citizen professor at the National University of Singapore's Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, and of his wife, and banned both from re-entering. The ministry called him 'an agent of influence of a foreign country' who worked with that country's intelligence agents to influence Singapore's foreign policy and public opinion. It did not name the country. Huang denied the charge.
cite: Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs statement, 4 August 2017
org_note: prc_state is used because the case is widely read as China, but Singapore's ministry did not name the country

n: Philip Chan — Singapore's first 'politically significant person'
d: Singapore's Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Act of 2021 lets the Home Affairs Ministry designate people at risk of being used by foreign actors, who must then disclose donations and foreign links. On 26 February 2024 the ministry designated Hong Kong-born businessman Philip Chan Man Ping, the first person listed. He was president of the Hong Kong Chamber of Commerce in Singapore and the Kowloon Club, a patron of two government-linked grassroots bodies, and had attended China's Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference, a united front body, as an overseas delegate. The ministry said he had shown he was susceptible to being cultivated by foreign actors.
cite: Singapore Ministry of Home Affairs designation, 26 February 2024

n: Alice Guo — Bamban mayor jailed for life over POGO trafficking
d: POGOs were Chinese-run online gambling firms licensed in the Philippines from 2016 that served players in China; Senate hearings in 2024 tied many to fraud, trafficking and torture. Alice Guo, elected mayor of Bamban, Tarlac in 2022, was linked by senators to the Zun Yuan Technology POGO hub raided in her town; the Ombudsman removed her from office on 13 August 2024 and barred her from public office. In June 2025 a Manila court voided her election, ruling she is a Chinese citizen, Guo Hua Ping, born in Fujian. On 20 November 2025 she was convicted of qualified human trafficking and sentenced to life in prison. A self-confessed Chinese spy, She Zhijiang, told Al Jazeera she was also a Chinese intelligence asset; she denies it and that claim is untested in court.
cite: Ombudsman decision, 13 August 2024; Manila RTC Branch 34, June 2025; trafficking verdict, 20 November 2025

n: Harry Roque — ex-presidential spokesman charged over POGO hub
d: Harry Roque was spokesman for President Rodrigo Duterte, under whom POGOs were legalised and expanded. In May 2025 the Angeles City Regional Trial Court, Branch 118, issued arrest warrants for Roque, businesswoman Cassandra Ong and 48 others on 11 counts of qualified human trafficking over Lucky South 99, a POGO hub in Porac, Pampanga, raided in June 2024. Prosecutors say Roque helped it seek a licence and was named as head of its legal department in a reapplication that the gaming regulator PAGCOR denied. Roque denies being its lawyer and has sought asylum in the Netherlands.
cite: Angeles City RTC Branch 118 arrest warrants (GMA News, 15 May 2025)

n: Philippines bans POGOs after Senate inquiry
d: The state gaming regulator PAGCOR licensed offshore gaming operators from 2016, and President Duterte declined China's 2019 request to shut them. After 2024 Senate hearings led by Risa Hontiveros and Sherwin Gatchalian, President Marcos announced a total ban in July 2024 and signed Executive Order 74 in November 2024 requiring all operations to stop by 31 December 2024. Congress made the ban law in the Anti-POGO Act, signed in October 2025.
cite: Philippine Senate hearings 2024; Executive Order No. 74 (2024); Anti-POGO Act (2025)

n: Chen Zhi — Prince Group head, adviser to Hun Sen, indicted in US
rank: adviser to Hun Sen and other leaders
d: Chen Zhi, born in Fujian, took Cambodian citizenship in 2014 and built the Prince Group, one of Cambodia's largest conglomerates. He held the honorary title Neak Oknha and served as an adviser to Hun Sen, interior minister Sar Kheng and National Assembly president Heng Samrin. On 14 October 2025 the US Justice Department indicted him for fraud and money laundering, calling him the head of a cyber-fraud empire run from scam compounds, seizing about 127,271 bitcoin (about US$14 billion), while the US and UK sanctioned 146 people and firms linked to the group. In January 2026 Cambodia said it had arrested him, revoked his citizenship and sent him to China to face charges.
cite: US Department of Justice indictment and OFAC/UK sanctions, 14 October 2025; Cambodian government statement, January 2026

n: Huione — firm co-run by PM Hun Manet's cousin named a laundering hub
rank: prime minister's cousin, director of Huione Pay
d: Huione Group is a Phnom Penh financial conglomerate whose payment arm Huione Pay has Hun To, a cousin of Prime Minister Hun Manet, as a major shareholder and director. In March 2025 the National Bank of Cambodia revoked Huione Pay's banking licence. In May 2025 the US Treasury's FinCEN found Huione Group to be a financial institution of primary money laundering concern, saying it laundered over US$4 billion in illicit funds between August 2021 and January 2025, including money from North Korean hackers and scam operations.
cite: FinCEN finding, 1 May 2025; National Bank of Cambodia, March 2025

n: RSS roots — 38 of 53 BJP ministers in Modi's second government
d: The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) is a Hindu nationalist volunteer organisation founded in 1925; the governing Bharatiya Janata Party grew out of its political wing. ThePrint counted in January 2020 that 38 of the 53 BJP ministers in Narendra Modi's second government (71%) had RSS roots, up from 41 of 66 (62%) in 2014. All eight members it listed on the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs, including Rajnath Singh, Amit Shah and Nitin Gadkari, had RSS links; Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar did not. It also counted 146 of 303 BJP Lok Sabha members with RSS links.
cite: ThePrint, 27 January 2020

n: C. P. Radhakrishnan — RSS member since 16, now Vice President
d: C. P. Radhakrishnan has been associated with the RSS and its earlier political wing, the Bharatiya Jana Sangh, since the age of 16, and later served as a BJP MP for Coimbatore and as governor of several states. He was elected the 15th Vice President of India and took office on 12 September 2025. The vice president also chairs the upper house of Parliament, the Rajya Sabha.
cite: Wikipedia: C. P. Radhakrishnan (citing Indian press)

n: Canada expels six Indian diplomats over use of Bishnoi gang
d: Sikh separatist Hardeep Singh Nijjar was shot dead in Surrey, British Columbia on 18 June 2023. In October 2024 the RCMP said 'agents of the Government of India' had used criminal groups, including the gang of Lawrence Bishnoi, who is held in an Indian prison, to target pro-Khalistan Sikhs in Canada, and Canada expelled six Indian diplomats including High Commissioner Sanjay Kumar Verma. India denies involvement and expelled Canadian diplomats in return. Canada listed the Bishnoi gang as a terrorist entity in September 2025, and in July 2026 US prosecutors charged Bishnoi with directing Nijjar's killing; that indictment does not allege an Indian government role.
cite: RCMP statement and Global Affairs Canada expulsions, October 2024; Canada terrorist-entity listing, September 2025

n: Pannun plot — Nikhil Gupta pleads guilty; RAW officer charged
d: US prosecutors charged that Vikash Yadav, an employee of India's Cabinet Secretariat, which houses the foreign intelligence agency RAW, directed a plot to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a US citizen and lawyer for the pro-Khalistan group Sikhs for Justice, in New York in 2023. His go-between, Nikhil Gupta, agreed to pay $100,000 to a hitman who was really an undercover officer, with a $15,000 cash advance on 9 June 2023. Gupta was extradited from the Czech Republic in June 2024 and on 13 February 2026 pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court to murder-for-hire, conspiracy and money-laundering conspiracy. Yadav was charged in a superseding indictment unsealed in 2024 and has not been brought to the US.
cite: US District Court, Southern District of New York: Gupta guilty plea, 13 February 2026
org_note: The Indian state's intelligence service is the actor; the brief allows state cases where named in the task

n: Gnanasara — BBS leader named to head 'One Country, One Law' task force
d: Bodu Bala Sena (BBS, 'Buddhist Power Force') is a Sinhala Buddhist nationalist monks' group founded in 2012, accused of stirring anti-Muslim violence. On 26 October 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa appointed its general secretary, Galagoda Aththe Gnanasara, to chair a presidential task force on 'One Country, One Law' to draft proposals on a single legal code. Justice Minister Ali Sabry said he had not been consulted, and the Bar Association said the task force would take over the work of Parliament and the Justice Ministry.
cite: Presidential gazette, 26 October 2021 (Daily FT)

n: Gnanasara — presidential pardon voided, BBS leader back in prison
d: In 2018 the Court of Appeal jailed BBS leader Gnanasara for six years for contempt of court during the case over the disappearance of journalist Prageeth Eknaligoda; President Maithripala Sirisena pardoned him in May 2019. He was jailed again for four years in March 2024 over statements about Islam, and for nine months in January 2025 for inciting religious hatred. On 10 September 2026 the Supreme Court declared the 2019 pardon arbitrary and invalid, and on 5 October 2026 the Court of Appeal ordered him to serve the rest of the contempt sentence.
cite: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, 10 September 2026; Court of Appeal order, 5 October 2026

n: Gotabaya Rajapaksa — defence secretary opens BBS training centre
d: On 9 March 2013 Defence Secretary Gotabaya Rajapaksa, brother of President Mahinda Rajapaksa, opened Meth Sevana, the Bodu Bala Sena's cultural and training centre in Galle District, as chief guest. In January 2013 President Rajapaksa and ministers met BBS leaders at the official residence, Temple Trees. Gotabaya Rajapaksa later served as president from 2019 to 2022.
cite: Colombo Telegraph, 14 March 2013; Wikipedia: Bodu Bala Sena

n: Ma Ba Tha drafts become Myanmar's race and religion laws
d: Ma Ba Tha (Association for the Protection of Race and Religion) is a Buddhist nationalist monks' group formed in 2014. In 2013–14 Myanmar's Ministry of Religious Affairs drafted four Race and Religion Protection Laws, covering religious conversion, marriage between Buddhist women and non-Buddhist men, monogamy and birth spacing, based on texts proposed by its members. Parliament passed them in 2015, the first being signed in May 2015.
cite: Human Rights Watch, 29 May 2014; Wikipedia: Ma Ba Tha

n: Myanmar army spokesman donates to banned Ma Ba Tha successor
d: Myanmar's state Buddhist clergy council ordered Ma Ba Tha disbanded in May 2017, and officials said its renamed successor was also outlawed. In June 2019, after members protested the civilian government's sedition case against the monk Wirathu, army spokesman Brigadier General Zaw Min Tun donated 30 million kyats to the successor group, the Buddha Dhamma Parahita Foundation. Zaw Min Tun is now the spokesman of the military government that took power in 2021.
cite: Wikipedia: Ma Ba Tha (citing Myanmar press)

n: Wirathu — junta drops sedition case and gives him top honour
d: Wirathu is a monk of the 969 movement and a leading figure of Ma Ba Tha, known for anti-Muslim sermons. In September 2021, seven months after the coup, the military government dropped the sedition charges against him and released him. In November 2022 he was awarded the title Thiri Pyanchi, one of the country's highest honours.
cite: Military government announcements, 2021–22; Wikipedia: Wirathu

n: Vietnam designates exile party Viet Tan a terrorist group
d: Viet Tan is a pro-democracy party founded by Vietnamese exiles in 1982 and based in the United States. On 4 October 2016 Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security designated it a terrorist organisation, saying it trained people to enter Vietnam and plotted sabotage. Human rights groups and foreign governments dispute the designation; the US government has said there is no evidence it is a terrorist group. Vietnamese courts have jailed people accused of membership.
cite: Vietnam Ministry of Public Security, 4 October 2016
